units.la: CRystalli historiam tractaturus, præsertim Phænomena mirandi hujus lapidis Physico examini subjecturus, Methodo consueta incipio ab Onomatologia, ubi statim denominatio ejus, omnibus ferè Europæ Gentibus communis notari meretur. Dicitur Latinis Crystallus, Crystallum, Chrystallus, Chrystallum, Cristallus, Cristallum. Germ. Crystall/Chrystall/Cristall. Gall. & Hisp. Cristall. Ital. Cristallo, Angl. & Belg. Crystall. Omnes videntur nominis originationem traxisse à Græcis, qui κρύσταλλον appellant, quasi κρυοσταλλον, à κρύος, frigus, alii à κρυμνὸς, & κρυμὸς, frigus, algor, glacies, & στέλλομαι, pro συστέλλομαι, quia est ὑπὸ κρύος συστελλόμενον ὕδωρ. Hesychius ait; κρύσταλλος, τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ ὑπὸ κρύος. Inde & vox Latinorum Crusta orta est. Κρύσταλλος ὕδατος Epiphanio dicitur aqua glaciata, ad differentiam κρύσταλλος λίθος. Ἄψακτον ὕδωρ apud eundem pro eodem sumitur, de Onychitis, quos ex aqua frigore concreta formari scribit. Τινὲς δὲ φασὶν αὐτὰς ἐξ ὕδατος ἀψάκτα πεπῆχθαι. Sic Sophocli apud Stobæum κρύσταλλος ἀψυχῆς [?]. Salmas: Exercit: in Solin: p.144. Alpium incolis Straalen/Straalstein/i.e. fulminis lapis dicitur: Vel quoniam vulgus sibi persuadet, Crystallos esse ἀεροπληΐς [?], à Cœlo descendisse, seu fulmine detrusos fuisse, sicut & duæ Crystalli majores hexagonæ Vitoduri in Bibliotheca pro Ceraunii, seu lapidibus fulminis ostenduntur, quæ in agro ab Urbe haud procul distante repertæ fuerint; cùm tamen de Ceraunorum existentia haud abs re dubitent modernorum multi. Vel potius, quia Crystallus radiat, à sole illustrata radios emittit, Weilen der Crystall straalet/Straalen von sich wirffet.
units.tr: Since I am about to treat the history of crystal, and especially to subject the phenomena of this wonderful stone to physical examination, I begin, by the usual method, with its nomenclature. Here its name, which is almost common to all the peoples of Europe, deserves notice. Among the Latins it is called Crystallus, Crystallum, Chrystallus, Chrystallum, Cristallus, Cristallum. In German, Crystall, Chrystall, Cristall. In French and Spanish, Cristall. In Italian, Cristallo. In English and Dutch, Crystall. All seem to have derived the origin of the name from the Greeks, who call it κρύσταλλον [krystallon], as if it were κρυοσταλλον [kryostallon], from κρύος [kryos], cold; others from κρυμνὸς [krymnos] and κρυμὸς [krymos], cold, frost, ice, and στέλλομαι [stellomai], for συστέλλομαι [systellomai], because water is contracted [συστελλόμενον] by the cold. Hesychius says: κρύσταλλος [krystallos] is water congealed by cold [τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ ὑπὸ κρύος]. From this also the Latin word crusta (crust) arose. Epiphanius calls κρύσταλλος ὕδατος [krystallos hydatos] aqua glaciata (glaciated water), to distinguish it from κρύσταλλος λίθος [krystallos lithos], the crystal stone. The same author uses ἄψακτον ὕδωρ [apsakton hydor] for the same thing, speaking of onychites, which he writes are formed from water concreted by cold. Some say that they are formed from water [τινὲς δὲ φασὶν αὐτὰς ἐξ ὕδατος ἀψάκτα πεπῆχθαι]. So in Sophocles, as cited by Stobaeus, κρύσταλλος ἀψυχῆς [krystallos apsychēs] (the text is uncertain). See Salmasius, Exercit. in Solin. p. 144. Among the inhabitants of the Alps it is called Straalen/Straalstein, that is, fulminis lapis, the lightning stone. Or because the common people are convinced that crystals are ἀεροπληΐς [aeroplēis] (thrown down by the air), having fallen from heaven or been hurled down by lightning, just as two large hexagonal crystals are shown in the library at Vitoduri as Ceraunia, that is, thunderstones, said to have been found in a field not far from the town; although many moderns reasonably doubt the existence of ceraunia. Or rather, because crystal shines, and when illumined by the sun it emits rays, Weilen der Crystall straalet/Straalen von sich wirffet, as the Dutch and German say: the crystal shines and throws out rays.

units.la: Cùm variæ reperiantur Species, variis etiam nominibus distinguuntur. Purissimas & pretiosissimas ἀκεντήτους [?], Acentetas appellabant, quia caelabantur tantum vitiosae, Apuleius Impunctam vocat. Pellucidae & diaphanae dicuntur Montanae, quia ut plurimum in montibus reperiuntur; Vulgò Crystalli montanae, Berg-Crystallen audiunt, quae e metallifodinis eruuntur, & à metallifodinis aliàs Fluores, Flüsse appellantur. Ubi ἐν πυρὶ monendum, plerumque à Scriptoribus confundi Fluores cum Crystallis. Quae fronti applicatae varios colores reddunt; Irides nuncupantur; Cùm tamen probè attendenti in omnibus Phaenomenon istud reperiatur. Obscuras, tenebrosas, Minium Crystalli, Excell: Archiater & Profess: D. D. Muralt: In Epist: ad Dn. Haak de monte Gletscher inserta Act: Philosoph: Angl: A. 1669. p. 251 nuncupat. Cardano de Subt. L. VII. p. 363; Praniunt elt Crystallus nigra & perspicua. Crystallos, quae vulgaribus duriores, Pseudo-Adamantes vocant, quae ipsae tamen veris Adamantibus adhuc molliores sunt, tales hinc inde colliguntur, ut Cornubiae in Anglia, in nostra Helvetia. Ipse in monte Groß Allbrig dicto, prope Lachsen[?] minores ἀμφίχρως[?] ob splendorem ac duritiem nobile hoc Epitheton promerentes juxta alios reperi. Crystallo multis angulis instructae Plin: L. XXXVII. C. X. Pangonii nomen imponit. Agricola de Ortu & Caus: subterran: L. IV. interpretatur de Crystallis Dodecagonis, cùm tamen vi vocis omniangula potius, quàm dodecagona interpretanda sit.
units.tr: Since various species are found, they are also distinguished by various names. The purest and most precious were called ἀκεντήτους [akentētous], Acentetae, because only faulty ones were engraved; Apuleius calls them Impunctam, unpierced. The clear and transparent are called Montanae, mountain crystals, because they are for the most part found in mountains; commonly they are called Berg-Crystallen, and those dug out of metal mines, which are otherwise called Fluores, Flüsse, are called so. Here it must be noted that in the phrase ἐν πυρὶ [en pyri], writers generally confuse fluors with crystals. Those which, when applied to the forehead, show various colours are called Irides, rainbows; yet this phenomenon is found in all of them, if one attends carefully. The dark, shadowy ones, Minium Crystalli, are named by the excellent physician and professor, Dr. Muralt, in his letter to Mr. Haak on the Glacier mountain, inserted in the Acta Philosophica Angliae, year 1669, p. 251. Cardan, De Subtilitate L. VII, p. 363, calls black and transparent crystal Praniunt. Crystals which are harder than ordinary ones, the Pseudo-Adamantes (false diamonds) they call, though these are still softer than true diamonds, are gathered here and there, as in Cornwall in England, and in our Helvetia. I myself found smaller ones, deserving this noble epithet on account of their lustre and hardness, on the mountain called Groß Allbrig, near Lachsen, as others also did. Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter X, gives the name Pangonius to crystal with many angles. Agricola, De Ortu et Causis Subterraneorum L. IV, interprets it as referring to dodecagonal crystals; yet by the force of the word it ought rather to be understood as many-angled than as twelve-angled.

units.la: Crystalli vox ambigua est, variéque usurpatur. Vel pro ipsa Glacie, haud dubiè ex communi falsa opinione, quòd à glacie generetur, ut apud Hippoc: S.V. Aph. 24. & Epiphanium, qui κρύσταλλον ὕδατι, aquam glaciatam, ad distinctionem κρυσταλλος λίθος vocat. Vel pro Vitro, vel pro corpore κρυσταλλοφανής, vitro haud absimili, ut Hesychius, κρυσταλλῶ [illegible, ~5 letters]. Glaciem quoque hodie de Vitro dicimus. Unde etiam Martialis.
units.tr: The word crystal is ambiguous and is used in various ways. Sometimes it means ice itself, undoubtedly from the common false opinion that it is generated from ice, as in Hippocrates, Aphorisms sect. V, aph. 24, and in Epiphanius, who calls κρύσταλλον ὕδατι [krystallon hydati], glaciated water, to distinguish it from κρυσταλλος λίθος [krystallos lithos]. Sometimes it means glass, or a body κρυσταλλοφανής [krystallophanēs], looking like crystal, not unlike glass, as in Hesychius, κρυσταλλῶ [krystallō] [illegible, about five letters]. Today we also speak of glass as ice. Hence also Martial:

units.la: Quum Tibi Niliacus portet Crystalla cataplus / Sunt mihi de circo pocula Flaminio.
units.tr: Since the Nilotic cup-bearer brings you crystal goblets, I have cups from the Flaminian circus.

units.la: Vel pro omnibus gemmis perspicuis & mollioribus, quae nullum colorem manifestum in se habent, ut Worm: Mus: p. 100. & Ansb: Boët: de Boot de Lap: & Gemm: L. II. C. 73. p. 221. Vel pro omnibus lapidibus perspicuis, gerentibus faciem Crystallinam, πάντων λίθων διαφανής, ut Diodorus; vel pro Selenite, seu Crystallo Islandica, ut Erasm: Bartholin. Hugenius &c. de qua fusius infra; vel pro Crystallo artificiali, quae Chymicis est lapillus fragilis per coagulationem & evaporationem factus, ut Crystalli Tartari, Nitri, Vitrioli, Veneris &c. omniumque Vegetabilium (quarum productio Chymicis Crystallisatio peculiari nomine insignitur.) Vel Pathologicè, pro pustulis per universum corpus dispersis, lupini magnitudine, albis, ac instar Crystalli diaphanis, quas cum Philyctaenis coincidere existimat
units.tr: Sometimes it means all transparent and softer gems, which have no manifest colour in themselves, as in Worm, Museum, p. 100, and Boetius de Boot, De Lapidibus et Gemmis L. II, c. 73, p. 221. Sometimes it means all transparent stones having the appearance of crystal, πάντων λίθων διαφανής [pantōn lithōn diaphanēs], as in Diodorus; sometimes it means selenite, or Icelandic crystal, as Erasmus Bartholinus, Huygens and others, of which more fully below; sometimes it means artificial crystal, which for chemists is a brittle little stone made by coagulation and evaporation, such as the crystals of tartar, nitre, vitriol, Venus, etc., and of all vegetables (whose production chemists mark by the special name crystallisation). Pathologically, it means pustules scattered over the whole body, the size of a lupine bean, white, and transparent like crystal, which he thinks coincide with philyctaenae.

units.la: CRystallus inter lapides pretiosos, quia ab aliis non nisi duritie differt, refertur à Kunkel: de Art: Vitr: P.II,p.120. In lapidum pretiosorum ignobiliorum numero ponit Alsted: Encyclopaed: L.XIII. Phys: P.IV.C.5. inter lapides mediæ naturæ, qui vulgaribus sint præstantiores, pretiosis vero ignobiliores Strauß: Isag: Phys: p.m.208. inter lapides pretiosos majores primo loco ponit Celeb: Basileensium D. & Prof. Emanuel König. Reg: Mineral: S.II.C.VI. p.102. tum quia corpus, & communem gemmarum omnium materiam præbet, tum quia notissimus est, tum & Adamanti, qui primò locatur inter gemmas minores, colore & figura affinis, nisi quòd præterquam alii lapides pretiosi, pellucidi, mollior, minúsque strictæ compagis. Qui lapides dividunt in figuratos & non figuratos, illi Crystallum ob regularem figuram ad prius genus referre possent, & eam quidem speciem, quæ non linearum ductus duntaxat & incisuras ostendit, ut Dendrites,&c. sed integro suo corpore peculiarem figuram repræsentat, uti quoque sunt Cornua Ammonis,Conchites,&c.
units.tr: Crystal is counted among the precious stones because it differs from the others only in hardness; it is so classed by Kunkel: de Art: Vitr: P.II,p.120. Alsted: Encyclopaed: L.XIII. Phys: P.IV.C.5. places it among the less precious stones. Strauß: Isag: Phys: p.m.208. places it among the stones of middle nature, which are superior to common stones but inferior to precious ones. The celebrated Basel physician and professor Emanuel König, Reg: Mineral: S.II.C.VI. p.102. places it first among the greater precious stones, both because it supplies the body and common matter of all gems and because it is very well known. Also, diamond, which is placed first among the lesser gems, is related to it in colour and shape, except that, unlike the other precious stones, crystal is transparent, softer, and of a less tightly bound structure. Those who divide stones into figured and unfigured could refer crystal to the first class because of its regular figure, namely the kind of figure that shows not merely lines, grooves and notches, as with dendrites, etc., but that represents a distinct shape in its whole body, as do ammonites, conchites, etc.

units.la: CAPUT III. Tradens. Phænomena in Crystallo occurrentia.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. Setting forth the phenomena occurring in crystal.

units.la: I. CRystalli locus varius est; Ordinariè & plerumque reperitur in montibus & Cavernis Saxorum, quæ Crystallino hoc hospite ita superbiunt, ut oculi spectatorum vix satiari possint; inveniuntur porrò in aliis aliorum lapidum ac minerarum cavitatibus, ut, Teste Worm: Mus: p.88. in conchæ striatæ genere Crystalli pellucidi, acuti & dentati trianguli, in Pyritis octoëdris, dodecaëdris, referente τω πάνυ Gesnero nostro in aureo de Fig: Lap: Tractatu p.25. Coeunt aliquando ad radicem in unum lapidem, multos autem mucrones de se spargunt, qualem habet Andr: Coesalpin: de Metall: L.II.C.19.p.99. Ex Indiis Orientalibus Illustri naturæ scrutatori Roberto Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virt: p.15, Allati pro raritate lapides; adeò duri, ut scintillas ederent, in quibus cavitas refert minutissimis politis lapidibus Crystallinis, quorum apices introrsum vergebant. Reperiuntur etiam in globis cavis, qui à Joh: Eusēb: Nieremberg: L.16. C. 1. Coccus mineralis vocantur. Ferrant: Imperat: Hist: Natur: L.24. C.19. Ventres Crystallini. Fort: Licet: In Litheosph: C.§2.p.265. Ovorum Solis nomine prædicat. Crescunt & in cavitatibus cornuum Ammonis, & speciatim etiam in iis, quæ in montibus Helvetiæ nostræ, Legerio & Rhandio colliguntur. Interdum Aratro eruuntur, à torrentibus deportantur, quandoque etiam in Vineis, agris, hortis, &c. reperiuntur.
units.tr: I. The place where crystal is found varies. It is usually and most commonly found in the mountains and in the caverns of rocks, which this crystalline guest so adorns that the eyes of onlookers can scarcely be satisfied. It is also found in other cavities of other stones and minerals: according to Worm (Mus. p. 88) in a striated shell-like kind, in clear, pointed, and toothed triangles; in octahedral and dodecahedral pyrites. Our most eminent Gesner [τῷ πάνυ], in his golden treatise on the figures of stones (p. 25), reports the same. Sometimes they grow together at the root into one stone but send out many points from themselves, as Andreas Caesalpinus has described (De Metallicis, L. II, c. 19, p. 99). From the East Indies, lumps of stone were brought to the illustrious investigator of nature Robert Boyle (De Gemmarum Origine et Virtute, p. 15), so hard that they gave off sparks; in them a cavity contained very small polished crystalline stones whose points faced inward. They are also found in hollow globes, which Johann Eusebius Nieremberg (L. 16, c. 1) calls "mineral berries" [Coccus mineralis]. Ferrante Imperato (Hist. Nat. L. 24, c. 19) calls them "crystalline bellies," and Fortunio Liceti (In Lithosphorum, c. 2, §2, p. 265) proclaims them under the name of "eggs of the sun." They also grow in the cavities of ammonites, and especially in those gathered in the mountains of our Helvetia by Leger and Rhand. Sometimes they are dug up by the plough, carried down by torrents, and sometimes found in vineyards, fields, gardens, and so on.

units.la: II. Crystallus plerúmque prædita est figurâ sexangulari in mucronem turbinata; Dantur & majores & minores sexangulares utrinque acutæ, quas Georg: Hieron: Velsch: Hecatost: I. Obs: 4c. p.54. Ἀμφήκης appellat; Jam à Geßnero Lib: C. p.18. & in Museo Septaliano C.IX.p.50.§.45. descriptæ. Quales & in monte Groß Ulbrig dicto reperias.
units.tr: II. Crystal is usually hexagonal, tapering into a point. There are also larger and smaller hexagonal crystals pointed at both ends, which Georg Hieronymus Welsch (Hecatost. I, Obs. 4, c. p. 54) calls "two-pointed" [Ἀμφήκης]. They have already been described by Gesner (Lib. de Crystallo, p. 18) and in the Museum Septalianum (c. 9, p. 50, §45). You may find such crystals on the mountain called Groß Ulbrig.

units.la: Ad meliorem Crystalli figuræ demonstrationem haud abs re erit, si demonstrationem terminorum, quam subtilissimus Nicol: Steno Differt: Prod: de Solido intra Solidum. p. 57. generaliter tantùm indigitavit, distinctiùs paulò in Fig. 1 explicemus.
units.tr: To demonstrate the figure of crystal better, it will not be out of place to explain a little more distinctly, in Fig. 1, the terms of the demonstration, which the most subtle Nicolaus Steno (Dissertationis Prodromus, De Solido intra Solidum, p. 57) had only indicated in general terms.

units.la: Crystallus, inquit, componitur ex duabus pyramidibus hexagonis (a b c d e a & k f g h i k) & columna intermedia itidem hexagona (b c d e i h g f b) Ubi angulos solidos extremos illos appello (bac, cad, dae, f k g, g k h, h k i.) qui vertices pyramidum constituunt, angulos verò solidos intermedios illos, (a b f, a c g, a d h, a e i, k f b, k g e, k h d, k i e,) qui in pyramidum cum columna unione constituuntur, eodem modo plana pyramidum (a c b, a d e, a e d, k f g, k g h, k h i,) plana extrema, & columnæ plana (b c g f, c d h g, d e i h) plana intermedia appello; planum baseos (α β γ δ ζ ε.) est sectio perpendicularis ad omnia plana intermedia, planum axis (a q r k t u a) est sectio, in qua est axis Crystalli, qui componitur ex axibus pyramidum, & axe columnæ.
units.tr: "Crystal," he says, "is composed of two hexagonal pyramids (a b c d e a and k f g h i k) and an intermediate column, likewise hexagonal (b c d e i h g f b). I call the extreme solid angles those (b a c, c a d, d a e, f k g, g k h, h k i), which form the vertices of the pyramids, and the intermediate solid angles those (a b f, a c g, a d h, a e i, k f b, k g e, k h d, k i e), which arise where the pyramids join the column. In the same way I call the planes of the pyramids (a c b, a d e, a e d, k f g, k g h, k h i) the extreme planes, and the planes of the column (b c g f, c d h g, d e i h) the intermediate planes. The plane of the base (α β γ δ ζ ε) is a section perpendicular to all the intermediate planes. The plane of the axis (a q r k t u a) is a section in which lies the axis of the crystal, which is composed of the axes of the pyramids and the axis of the column."

units.la: III. Hisce terminorum significationibus, sive partium Crystalli denominationibus nunc præmissis, haud difficile erit intelligere Phænomena in Crystallis ipsis hexagonis variantia, à Laudato Stenone Diss: Prodr: cit: p.60. & 61. Ordine notata, ut, quòd plana intermedia in quibusdam Crystallis majora, in aliis minora sint, in quibusdam omnino desiderentur; quòd plana intermedia fere semper striata sint, plana verò extrema, materiæ sibi appositæ indicia conservent: quòd axis pyramidum non semper constituat eandem rectam cum axe columnæ; quòd plana extrema raro sint æqualia inter se; Unde sequitur inæqualitas planorum intermediorum; quòd plana extrema non semper sint triangularia, sicut nec semper quadrilatera sint omnia plana intermedia; quòd angulus solidus extremus resolvatur in plures angulos solidos, idémque angulis solidis intermediis frequenter contingat, quòd idem planum communiter dictum, non habeat partes suas omnes in eodem plano sitas, sed in planis diversis, supra illud diversè exstantibus; quòd planum communiter dictum, multis in locis, non planum, sed gibbum conspiciatur; quòd tandem in planis intermediis inæqualitates oriantur scalarum gradibus similes. Interdum pyramides ipsæ non sunt altius elevatæ, sed quodammodo depressæ. Ita in Museo nostro Tigurino extat inter alias Mater Crystalli perrara, absque cuspidibus, cujus scilicet Crystalli juxta invicem adsurgentes sunt hexagonæ, planis pyramidalibus tribus depressis, iisque pentagonis tectæ. Uti eam Fig. 2. exhibet. Est mihi Crystallus perspicua utrinque acuta, cujus quidem columna sex cingitur lateribus, pyramis etiam una totidem, altera tria tantum habet plana, hanc inter rariores asservo, & Fig. 3. ob oculos pono.
units.tr: III. With these meanings of the terms, or names of the parts of the crystal, now set out, it will not be difficult to understand the phenomena that vary in hexagonal crystals themselves, which Steno, cited above (Dissertationis Prodromus, pp. 60 and 61), notes in order: that the intermediate planes are larger in some crystals, smaller in others, and altogether lacking in some; that the intermediate planes are almost always striated, while the extreme planes keep traces of the matter applied to them; that the axis of the pyramids does not always make the same straight line with the axis of the column; that the extreme planes are seldom equal to one another, whence follows the inequality of the intermediate planes; that the extreme planes are not always triangular, just as not all the intermediate planes are always quadrilateral; that an extreme solid angle is resolved into several solid angles, and the same often happens to the intermediate solid angles; that a plane commonly so called does not have all its parts lying in one plane, but in different planes standing out variously above it; that a plane commonly so called, in many places, is seen not as a plane but as a hump; and finally that in the intermediate planes arise inequalities similar to the steps of a staircase. Sometimes the pyramids themselves are not raised high but are somehow depressed. Thus in our Zurich museum there exists, among others, a very rare "mother of crystal," without points, in which the crystals rising beside one another are hexagonal, with three depressed pyramidal planes, which are themselves covered by pentagons, as Fig. 2 shows. I myself have a clear crystal pointed at both ends, whose column is indeed surrounded by six sides, and one pyramid likewise has six, while the other has only three planes; I keep this among the rarer specimens and place it before the eyes in Fig. 3.

units.la: IV. Crystalli, licèt hexagonæ ut plurimùm sint, variant tamen maximè figura. Memorat Olig: Jacobæus Mus: Reg: Dan: S.VII.p.37, Triangularem cui stipulæ inclusæ. Georg: Hieron: Velsch.l.c. Seriem talium anomalarū Crystallorum recenset, variis etiam & novis nuncupat nominibus. Parvam, qua Virile membrum repræsentat, ἀνδρειοειδὴν[?] repræsentat. Sicut porrò ἀμφίκηκης[?] minima hexagona, sed tamen & heptagona, tetragona & trigona; Polystagonia cum appendice quadrangulari, διφυὴς[?] pentagona plane irregularis, & vicissim regularis cum appendice digona; ἀνισοέδρῳ[?] basi lactea, ἑξταχαγδεκαέδρῳ[?] major & minor, Decagona pentadecaedros, octaedros, decaedros; hendecaedros digona irregularis. Tetrastalagmias pulcherrima, & distalagmias bicornis, & polystalagmias. Hexagona inæqualibus & irregularibus angulis, διxέφως[?], Octogona epigona, distalagmias pentagona, Enneagona inæqualis, dodecagona heptapleuros, digona appendice irregulari, pentagona minor matrice petrosa, & altera scabrosa. Hexacaedecagona, anomala polystalactica heptaedra, heptagona inæqualis, anisogona basi lactea, & Diphyes cardioides. Worm: Mus: p.100. Frid: Lachmund: Oryctograph: Hildesheim: S.III.C.7. Joh: de Laët de Gemm: & Lap: L.I. C.15. p.58. Nascuntur etiam globosa Olivari utrinque in apicem terminata, ovali & hemisphærica figura. Plin: Hist: Nat: L.37.C.10. Agricol: Geßn: L.C.p.25. Interdum dodecagonæ reperiuntur. Hisce adjungo, quas primo loco nominare debuissem, Crystallos rarissimas Trigonas, è congerie plurium minorum constantes, & à radice latiori in Pyramidem desinentes,
units.tr: IV. Crystals, although they are mostly hexagonal, nevertheless vary greatly in figure. Olig Jacobaeus (Mus. Reg. Dan. S. VII, p. 37) records a triangular one with straw enclosed inside. Georg Hieronymus Welsch (l.c.) lists a series of such anomalous crystals and gives them various new names: a small one that represents the male member, called "manlike" [ἀνδρειοειδής]; likewise the very small hexagonal "double-edged" [ἀμφίκηκης], but also heptagonal, tetragonal, and trigonal ones; the "polystagonal" with a quadrangular appendage; the "two-natured" [διφυής], a plainly irregular pentagon, and conversely a regular one with a two-cornered appendage; the "unequal-faced" [ἀνισοέδρος] with a milky base; the sixteen-faced [ἑξταχαγδεκαέδρος], larger and smaller; decagonal, pentadecahedral, octahedral, decahedral; hendecahedral, irregular two-cornered. The "tetrastalagmias" very beautiful, the "distalagmias" two-horned, and the "polystalagmias." Hexagons with unequal and irregular angles, "two-lighted" [διξέφως]; octagons, "epigonal"; the pentagonal distalagmias; the unequal enneagon; the dodecagon "seven-sided"; the two-cornered one with an irregular appendage; the smaller pentagon with a stony matrix, and another rough one. The hexadecagonal, the anomalous polystalactic heptahedral, the unequal heptagonal, the anisogonal with a milky base, and the heart-shaped double crystal [Diphyes cardioides]. See Worm (Mus. p. 100), Friedrich Lachmund (Oryctographia Hildesheimensis, S. III, c. 7), Johannes de Laët (De Gemmis et Lapidibus, L. I, c. 15, p. 58). Globular olive-shaped ones also arise, terminating at both ends in a point, of oval and hemispherical figure (Pliny, Hist. Nat. L. 37, c. 10; Agricola; Gesner, L. c., p. 25). Sometimes dodecagonal ones are found. To these I add, though I ought to have named them first, the very rare trigonal crystals, made up of a heap of several smaller ones and ending in a pyramid from a broader base.

units.la: Viro Illustrissimo ac Excellentissimo, Petro Valkenierio, Potentissimorum Foederati Belgii Ordinum ad Respu- blicas Helvet: & Rhet: Ablegato Extraordinario, Montis-
units.tr: To the most illustrious and most excellent Peter Valkenier, Extraordinary Envoy of the most powerful Lords States of the United Netherlands to the Swiss and Rhaetian Republics, Montis-

units.la: beligardo transmissas, quas curioso Lectori Fig.4. ob oculos ponere constitui, quæ non valde dissimiles sunt iis, seu Crystallis, seu selenitis, qui Altdorfi Noricorum ad molam Brethal, saxo cuidam adnati, & fœtura flavescente obducti reperiuntur.
units.tr: beligardo transmitted, which I have decided to set before the curious reader at Fig. 4. They are not very unlike those crystals or selenites that are found at Altdorf in Noricum, near the Brethal mill, growing on a certain rock and covered with a yellowish crust.

units.la: V. Omnis Crystallus adeò perspicua & diaphana est, ut feré aquam puram, limpidam, vel congelatam æquet. Basis, seu infima pars Columnæ, subinde pura & diaphana, plerumque tamen albicans, & variis impuritatibus est referta.
units.tr: V. Every crystal is so clear and transparent that it nearly equals pure, limpid or frozen water. The base, or lowest part of the column, is sometimes pure and transparent, but for the most part it is whitish and full of various impurities.

units.la: VI. Cui colorum divisio Antiquis usitata in veros & apparentes non displicet, is ad illorum Classem referet Crystallum tam nigram quàm atramentum, Mus: Septal. L. C. §. 46. Velsch. L. C. Rubras, Virides, Cœrulèas, Citrinas, Amethystinas. Card: de Subt: L. VII. p. 362. Mus: Worm. p. 99. Quasdam dimidia parte albas, & dimidia virides, alias totas albas, ac quasdam virides & summè perfectas vidisse, testatur Joseph: Acost. In cavitate Crystallis plena, aquea, lucidissimæ, albæ & Amethystinæ erant. Nicol: Steno Diss: Prod: cit: p. 69. In Italia Crystallum amplam, cujus pars pyramidalis colore viridi tincta, sed lentior ac pallidior evadebat, antequam basin attingeret, quidam asservabat, Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virtut: p. 13. Colore croceo, purpureo & rubiginoso tinctas habebat Worm: Mus: p. 100. Ad apparentiam colorum spectat, quando Crystallus supposito aliquo colore, cùm ex adverso spectatur, infecta tota videtur, Athanas: Kirch: Mag: Art: Lucis & Umbræ, p. 80. Ita datur Crystalli species, quæ exposita solis radiis per januam, fenestram &c. radios projicit in proximum parietem, ex effectu Iris nominatur, etiam fronti applicata tales colores repræsentat, Gesner. L. C: p. 68. 69. Ansh: Boët: de Boot: L. C: p. 221. Mus: Worm: p. 100. Licèt, ut supra dictum, colores hi in omnibus Crystallis diaphanis & perspicuis observantur; porrò, si fissura ab ictu vel percussione Crystallo infligatur, offerunt sese, è medio licèt lapidis, itidem colores pulchrè variegati.
units.tr: VI. Those who do not object to the division of colours used by the ancients into true and apparent colours will assign to that class the crystal that is as black as ink, Mus: Septal. L. C. §. 46. Velsch. L. C. red, green, blue, yellow and violet, Card: de Subt: L. VII. p. 362. Mus: Worm. p. 99. Joseph: Acost. testifies that he saw some that were half white and half green, others wholly white, and some green and most perfect. Nicol: Steno Diss: Prod: cit: p. 69. In a cavity full of water, the crystals were very bright, white and violet. Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virtut: p. 13. In Italy a certain man kept a large crystal whose pyramidal part was tinted with green, but which became paler and fainter before it reached the base. Worm: Mus: p. 100. He had one tinted with saffron, purple and rust colour. It belongs to the appearance of colours when a crystal, with some colour placed behind it, looks wholly tinted when viewed from the opposite side. Athanas: Kirch: Mag: Art: Lucis & Umbræ, p. 80. So there is a species of crystal which, when exposed to the rays of the sun through a door, window and so on, casts the rays on the nearest wall, and is called the iris from this effect; applied to the forehead, it also shows such colours. Gesner. L. C: p. 68. 69. Ansh: Boët: de Boot: L. C: p. 221. Mus: Worm: p. 100. Although, as said above, these colours are observed in all transparent and clear crystals, yet if a crack is made in the crystal by a blow or a strike, beautifully variegated colours also appear from the middle of the stone.

units.la: VII. Huc etiam commodè referri potest Crystallus Islandica, in peculiaribus Tractatibus à Viris in Orbe Erudito notissimis, Erasmo Bartholino, & Christiano Hugenio descriptæ. Est autem meo judicio hæc ipsa, quam sub nomine Massæ Crystallinæ quadratæ (seu Rhomboidalis potius) describit in Mus: Septal: Paul: Maria Terzag: l. C. §. 54. atque pro Gyp-si specie potius, quam Crystallo agnovit. Ut sanè, qui non figuram duntaxat, sed & friabilitatem, divisibilitatem in lamellas. &c. attendit, & descriptiones ab Auctoribus factas probè perpendit, facilè nobiscum consentiet, precariam esse ejus inter Crystallos recensionem & Selenitæ Rhomboidalis titulo melius insigniri, sicut ejus meminit Stenò Prodr: Diss: Citat: p. 79. Quia est ad instar selenitæ in lamellas scissilis, & integra quælibet massa in corpuscula minora & minima ejusdem figuræ cum toto, i.e. Rhomboidalia potest dividi. Unde eadem hæc Crystallus Islandica in Museo Societ: Regiæ Angl. p. 309. memorata appositè Crystallus Talcosa nominatur. Non tamen esse hanc, sive Crystallum, sive Selenitem, Islandiæ propriam, sed & Helvetiæ incolam, vel inde patet, quia ex variis ad nos delata fuit locis, ex Rhetia, Ditione Bernensi, Glaronensi, vico ditionis Suitensis, ad Lacum, Sachen/dicto, Thermis Schinznacensibus. Quandoquidem in Crystalli Islandicæ ad Opticæ leges instituto examine varia congessit Phænomena Erasm: Bartholin: in Tractatu huc in finem Haffniæ, 1670. in 4to edito, non abs re erit præcipua, eáque Curiosiora, paucis indigitare. Ut, quòd si Prismati talì Crystallino aliquid supponatur, quicquid etiam sit, duplex in superficie appareat, unde eam Disdiaclasticam quoque vocat Exp. VII. Et quidem apparentia utraque dilutiore colore, interdum pars una obscurior altera. Exp. VIII. Item, una ex duabus hisce imaginibus altera elevatior. Exp. IX. Detur item locus aliquis, in quo tantum una & simplex, per prisma hoc aspicientibus apparet imago, non secus ac per aliud aliquod diaphanum. Exp. X. Sit & locus aliquis, ubi objectum appareat sextuplum, Exp. XI. Quòd item una ex duabus imaginibus sit mobilis, sive sequatur motum prismatis, altera permanente fixa & immota. Exp: XIII. Quòd item possit fixa species reddi mobilis, & mobilis fixa in eodem Crystallo, nec non utraque mobilis. Exp: XIV. Quòd etiam mobilis illa species, non incertis vagetur legibus, sed circa fixam rotetur semper. Exp: XV.
units.tr: VII. The Iceland crystal can also conveniently be referred here; it has been described in special treatises by men most famous in the learned world, Erasmus Bartholin and Christiaan Huygens. In my judgement it is the same thing that Paolo Maria Terzaghi, in the Museum Septalianum, describes under the name of a quadrangular (or rather rhomboidal) crystalline mass, and acknowledges as a kind of gypsum rather than a crystal. Anyone who attends not only to its shape but also to its friability, its divisibility into thin plates, and so on, and who carefully weighs the descriptions given by the authors, will readily agree with us that its inclusion among the crystals is doubtful, and that it is better named rhomboidal selenite, as Steno also mentions it in the Prodromus Dissertation cited, p. 79. Because it is like selenite, splitting into plates, and any whole mass can be divided into smaller and very small bodies of the same figure as the whole, that is, rhomboidal. Hence this same Iceland crystal, mentioned in the Museum of the Royal Society of England, p. 309, is fittingly called talc-like crystal. That it is not peculiar to Iceland, but is also found in Switzerland, is clear from the fact that it has been brought to us from various places: from Rhaetia, from the territory of Bern, from Glarus, from the village of the Schwyz territory on the lake called Sachen, and from the Schinznach baths. Since Erasmus Bartholin, in his treatise published for this purpose at Copenhagen in 1670, in quarto, has examined the Iceland crystal under the laws of optics and gathered various phenomena, it will not be out of place to point out briefly the principal and more curious of them. For example, if anything is placed beneath such a crystalline prism, whatever it may be, a double image appears on the surface, for which reason he also calls it disdiaclastic (Exp. VII). And indeed both images are of a rather paler colour, sometimes one part darker than the other (Exp. VIII). Likewise one of these two images is higher than the other (Exp. IX). There is also some place in which, to those looking through this prism, only one single image appears, just as through any other transparent body (Exp. X). There is also a place where the object appears sixfold (Exp. XI). Likewise one of the two images is movable, following the motion of the prism, while the other remains fixed and immobile (Exp. XIII). Likewise the fixed image can be made movable, and the movable one fixed, in the same crystal, and both can be movable (Exp. XIV). Likewise that movable image does not wander according to uncertain laws, but always revolves about the fixed one (Exp. XV).

units.la: VIII. Superficies Crystalli exterior non ita est lævis & polita semper, quin variis obnoxia sit inæqualitatibus & inquinamentis. Sic Velsch: Lib. C. Ex sylva Hercynia haud procul Pulaco asportavimus Crystallum densissimâ fœturâ in saxo luxuriantem, guttisque aureis, seu verius sabulo aurifero undique conspersam. Aliam similem, in qua Massulæ marcasitæ aureæ eminent angulares, Octaedræ, decaedræ, & dodecaedræ grandes & ponderosæ. Gesn: l.C. p. 18. In quibusdam, quæ Blochebergi reperiuntur, magnus est mucro, corpus exiguum, lateribus nisi scabritie infestantur, ferme tantus est lævor, ut vix arte possit æquari. Mus: Septal. l. 3. §. 24. Massa Crystallina quadrata, s. Rhomboidalis, durissimâ auri minerâ naturaliter obducta. Est mihi frustum Crystallinæ pyramidis, in cujus planitie figuræ quædam lineares, foveolæ acu quasi exsculptæ cernuntur. Fig: 5. ad A. mica insuper hinc inde sparsum. Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virtut: p. 24. Observatur in Adamantibus Cornubiensibus exiguus lapis, ejusdem generis composuisse quasi unum corpus cum majore, ita ut minor majori fuerit insertus, separatione facta remanebat in majore cavitas, quæ concinnè sese ad minorem adaptabat. In Rarithecio nostro Tigurino asservatur, inter alia, Minera Crystalli hexagona pyritæ Silicei crustæ innatæ, ubi plana pyramidalia obscuri & nigricantis sunt celoris, & insuper bullulis exiguis, veluti variolis conspersa. Quarum etiam meminit Steno Diss: Prod: Cit: p. 62. Vide Fig. 5. ad B.
units.tr: VIII. The outer surface of a crystal is not always so smooth and polished that it is not exposed to various unevenness and stains. Thus Velsch, in the work cited, says: "From the Hercynian forest, not far from Pulaco, we carried off a crystal growing very thickly on the rock, and sprinkled everywhere with golden drops, or rather with auriferous sand." Another similar one, in which golden marcasite masses stand out as angular, large and heavy octahedrons, decahedrons and dodecahedrons. Gesner, l.c. p. 18. In some found at Blochberg there is a large point and a small body; the sides are troubled by roughness, but otherwise the smoothness is so great that it can scarcely be made even by art. Museum Septalianum, l. 3, §. 24. A quadrangular or rhomboidal crystalline mass, naturally covered with a very hard gold ore. I have a piece of a crystalline pyramid, on whose flat surface certain linear figures and little pits can be seen, as if carved with a needle (Fig. 5 at A), with mica also scattered here and there. Boyle de Gemm: Orig. & Virtut. p. 24. In the Cornish diamonds a small stone is observed which, of the same kind, has grown together as if one body with a larger one, so that the smaller was inserted into the larger; when they were separated, a cavity remained in the larger which fitted neatly to the smaller. In our Tigurine cabinet is kept, among other things, a mineral of hexagonal crystal, grown on a siliceous crust of pyrites, where the pyramidal flat faces are of a dark and blackish colour, and besides are sprinkled with tiny bubbles, as if with pox marks. Steno also mentions these in the Dissertation Prodromus cited, p. 62. See Fig. 5 at B.

units.la: IX. Multa vitia Crystallo innasci solent, Plin: Hist: Nat: L. 37. C. 2. & Ansh: Boët: de Boot: Lib: C. p. 221. Festucæ, Nebulæ, Atomi, rubigo, & ferrugini quid simile, scabrities, Vomica, muscæ, formicæ, palæ, Plumbago, Nix, Salia, quæ Martialis Nitrum vocat.
units.tr: IX. Many faults are wont to grow in crystal: Plin: Hist: Nat: L. 37. C. 2. & Ansh: Boët: de Boot: Lib: C. p. 221. Straws, clouds, atoms, rust and something like iron rust, roughness, a vomica, flies, ants, scales, plumbago, snow, salts, which Martial calls nitre:

units.la: Et turbata levi quæstas Crystallina Nitro.
units.tr: And crystal, clouded by a little nitre, ...

units.la: Et Du Hamel. de Meteoris & Fossilibus Lib. II. Cap. VII. pag. 453. per maculam minutiori muscæ persimilem explicat, cui item capillus, aliud gemmarum vitium, est, veluti quædamscissura, quæ radios regerit, ac perspicuitati obest. Possedit Velsch: Hecatost: l. Cit: l. Crystallum in qua Aculeus Erinacei inclusus coaluit; forte eadem hæc est cum iis, quas habet Mus: Septal: l. c. §. 3. 4. 6. 15. 20. In quarum visceribus pili variæ crassitiei nigri conspicui sunt, & hæ, opinor, nihil aliud sunt, quàm Antimonium elegantissimè, ac pilorum adinstar Crystallifatum, ejusmodi Crystallum, quam ipse ex Valesia asportavi, in gratiam Curiosorum in Fig: 6. exprimere volui. Tale Antimonium Crystallifatum in minera Crystallorum, non quidem semper in mediis corporibus, sed extrà observatur, uti talem in Bibliotheca nostra Civica videre licet. Memorantur porrò in Crystallorum corpore à Velsch: l. c. Venæ Cruentæ. Mus: Septal: l. c. §. 7. 9. 11. 13. 44. 49. 50. 55. Fort: Licet: de Sponst: Vivent: Ort: L. II. C. 21. p. 215. Velsch: l. c. Olig: Jacob: Mus: Reg: Dan: S. VII. p. 37. Gramen viridissimum, fœnum resiccatum, Muscus, frusta ligni, stramina, Folium Oliuæ, Vermiculi. Card: de Subt: L. VII. p. 362. Boyle de Gen: Orig: & Virt: p. 24. Mus: Septal: l. c. §. 27. 28. 29. 33. In medio Crystalli gutta aquæ conclusa, quæ facilè motu observari potest, Crystallo imprimis situm mutante. Card: l. c. Joh: Jonst: Thaumatog: Nat: Cl. 4. C. 20. p. 172. In mucrone rarius, frequenter in corpore Argentum rude, & quidem plumbaginis coloris, Mus: Septal: l. c. §. 8. In visceribus ipsius exsurgit argentum purissimum.
units.tr: And Du Hamel. de Meteoris & Fossilibus Lib. II. Cap. VII. pag. 453. explains it by a spot much like a very small fly. Another flaw of gems is the hair, which is like a kind of cleft that reflects the rays and hinders clearness. Velsch, Hecatost. l. cit. l., had a crystal in which a hedgehog's spine was enclosed and had grown fast. Perhaps this is the same as those which the Museum Septalianum, l.c. §§ 3, 4, 6, 15, 20, has. In their interiors black hairs of various thickness are visible, and these, I think, are nothing other than antimony, most elegantly crystallised and like hairs. I wished to show in Fig. 6, for the benefit of curious readers, such a crystal as I myself carried from Valais. Such crystallised antimony is observed in a mineral of crystals, not always in the middle of the bodies but on the outside, as can be seen in such a specimen in our Civic Library. Further, blood-red veins are mentioned in the body of crystals by Velsch, l.c. Museum Septalianum, l.c. §§ 7, 9, 11, 13, 44, 49, 50, 55. Fort: Licet: de Sponst: Vivent: Ort: L. II. C. 21. p. 215. Velsch: l.c. Olig: Jacob: Mus: Reg: Dan: S. VII. p. 37. Very green grass, dried hay, moss, pieces of wood, straws, olive leaves, little worms. Card: de Subt: L. VII. p. 362. Boyle de Gen: Orig: & Virt: p. 24. Mus: Septal: l.c. §§ 27, 28, 29, 33. In the middle of a crystal a drop of water is enclosed, which can easily be seen to move, especially when the crystal changes its position. Card: l.c. Joh: Jonst: Thaumatog: Nat: Cl. 4. C. 20. p. 172. At the point, more rarely, and frequently in the body, is crude silver, indeed of the colour of plumbago. Museum Septalianum, l.c. §. 8. In the interior of it rises the purest silver.

units.la: X. Magnitudo in omnem dimensionem variat, aliæ amplissimæ sunt, ut habet Plin: l. C. quæ in Capitolio Livia Angusta dicaverat, librarum circiter quinquaginta. Id: juxta Gemmam Topasion in Insula Nerone cubitalis effossa. Ath: Kirch: Mund: Subl: l. C. p. 188. Crystallus eruta in montibus Cupriferis, plùs quàm centenarium ponderabat. Ipse in Valesia superiore vidi Crystallum sexcentas libras superantem, cortice flavo præditam, quæ intus pellucidita te sua Vitrum Venetum æquabat. Ex Norvegia Crystalli teste Worm: Mus: p. 100. diversæ magnitudinis afferuntur, minutæ crassitiei pennæ gallinaceæ, longitudine dimidii digiti, hexangulæ oblonga acuminatæ.
units.tr: X. Their size varies in every dimension. Some are very large, as Pliny reports of the one that Livia Augusta had dedicated in the Capitol, weighing about fifty pounds. Likewise, according to Topasion, a crystal dug up on the island of Nero was a cubit in length. Kircher, Mundus Subterraneus, l.c., p. 188. A crystal dug out of the copper mountains weighed more than a hundred pounds. I myself saw in Upper Valais a crystal weighing more than six hundred pounds, with a yellow rind, which inside rivalled Venetian glass in its transparency. From Norway, according to Worm, Museum, p. 100, crystals of various sizes are brought: some are thin, like a hen's feather, half a finger long, six-sided, oblong and pointed.

units.la: XI. Quædam maximè duritie pollent, ut Worm: l. C. Crystalli globosæ duriores sunt vulgaribus, ac pro Pseudo-adamantibus venduntur. Quibusdam prædurum fragileque centrum inest, Auctoribus Plin: Hist: Nat:L.C.Jonst:Not:Reg:Mineral:p 35.
units.tr: XI. Some are exceptionally hard, as Worm (l.c.) notes: globular crystals are harder than ordinary ones, and are sold as pseudo-diamonds. Some have a very hard but brittle centre, according to Pliny, Natural History, l.c., and Jonston, Mineralogy, p. 35.

units.la: XII. Aliquando Crystalli loco decussæ regenerantur. Sic Bened. Cerut: ad Mus: Calceolar: S.III. Extat in ditione Bergomensi mons quidam, Salvinum accolæ nominant, in quo reperitur maxima Crystallorum copia variis figuris Geometricis notatarum, præcipue verò quæ quantitate parvæ, sexangularem figuram egregiè referunt. Quòd si aliqua harum pars a loco eximatur, non longo interposito temporis spatio, aliæ veluti ab eadem minera, eodem in loco propullulare visuntur. Hertod: Tartaro-Mast: Morav: p.63. Pseudo-adamantes decussi spatio duorum vel trium annorum regenerantur, ut verè dici possit unum alium gignere. Contrarium, experientia duce, referunt Incolæ Helvetiæ, Urienses, Suitenses, Subsylvani, Glaronenses, Valesii, apud quos Crystalli uberrimè producuntur; Scilicet, in illis locis, in quibus prius reperiebantur, non regenerari. Idem contra celebrem Rerum Indicarum Scriptorem asserit Steno Diff: Prod:Cit: p.74. Adamantes in terra, unde semel eruti sunt, certo annorum spatio non renascì.
units.tr: XII. Sometimes crystals regenerate in place of those removed. Thus Benedetto Cerutti, on the Calceolarian Museum, sec. III: in the district of Bergamo there is a certain mountain, which the locals call Salvinum, in which there is a very great abundance of crystals marked with various geometric figures, especially those small ones which closely resemble a six-sided figure. If some part of these is taken from the place, after no long interval of time others appear to sprout from the same ore, in the same place. Hertodt, Tartaro-Mastix Moraviae, p. 63: pseudo-diamonds that have been dug out regenerate within a space of two or three years, so that it may truly be said that one begets another. The inhabitants of Switzerland report the opposite, based on experience: the people of Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Glarus and Valais, where crystals are produced most abundantly, say that in those places where they were first found they do not regenerate. Steno, in his Dissertation on the Prodromus, p. 74, asserts the same against the famous writer on Indian affairs: diamonds in the earth, once dug out from where they were, do not grow again within a certain span of years.

units.la: XIII. Crystallus chalybe, vel alio lapide percussa scintillas emittit. Peculiare quoddam circa id observavit Casatus de Igne, p.145. Crystallus, si Chalybe percutiatur, scintillas erumpere sulphureum quid redolentes deprehenditur, cùmque Crystallus in hexagonum prisma exsurgat, deinde in Pyramidem hexagonam desinat, observatur ex pyramide percussa admodum paucas scintillas emicare, ex prismate aliquanto plures, sed ex basi, seu radice admodum frequentes, & acriorem sulphuris odorem emittentes. Ope etiam Crystallini prismatis radii solis ita concentrari possunt, ut objecta combustibilia statim accendat. Albert:Magn:Libell:de Lap:Virt:p.153.
units.tr: XIII. Crystal, when struck with steel or another stone, gives off sparks. Casati, On Fire, p. 145, observed a peculiar thing about this: it is found that when crystal is struck with steel, sparks burst forth smelling somewhat of sulphur; and since crystal rises as a hexagonal prism and then ends in a hexagonal pyramid, it is observed that when the pyramid is struck, very few sparks flash out, more from the prism, but from the base or root very many, giving off a sharper smell of sulphur. Also, by means of a crystalline prism, the rays of the sun can be so concentrated that they set fire to combustible objects at once. Albertus Magnus, Libellus de Virtutibus Lapidum, p. 153.

units.la: XIV. Dissentiunt Auctores, an Crystallus calorem ferat, necne? Matthiol:Comm:inLib:V.Diosc:p.881. Consentit, quia ex ea pocula parentur. E Contrario Georg: Agricol: de Nat: Fossil:L.VI.p.284. dissentit, & ab infusione liquoris calidi rumpi dicit.
units.tr: XIV. Authors disagree whether crystal bears heat or not. Matthiolus, Commentary on the Fifth Book of Dioscorides, p. 881, agrees, since cups are made from it. On the contrary, Georg Agricola, On the Nature of Fossils, Book VI, p. 284, disagrees, and says that it is broken by pouring in a warm liquid.

units.la: XV. Robert:Boyle de Gem:Orig:& Virt:p.9. Sæpe in Crucibulo Crystallum candere feci, deinde frigidâ calorem ejus extinxi, ubi etiam partibus non dissilientibus, sed corpore pristinam figuram retinente, multitudo exiguarum fissurarum per hanc operationem productarum pellucediate abolita albedinem induxit. Ib: Si Crystallus ignita in plena solutione Cochinellæ in Spiritu Vini factæ, extinguatur, satis rubrarum particularum solutionis occupabit fissuras Crystalli, Pulcherque ei conciliatur color.
units.tr: XV. Robert Boyle, On the Origin and Virtues of Gems, p. 9: I have often made crystal glow in a crucible, then extinguished its heat with cold water; here too, without the parts flying apart, but the body retaining its former shape, a multitude of tiny fissures produced by this operation, with the transparency gone, induced a whiteness. Ibid.: If red-hot crystal is quenched in a full solution of cochineal made in spirit of wine, enough of the red particles of the solution will fill the fissures of the crystal, and a beautiful colour is given to it.

units.la: XVI. Crystallus etiam Chymica arte absque ignitione, sine ullis fissuris, coloribus imbui potest, qualem habebat flammeo Rubino simiem Septal:Mus:Cit:f.16. Liquore quodam Crystallum in Rubinum mutabat colore tantùm,non verò etiam duritie,quam pro sedecim Imperialibus venditabat Job:Agricol:Tract:de Sulph:p.m.873. Crystalli petrosæ pulchris coloribus per vapores minerales tinguntur,licèt colores hoc modo producti non soleant Crystallos illos multùm invadere,penetratióque illorum adjuvetur non debili caloris gradu, tamen partes Crystalli plenariam suam duritiem obtinuerunt,ut post colorationem secari & poliri in modum aliarum Crystallorum possit. Boyle de Gemm:Orig:& Virt:p.10.
units.tr: XVI. Crystal can also be dyed with colours by chemical art, without heating and without any fissures, such as that which Septalius, Museum, cited above, f. 16, had, resembling a flame-coloured ruby. By a certain liquor he changed crystal into ruby in colour only, not in hardness, which he sold for sixteen imperial pieces. Johann Agricola, Treatise on Sulphur, p. 873: crystals of rock are tinged with beautiful colours by mineral vapours, although colours produced in this way do not usually penetrate those crystals deeply, and their penetration is aided by a moderate degree of heat; nevertheless the parts of the crystal retain their full hardness, so that after colouring they can be cut and polished in the manner of other crystals. Boyle, On the Origin and Virtues of Gems, p. 10.

units.la: XVII. Crystallus, attritu, accepta caloris animâ trahit ad se paleas,chartam,aliáque corpora leviora,propius admota attrahit,& complexu tenet. Sicuti id de Crystallo Islandica quoque testatur Erasm: Bartholin:Exp:II.p.3.
units.tr: XVII. Crystal, when rubbed, having received the spirit of heat, draws to itself straws, paper and other lighter bodies, and, when brought close, attracts them and holds them in its embrace. Erasmus Bartholin testifies to this also of Iceland crystal, Experiments II, p. 3.

units.la: CAPUT IV. Proponens Hypotheses Veterum & Recen- tiorum, cum modesta ἐπιχρίσει
units.tr: CAPUT IV. Setting out the hypotheses of the Ancients and the Moderns, with modest criticism [ἐπιχρίσει]

units.la: PHænomena in Capite præcedenti recensita antequam Methodo mihi proposita solvam,haud abs re erit aliorum, seu Veterum, seu Recentiorum placita proponere, ut eò melius patescat, quid illorum valuerint humeri, quid ferre recusaverint,in quo nobiscum consentiant, vel dissentiant ; Atque primò in scenam produci posset ingens Scriptorum numerus,qui Crystallum ex aquâ glaciatâ nivali, vel glaciê ipsâ oriri existimârunt. Ita Hesychio Crystallus definitur τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ ὑπὸ χρύσεος. Et Aristoteli Analyt:Poster:L.II.C.XII.: χρυσταλλος dicitur ὕδωρ πεπηγὸς. De quibus tamen locis dubium omnino videtur, an χρύσταλλον intelligat λίθον, vel annon potius ipsam aquam frigore concretam, sive glaciem. Diodorus Lib.II. Expressis verbis scribit, τὰς χρυσταλλος λίθος ἔχειν τὴν σύστασιν ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ χάρᾳ πηγέντος. Ubi tamen vult Salm: in Solin:p,144. Diodorum per χρυσταλλος λίθος non intelligere Crystal-los,sed Adamantes,quòd in eodem textu adjiciat Auctor cogi, vel congelari ἀπὸ ὑπὸ ψύχους, ἀπὸ ὑπὸ θείας δυνάμεως, quum loquatur de Arabiæ Lapidibus , ubi locorum Crystallus non gignitur, & omnes alii Crystallum ὁμοιουμένον scribant frigore & longæva nive densari, ἀσπιδές διαμένειν, cùm Crystallus sit fragilis,& πολυμόρφως βαφῆναι, ἀναξυμιάσει πνεύματος dicatur , quod rursus non congruere posset Crystallo, quia uniformis est,nec pluribus coloribus naturâ imbuitur;cùm in candido tantùm transluceat, Plin: Hist: Nat: L.37.C.2. Crystallus dicitur geluvehementiore concreta. Joh:Grammat:II. Post:Comm: p.23. Est congelatio aquæ per totalem privationem calidi. Isidor:L.XVI.C.13. Nix glacie durata per annos. Senec:L.III. Quæst: Nat:C.25. Aqua cœlestis minimum in se terreni habens, cùm induruit longioris frigoris pertinaciâ spissatur magis ac magis, donec omni aere excluso in se toto compressa est, & humor qui fuerat, lapis effectus est. August: de Mirab:Script:L.I.C.V. Et in Enarrat:Ps.147. Crystallus gignitur à nive per multos annos non resoluta, & ita congelascente. Statius: Raráque longævis nivibus Crystalla gelari.
units.tr: Before I resolve the phenomena recorded in the preceding chapter by the method I have proposed, it will not be out of place to set out the opinions of others, whether ancient or modern, so that it may be clearer what their arguments were worth, what they were unable to bear, and where they agree or disagree with us. First of all, an immense number of writers could be brought onto the stage who believed that crystal arises from frozen water, or from snow-ice, or from ice itself. Thus Hesychius defines crystal as "water congealed by cold" [τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ ὑπὸ χρύσεος]. And Aristotle, in the second book of the Posterior Analytics, says that crystal is "water congealed" [ὕδωρ πεπηγὸς]. Yet in these passages it seems entirely doubtful whether they mean a stone by crystal, or rather water itself, solidified by frost, that is, ice. Diodorus, in his second book, writes in express words that crystal stones have their substance from water and air hardened by cold [τὰς χρυσταλλος λίθος ἔχειν τὴν σύστασιν ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ χάρᾳ πηγέντος]. Yet Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 144, holds that Diodorus by "crystal stones" does not mean crystals but diamonds, because in the same passage the author adds that they are compressed or congealed by cold or by a divine power [ἀπὸ ὑπὸ ψύχους, ἀπὸ ὑπὸ θείας δυνάμεως], while speaking of the stones of Arabia, where crystal is not produced at all. Moreover, all the others write that crystal is made dense by frost and long-lasting snow, and that it remains unbroken [ἀσπιδές διαμένειν], whereas crystal is brittle, and it is said to be dyed in many colours [πολυμόρφως βαφῆναι] by an infusion of air, which again could not fit crystal, since it is uniform and by nature not imbued with several colours, being transparent only in whiteness. Pliny, Natural History, book 37, chapter 2, says that crystal is formed from very severe frost. John Grammaticus, in his Posterior Commentary, p. 23: it is the congealing of water through the total privation of heat. Isidore, book 16, chapter 13: snow hardened into ice over the years. Seneca, Natural Questions, book 3, chapter 25: heavenly water, having the least earthy matter in itself, when it hardens through the persistence of a longer frost, is thickened more and more, until, with all air excluded, it is compressed entirely within itself, and the moisture that had been becomes stone. Augustine, On the Wonders of Scripture, book 1, chapter 5, and in his commentary on Psalm 147: crystal is produced from snow that has not melted for many years and has thus congealed. Statius: "and crystals frozen from snows that last for ages."

units.la: Albertus Magnus I. Mineral: Tractat: II. Crystallus habet naturam aquæ, & fit vi frigoris. Conimbricens: Tractat: VII. de Meteoris C.V. Est glacies in perfrigidis regionibus concreta. salmas: in Solinum pag. citat. Humor perspicuus frigore concretus Crystallum generat. Theophrast: Paracels: In Fragm: de Morb: Gall: p.m.658. Crystallus est centrum glaciei, frigoréque spiritus ipsius coagulatur. Et in Tract:V.de Element:Ignis Text:IV. Crystallos ac Beryllos generari vult ex stellis nivalibus, atque nihil aliud esse quàm coagulatam aquam nivalem. Encel:de Metall.L.III C.18. Est glacies ad lapidis duritiem evecta. Crystalli Origo est ex aqua, seu aqueo humore, vi frigoris intensioris, ac diuturnioris, in lapideam duritiem concreta. Kunkel: de Arte Vitr:P.II.p.120. Crystallus nihil aliud est, quàm glacies congelata, non solùm vi frigoris, sed & caloris subterranei; Lamb: Dan: Phys: Christ: P.II.C. 25. Est aqua magno & diuturno frigore congelata & induratata. Croneburg: de Comp.Med:L.IX.p.134. Crystallus fit ex succo purissimo, frigore intra terram densato; Seidel: Phys: p.375. Est aquea substantia pura, ac frigore concreta. Agmen claudit Celebris ille Polyhistor Morhoff: cui in Tract:deScypho Vitreo per certum humanæ vocis sonum fracto:p.35. Verosimile fit per seculorum aliquot tractus in veram Crystallum consolidari glaciem posse; In quam tamen sententiam se non descendere potuisse fatetur, nisi auctoritate Virorum Celeberrimorum, Helvetiorum, ad id fuisset persuasus. Hanc tamen mentem mutavit in Coll: Hist: Nat: MSC P.II. c.31. Ubi Crystallum æquè ac alios lapides gigni concipit ex solido aliquo principio & aqua, quæ duo primùm instar succi inspissentur, & postea in lapidis duritiem abeant, humore arctius cum particulis arenariis unito.
units.tr: Albertus Magnus, Mineralogy, tractate 2: crystal has the nature of water and is formed by the force of frost. The Coimbra commentators, tractate 7 on Meteors, chapter 5: it is ice congealed in the very cold regions. Salmasius, on Solinus, the page cited: a clear moisture congealed by frost generates crystal. Theophrastus Paracelsus, in the fragment on the diseases of the gall, p. 658: crystal is the centre of ice, and its spirit is coagulated by cold. And in tractate 5 on the element of fire, text 4, he holds that crystals and beryls are generated from snowy stars, and that they are nothing other than snow-water coagulated. Encelius, On Metals, book 3, chapter 18: it is ice raised to the hardness of stone. The origin of crystal is from water, or a watery moisture, hardened into a stony hardness by the force of a more intense and more lasting cold. Kunckel, On the Art of Glass, part 2, p. 120: crystal is nothing other than ice congealed, not only by the force of cold but also by that of subterranean heat. Lamb, Christian Physics of Daniel, part 2, chapter 25: it is water congealed and hardened by a great and long-lasting cold. Croneburg, On the Composition of Medicines, book 9, p. 134: crystal is formed from the purest juice, thickened within the earth by cold. Seidel, Physics, p. 375: it is a pure watery substance, congealed by cold. The famous polymath Morhof closes the line. In his tractate on a glass cup broken by a certain sound of the human voice, p. 35, he says that it is possible for ice, over a series of centuries, to be consolidated into true crystal; yet he confesses that he could not go so far in this opinion, unless he had been persuaded of it by the authority of very famous men of Switzerland. However, he changed this view in his Collection of Natural History, manuscript, part 2, chapter 31, where he conceives that crystal, like the other stones, is generated from some solid principle and water, which two first thicken like a juice, and afterwards pass into the hardness of stone, with moisture more closely united to sandy particles.

units.la: Quibus pro materia Crystalli aqua congelata, vel nix, vel glacies ipsa non arrisit, illi aliam quæsiverunt. Vel ex succo puro, vel ex humore sui generis, quem non denominant. Ita Georg:Agricol:de Ort:& Caus: subt.L.IV.p.58. Et de Nat:Fossil:L.VI.p.282. Crystallus constat ex succo purissimo quem frigus intra terram conglutinavit. Et Andr:Matth:in Lib: V.Diosc:Comm.p.m.881. Ut & Georg: Eras: Ollinger:de Signat:Med:p.m. 422. Ex humore omnium purissimo & eo ipso, quo in terra visceribus Adamas, & alii id genus lapides gignuntur. Sengu erd:Colleg:Phys:p.204. Ex succo lapidescente puriore, cui multum aquæ materiæ admixtum est. Card: de Subt: L.VII.p.361. Crystallus constat ex humore sui generis. Henr: Alsted. Indic:Fossil:p.m.1948. Ex succo quodam, quem frigus intra terram conglutinavit. In Disp: Galeno-Chymic: Hanov:A.1631.p.m.302. Ex humore aqueo & purissimo, non frigore, sed divini cujusdam caloris virtute concreto, & p 303. Ex humore sui generis Crystallino, tum à causa universali, tum potentia quadam terrestri lapidescente. Daniel: Hartnacc: Admirand: Phys:p.411. Et Strauss: Isagog: Phys:p. m.211. E succo lapidescente proprio, quem forma propria elaborat. Quibus addimus Velsch:Hecatost: I. Obs:38. ita ratiocinantem: Gemmæ omnes ex Crystallo generantur: non autem ex Crystallo proprie ita dicto, sed quæ huic similLima, corpus nempe liquidum, lapidifico, ut vocant, succo plus minus turgidum, diaphanum, & variæ figuræ capax, &c.
units.tr: For those who did not favour ice, snow, or frozen water as the matter of crystal, these writers sought another. Either a pure juice, or a moisture of its own kind, which they do not name. Thus Georg Agricola, On the Origin and Causes of Subterranean Things, book 4, p. 58, and On the Nature of Fossils, book 6, p. 282: crystal consists of the purest juice, which cold has glued together within the earth. And Andreas Matthiolus, in his commentary on Dioscorides, book 5, p. 881, as well as Georg Erasmus Ollinger, On the Signatures of Medicines, p. 422: from the purest of all moistures, and the very one from which adamant and other stones of that kind are generated in the bowels of the earth. Senguerd, Physics Lectures, p. 204: from a purer petrifying juice, in which much watery matter is mixed. Cardanus, On Subtlety, book 7, p. 361: crystal consists of a moisture of its own kind. Henry Alsted, Index of Fossils, p. 1948: from a certain juice, which cold has glued together within the earth. In the Galeno-Chymical Disputation at Hanover, 1631, p. 302: from a watery and most pure moisture, not congealed by cold but by the power of some divine heat, and p. 303: from a crystalline moisture of its own kind, both from a universal cause and from a certain earthly power that petrifies. Daniel Hartnack, Admirable Physics, p. 411; and Strauss, Introduction to Physics, p. 211: from a proper petrifying juice, which a proper form elaborates. To these we add Velschius, Hecatostes I, Obs. 38, reasoning thus: all gems are generated from crystal, but not from crystal properly so called, rather from what is most like it, namely a liquid body, a petrifying juice, as they call it, more or less swollen, transparent, and capable of various shapes, etc.

units.la: {A}Alii aquam equidem, vel succum quendam purum pro materia agnoscunt, efficientem autem; quam modò allegati Auctores Spiritum Gorgoneum, vel lapidificum vocant; coagulantis Salini titulo insigniunt; Ita Theoph: Parac: In Fragm: de Morb: Gall: p.c. vult Crystallum substantiam suam & coagulationem sumpsisse à diaphaneitate salis glaciati; Et de Meteor: p.m 87. Crystalli generantur ex aqua, quæ aqua, seu materia in se habet Spiritum coagulantem, qui statim coagulat. Consentit Hertod: Tartaro-Mast: Morav: p.62. Genesin hujus lapidis ita concipiens: Crystallus non nascitur ex nivium liquefactarum purissimis aquis, vi Spiritus coagulativi, in Crystallum conversis, sed potius, cum tellus spiritibus Salinus, Nitrosis, &c. donata sit, qui igne subterraneo in vaporem versi, per intimas & insensibiles telluris fibras exaltati, ubi in glebas sale turgidas inciderint, subitò magnetismo quodam exaltati, partes subtiliores ad partes similes confluunt, quæ cum subtilissimæ sint & diaphanæ omnes, hæ unitæ in loco appropriato, Spiritu lapidifico iis insito cooperante, in substantiam Crystallinam coalescunt. Et jam supra Laudatus Exc: D:D.König: Reg: Mineral:S.II.C.VI.p. 104. Videtur Crystallus aquæ certæ natales attribuere, quæ particulis arenosis dissolutis prægnans, à sale quodam austero magis figitur, & in tale corpus diaphanum abit. Etthmyll: Schröd: Dilucid: Mineral:p.223. Crystallus est simplicissima aqua à Salino principio interno coagulata. Jüngken Chym: Exper: p.286. Aqua peculiari quadam materia subtiliori imbuta, & Spiritu quodam coagulata. Bernhard: Palisçy, Tractat: Gall: de Orig: Metall: Lapid: & Font: Crystallum, ut alios lapides vult produci ex aqua congelante, per quam, explicante Sorello, nihil aliud quàm Salem intelligit, aut aliquam substantiam lapidificam. Jungimtus his Kircherum, qui Mund: subt: L.VIII.S.I.p.19. Gemmarum atque Crystallorum Genesin sequentibus inter alia verbis exprimit: In montibus, ubi plurimùm purgatissimi Salis intra concava montium tium latet, fit, ut calore subterraneo agente, alia Salina corpora per Vaporem Salinum, & ab omnibus aliis grossioribus partibus purgatissimum eleventur, qui per intimas terrarum rimas exaltati, ubi sympathicum illis subjectum reperiat, ibidem etiam naturae quodam interveniente magnetismo, partium similium ad partes similes attractus consurgat, quae paranympho spiritu coagulativo, dum miro conjugio copulantur, inde tandem Crystallus illa diaphana, ex unione diaphanorum corpusculorum nascitur. Qui pro fundamento consistentiae, & soliditatis terram, vel solam, vel cum sale adscisc unt[?] illi Crystalli etiam productionem inde derivant; Ita Franc: Rueus de Gemm: Ort: L.I.C.I.p.175. Lapides pellucidi ex aqua praesertim consistunt, cui subtilis quaedam terrea, nec obscura materia immixta est, ut in Crystallo, glaciei speciem plane referente videre est, Et Le Febure Chym: P.II.p.522. Crystallus constat ex purissima quadam terra, & paucula aqua, quae terram vi Salis appropriati, sive in se contenti, & lapidescentis fermenti dissolvit.
units.tr: {A} Others indeed recognise water, or some pure juice, as the matter, but as the efficient agent they name a spirit, which the authors just cited call Gorgonean or petrifying, and mark with the title of a coagulating salt. Thus Theophrastus Paracelsus, in the fragment on the diseases of the gall, chapter c, holds that crystal took its substance and coagulation from the transparency of glaciated salt; and in his work On Meteors, p. 87: crystals are generated from water, which water, or matter, has in itself a coagulating spirit that coagulates at once. Hertodt agrees, in his Tartaro-Mastix of Moravia, p. 62, conceiving the genesis of this stone thus: crystal does not arise from the purest waters of melted snows, turned into crystal by the force of a coagulating spirit, but rather, since the earth is endowed with saline and nitrous spirits, etc., which, turned into vapour by subterranean fire and raised through the inmost and insensible fibres of the earth, when they fall upon clods swollen with salt, are suddenly lifted up by a certain magnetism; the subtler parts flow together to like parts, and since all of these are most subtle and transparent, they, united in a fitting place, coalesce into a crystalline substance, the petrifying spirit inherent in them cooperating. And the already cited most excellent Dr. König, Royal Mineralogy, part 2, chapter 6, p. 104, seems to ascribe to crystal a certain watery birth, which, pregnant with dissolved sandy particles, is fixed more firmly by a certain austere salt and passes into such a transparent body. Ettmüller, Schröder's Dilucidation of Mineralogy, p. 223: crystal is the simplest water, coagulated by an internal saline principle. Jüngken, Chemical Experiments, p. 286: water imbued with a certain peculiar and subtler matter and coagulated by a certain spirit. Bernard Palissy, Treatise on the Origin of Metals, Stones and Springs, wants crystal, like other stones, to be produced from congealing water, by which, as Sorellus explains, he means nothing other than salt, or some petrifying substance. To these we join Kircher, who in Mundus Subterraneus, book 8, section 1, p. 19, expresses the genesis of gems and crystals among other words thus: in mountains, where a great deal of very pure salt lies hidden within the hollows of the mountains, it comes about that, with subterranean heat acting, other saline bodies are lifted up by saline vapour, purged most thoroughly of all the other grosser parts; these, raised through the inner cracks of the earth, where they find something sympathetic to them, there too, by a certain magnetism of nature intervening, rise by attraction of like parts to like parts; and these, when with a wondrous marriage they are joined, the coagulating spirit serving as bridesmaid, at last crystal is born, that transparent thing, from the union of transparent corpuscles. Those who take earth, either alone or with salt, as the foundation of consistency and solidity, derive the production of crystal from this as well. Thus Franciscus Ruaeus, On the Origin of Gems, book 1, chapter 1, p. 175: transparent stones consist chiefly of water, in which a certain subtle earthy matter, not obscure, is mixed, as may be seen in crystal, which plainly resembles ice. And Le Febure, Chemistry, part 2, p. 522: crystal consists of a very pure earth and a little water, which the earth dissolves by the force of a salt appropriate to it, or contained within it, and of a petrifying ferment.

units.la: Ab ipso fluido in solidam substantiam mutato, Crystallum deduxit Gabriel. Fallop: de Metallis & Fossil: C.VIII.p.108. Cujus philosophandi genus vere Scholasticum ut eo magis patescat, propria ejus verba adducere non pigebit, ita autem ille: Quod humidum totum aliquando in terreum mutetur, & retineat suam luciditatem, argumento est Crystallus, quae, quamvis tota terrestris sit, tamen lucida est, quia humidum redundans totum est transmutatum, quia si Crystallus comburatur, nihil humidi resudat, & generatur tantum cineris, quanta erat quantitas Crystalli. Igitur qui consumptionem humidi superabundantis intelligentis transmutationem illius humidi in terram, quae transmutatio fit ab intenso frigore, & siccitate, quae secum juncta est, humidum autem illud in terram transmutatum reservat pristinam luciditatem, & miscetur cum aliis partibus terreis, & fit lapillus pretiosus.
units.tr: Gabriel Fallopius, in his work on metals and fossils, chapter 8, page 108, derives crystal from the fluid itself, changed into a solid substance. Since his way of philosophising is truly scholastic, it will be clearer if I do not hesitate to give his own words. He writes: "That a moist substance is sometimes changed entirely into earth and yet keeps its clarity is shown by crystal. Although crystal is wholly earthy, it is nevertheless clear, because the surplus moisture has been wholly transformed. For if crystal is burned, no moisture oozes out, and only ash is produced, equal in quantity to the crystal itself. Therefore, whoever understands the consumption of the superabundant moisture as its transformation into earth, a change brought about by intense cold and by the dryness that is joined with it, will see that this moisture, changed into earth, keeps its former clarity, mixes with the other earthy parts, and becomes a precious stone."

units.la: Recentiores Philosophi celebriores, licet lapides vulgares, vel etiam pretiosos opacos ex arenulis tanquam totidem filiculis, iisque nunc crassioribus, nunc subtilioribus coaluisse dicant, tamen circa lapides pellucidos, quales sunt Crystalli nostrae, & gemmae pleraeque, aliter sentiunt, tales nempe e fluido concrevisse, quamvis paradoxon videatur, solidissima atque durissima corpora, aliquando fuisse fluida vel liquores. Et speciatim Robert: Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virt: Totus in id incumbit, ut demonstret fluiditatem primam gemmarum, argumenta desumens solidissima, ut p.2. I. A diaphaneitate, quum non probabile sit, corpora, quae nunquam fuere fluida, ita ordinate dispositis gaudere partibus constituentibus, prout pellucidi-tas requirit; quam quae aliquando substiterunt in forma liquida, qua durante radii lucis facile poterant quaqua penetrare, & solida corpuscula disponere, modo ad constitutionem pellucidi corporis requisito. II. Ab externa figuratione, cum non facile imaginatu sit, quomodo gemma acquirat concinnam, angularem & determinatam figuram, absque quo è fluido concrevit, vel liquido circumdatum, vel magna ejus parte contiguum fuerit. Quod argumentum p.6. porrò confirmat, Ex coalitione duorum vel plurium istius generis lapidum, quam nonnunquam observavi, & congruitate figurae nonnullorum cum figuris illarum partium aliorum, quae eis contiguae erant, & post formatae videbantur. III. Ab interna textura gemmarum, quarum quaedam videntur in sua coagulatione (ex particulis exiguis per convenientem juxta positionem invicem associatis & harum rursus e planis, & maximè tenuibus lamellis S. bracteis) imitari diversas substantiarum illarum, quae pro certo aliquando fuerunt fluidae. IV. p.8. A coloribus gemmarum, quorum plerique omnino videntur esse adventitii illisque participati, sive à succo quodam minerali colorato, sive à quadam minerali exhalatione tingendi virtute praedita, quoad gemma erat vel in solutis principiis, vel constabat ex textura satis aperta, ut per eam penetrarent vapores minerales. Hoc autem argumentum illustrat ex diversis observationibus ab ipso factis, ut, quòd multae gemmae colore suo priventur, si nimis diu in igne jacuerint, imò omnes exceptis Granatis Bohemicis; Quòd colores diversarum gemmarum igne possint alterari, si non destrui, quòd plurimis locis in quibus reperiuntur gemmae coloratae, vicinae sint fodinae minerales, seu venae metallorum, imò gemmae ipsae nonnunquam reperiantur in ipsis venis metallicis; quòd ex quibusdam gemmis per menstrua obtineri possint tincturae, seu verae extractiones; Quòd gemmae, ad eandem speciem gemmariis relatae, possint diversissimis coloribus esse tinctae, ut Sapphiri albae, coerulea &c. quòd tandem reperiantur nonnunquam gemmae partim tinctae, partim colore carentes, quasi tingens pigmentum commixtum uni parti materiae, ex qua lapis constabat, dum esset liquidus vel mollis, non satis copiosus fuerit, ut se diffunderet in totum, & omni illi portioni, quam tingit, praeberet aequè intensum colorem. V. p.14. Quòd diversae eedem pellucidae gemmae sibi habent commixta metallica, vel alia extranea mineralia corpora per minima, unde rationi maximè conveniens judicat, ejusmodi mixturam fuisse perfectam, mixtis corporibus existentibus fluidis, siquidem conceptu difficile sit, qua alia ratione, corpuscula metallica fuerint deducta in gemmas, adeoque compacta, seu solida & dura corpora, & contrà facillimum comprehensu sit, quomodo inter metalla & lapides compactae fuerint mixturae adeò exquisitae, Hypothesi de fluiditate admissa. Quibus ultimò addit ex Anonymo Auctore Gallico Observationes curiosas, quòd in Indiis Orientalibus lapides gemmei ex petra aut locis vicinis extracti pulchro ut plurimum colore sint exornati, sed extracti ex terra participent de colore terrae in qua reperiuntur. Tandem, postquam opiniones aliorum, qui pro figura tam ordinata, & Geometrica explicanda ad facultatem quandam seminalem & plasticam, vel distinctum principium architectonicum confugiunt, refutasset p. 17. 18. ut & in Tract: de Orig: Form: & Qualitat: ostendit, corpora, tam gemmea quàm Salina, posse induere figuras illas, ex coalitione talium singulorum invisibilium corpusculorum, quæ per motum fluidi, cui innatabant, perque diversas circumstantias auxiliares determinentur, ut concurrant, vel cohæreant, hoc potius quàm alio modo. Consentiunt Boylio ex Recentioribus sanioribus plurimi, ex quibus nominasse sufficiat Fidum illum Cartesii Achatem, Anton: Le Grand: Princ: Philos: P.VI.p.312. Celeberrimum per orbem Eclecticum; Christ: Sturm: Phys: Conc: Part: Specialis: S.I. C.I. p.196. Et Stenon: Diss: Prod: Cit: p. 56--59.
units.tr: Among the more famous recent philosophers, although they say that common stones, and even precious stones that are opaque, have coalesced from tiny grains of sand, as it were, now coarser and now finer, yet concerning transparent stones, such as our crystals and most gems, they think otherwise. They hold that such stones have condensed from a fluid, although it may seem a paradox that the most solid and hardest bodies were once fluid or liquid. Robert Boyle, in his work on the origin and virtues of gems, especially labours to show the original fluidity of gems, drawing his arguments from the most solid things. (I) From transparency: since it is not probable that bodies which were never fluid should have their constituent parts so orderly arranged as transparency requires, whereas bodies that once stood in liquid form, while that form lasted, could easily let the rays of light penetrate every way and arrange the solid particles in the way needed for the structure of a transparent body. (II) From external shape: since it is not easy to imagine how a gem acquires a neat, angular and determinate shape unless it condensed from a fluid, or was surrounded by a liquid, or lay in contact with it for a large part of its surface. Page 6 further confirms this argument: "From the coalescing of two or more stones of this kind, which I have sometimes observed, and from the fit of the shape of some with the shapes of the parts of others that were contiguous to them and seemed to have been formed afterwards." (III) From the internal texture of gems, some of which seem, in their coagulation (from tiny particles, united by suitable mutual position, and these again from flat and very thin plates or leaves), to imitate those various substances that were certainly once fluid. (IV) Page 8: From the colours of gems, most of which seem to be wholly adventitious and imparted to them, whether from some coloured mineral juice or from a mineral exhalation endowed with the power of dyeing, provided the gem was either in dissolved principles or consisted of a texture open enough for mineral vapours to penetrate through it. He illustrates this argument with various observations made by himself: that many gems lose their colour if they lie too long in fire, indeed all of them except the Bohemian garnets; that the colours of various gems can be altered by fire, if not destroyed; that in most places where coloured gems are found, mineral mines or veins of metals are nearby, and gems themselves are sometimes found in the metal veins; that from some gems tinctures, or true extracts, can be obtained by means of solvents; that gems belonging to the same species can be dyed in very different colours, as white, blue and so on sapphires; and finally that gems are sometimes found partly tinted and partly colourless, as if the tinging pigment, mixed into one part of the matter of which the stone consisted while it was liquid or soft, was not abundant enough to spread through the whole and give equally strong colour to every portion it tints. (V) Page 14: that the same transparent gems have metallic or other foreign mineral bodies mixed in them in very minute amounts. Hence he judges it most reasonable that such a mixture was made perfect while the mixed bodies were fluid, since it is hard to conceive by what other means metallic corpuscles could have been brought into gems and so compacted into solid and hard bodies, whereas, once the hypothesis of fluidity is admitted, it is very easy to understand how such exquisite mixtures of metals and stones were formed.
