Finally he adds, from an anonymous French author, curious observations: that in the East Indies, gemstones extracted from rock or from nearby places are for the most part adorned with a beautiful colour, but those extracted from earth take on the colour of the earth in which they are found. At last, after refuting, on pages 17 and 18, the opinions of others who, to explain such orderly and geometrical figures, take refuge in a certain seminal and plastic faculty or a distinct architectonic principle, he also shows in his Tract on the Origin, Form and Qualities that bodies, both gemlike and saline, can take on those figures from the coalition of such single invisible corpuscles, which are determined by the motion of the fluid in which they floated, and by various auxiliary circumstances, so as to come together or cohere in this way rather than in another. Most of the saner recent writers agree with Boyle, among whom it is enough to name that faithful Achates of Descartes, Antoine Le Grand, Principles of Philosophy, part 6, page 312, the most celebrated Eclectic in the world; Christoph Sturm, Physics, Concerning Particular Parts, section 1, chapter 1, page 196; and Steno, Dissertation Prodromus, cited, pages 56-59.

units.la: Causam efficientem materiam ad Crystallinam formam & duritiem disponentem quòd spectat, ex hactenus allatis Auctorum textibus palàm fit, Alios præcipuas partes tribuere frigori; Alios calori, seu solari, seu subterraneo; Alios utrumque conjungere; Alios tandem & astra in subsidium vocare, sicuti huc adduci meretur locus in Christi. Vielbeur: descript: Mater: exot: p.34. Ex hisce, inquit, (aquis mineralibus,) à Saturno generatur, Crystallus, cum suo frigido ascendentali; Si exaltatio Saturni, Cœlo sereno, & conjunctionem cum Luna faciat, fiunt Crystalli clarissimi, sin vero nebuloso, & conjunctionem cum Marte instituat, non adeò diaphani producuntur.
units.tr: As far as the efficient cause that disposes matter to the crystalline form and hardness is concerned, it is clear from the texts of the authors cited so far that some assign the chief part to cold, others to heat, whether solar or subterranean, others join both, and others at last call the stars to help. The passage in Christoph Vielbeur, Description of Exotic Materials, page 34, deserves to be cited here. He says: "From these (mineral waters) crystal is generated by Saturn, with its cold ascendant. If Saturn's exaltation, with a clear sky, makes a conjunction with the Moon, the clearest crystals are produced; but if the sky is cloudy and he makes a conjunction with Mars, they are produced not very transparent."

units.la: Variis nunc Auctorum variorum expositis de Crystalli generatione opinionibus, modestam de his omnibus subjungam ἐπιχείρησιν[?], & diversa sententiarum, ubi id fieri licet; conciliabo, reliqua pauciora, minùs vera visa, levi censoriâ virgulâ perstringam. Atque primùm, eos quòd attinet, qui Crystalli originem ex Glacie, vel aqua glaciata petunt, videntur illi à vero quàm maximè aberrare, & falsa similitudinis niti hypothesi, quum ex vulgato veriverbio, simile non sit idem; & exactiùs rem ponderanti plures omnino obveniant Crystalli & glaciei differentiæ, quàm convenientiæ. Ut autem rationes, quæ falsitatem hujus opinionis ostendunt, ordine disponam, Dico I. Ex illorum Hypothesi, nullibi posse reperiri Crystallos, nisi ubi perpetua nive tecta sunt montium cacumina, vel saltem in annos absque liquefactione durant, cùm tamen certum sit, & indubiis, tam Veterum, quàm Recentiorum testimoniis comprobatum, in calidissimis etiam Asiæ, Africæ & Americæ, imò sub zona torrida sitis regionibus Crystallos reperiri. Licèt Garcias ab Horto L.I.C.47. Nullam per universam Indiam Crystallum reperiri velit; & inde forte Salmas: in Solin: p.143, Per totam Indiam non nasci asserat. Cùm tamen ipse Plin: Hist: Nat: L.37.C.2. Orientem Crystallum mittere, & Indicæ nullam præferri scripserit. Ex Recentioribus tradit Robert: Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virt: p.26. Madagascar, aliásque regiones zonæ torridæ abundant. abundare Crystallo. Et Vietheurn[?]: descript: Exot: p.33. In India Occidentali montes Crystalliferos reperiri asserit prope flumen Winacopora, quod se exundat in Oranke, & fluit supra cacumen montis Crystalliferi. Item in Peking, Provincia China. Neuhof Sinische Reis-Beschreibung. p.303. Zei-lonenses etiam Crystallos memorant Act: Lips: S. p.40. Ast quid opus plura hanc in rem afferre testimonia, cum nemo non gemmarum durissimarum & pretiosissimarum loca natalia agnoscat sub ipsa Zona torrida, quae tamen ejusdem omnino videntur, & sunt, cum Crystallo speciei, & Originis, & ab hac non nisi duritie differunt. Ut jam taceam, reperiri Crystallos in profundissimis etiam fodinis metallicis, ubi tamen calor potius quam frigus regnat, vel saltem glaciei & aquae congelatae nullus conceditur locus. II. Quod in ipsis montibus, quos a glacie perpetua ibi existente sine dubio Glaciales, sive Gletscheros nominant Helvetii, reperiantur Crystalli, non statim inferre licet, eas ex tali glacie nasci, quid? Quod potius ex hac Hypothesi sequeretur integras rupes & corpora, glacialia in Crystallum abire, quod tamen experientiae omnino est contrarium, sicuti in testem Helmont: Invent:Tart:N:14. adducit Paracelsum. Immemorem se in suis Helvetiorum rupibus vidisse glaciem immani frigore forte a mille annis constrictam jacere, nec tamen Crystallum esse, sed permanere glaciem, ut ab initio. Ipse ego, dum montes hos glaciales curiositatis ergo invisi, experientia didici, glaciem inveteratam, & ante plura forte secula induratam, durissimam quidem esse & difficulter exscindi, liquescere tamen statim, licet recente tardius, atque ita diffluere, ut nihil solidi, lapidei remaneat; Oculatus item testis sum, non effodi Crystallos ex ipsa glacie inveterata, vel sub glacialibus illis rupibus, nisi forte raro, sed e Saxis & cavernis inde haud longe distantibus, atque ibi nonnisi magna vi & ferro avelli; Ut hinc III. Argumenti loco pateat ingens inter Crystallum & glaciem differentia, dum haec per mille licet annos a nova jugiter adnascente ei impacta, tamen levi igne liquefit, illa autem fere nulla ignis vi dissolvi potest, & citius calcinationem, quam liquefactionem subit. Inter rarissima quippe, imo casualia, qualia Alchymistis plura sunt, experimenta numeratur illud Joachim: Beccher Phys: Subt: L. I. S.III. C.2. p.144. Cui contingit, inquit, quod Crystallum solveremus. Operationem ipsam non adjungit, sed facti duntaxat veritatem insinuat, hanc solam addens circumstantiam, quod solvente, sive menstruo abstracto, in fundo vasis remanserit Crystallus pellucidissima gelatinosae consistentiae, cerae adinstar tractabilis, & levi igne solubilis. Rarissimum hoc esse Phaenomenon, ipsa, quam mox subjungit, exclamatio, Viri in Chymica arte aliās versatissimi, satis superque testatur. Mirum profecto producium! quod etiamnum miraculi instar apud nos servamus. IV. Accedit alia glaciem à Crystallo discernens Circumstantia, quòd illa aquæ supernatet, hæc, ut omnes alii lapides, inferiora, sive fundum petat; Id quod equidem omnibus notum, & expertu facile est. Exactius tamen & Hydrostaticè examinavit Rob: Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virt: p.26. in Crystallo petrosa prorsus pellucida, & colore omni carente (ut probabilem præberet rationem arbitrandi, illam destitutam esse mixturis adventitiis) atque tenera bilance examinato ejus pondere in aere, deinde in aqua, comperit pondus ejus ad pondus aquæ æqualis quantitatis eandem habere rationem, quàm 2. & fere 2/3 ad 1. atque vel hoc solo concludit, quàm leviter & sine ratione multi viri literati, cùm Antiqui, tum Recentiores, statuant, Crystallum non esse nisi glaciem diuturno & vehementi gelu extraordinariè duratam, cùm tamen quantitas glaciei sit levior æquali quantitati aquæ. V. Figuræ regularitas in gemmis & Crystallis conspicua, hanc de Ortu ex glacie opinionem, si non prorsus evertit, non parùm tamen infringit, cùm ad figuræ tam ordinatæ, & Geometricæ productionem requiratur, vel moduli aptitudo, vel ipsius materiæ ad eam dispositio, quorum tamen neutrum, de glacie, vel aqua conglaciata dici potest, & porrò conceptu difficile, imò, verè dicam, impossibile sit, quomodo sive glacies, sive aqua lateribus, & parietibus saxorum ita adhærescant, ut figura prodeat & identitas, & regularitas. VI. Tandem, convellendæ huic opinioni inservit scintillarum emissio in Crystallorum percussione observabilis, quæ in glacie indurata, vel aqua congelata concipi vix potest, & sulphuris inexistentiam necessariò infert, licèt Sulphur Crystallorum purius sit, subtilius, & minùs terrestre, quàm quod Silicibus inest, quia minùs fœtidum, & scintillæ clariores, minusque coloratæ sunt.
units.tr: Having now set out the various opinions of different authors on the generation of crystal, I will add a modest attempt at reconciliation [ἐπιχείρησιν] of all of them, and where it is possible I will bring the differing views together. The few remaining opinions, which seem less true, I will touch on briefly with a light critical stroke. First, as to those who derive the origin of crystal from ice, or frozen water, they seem to me to stray very far from the truth and to rest on a false hypothesis of resemblance, since, as the common saying goes, a likeness is not identity; and when the matter is weighed more carefully, there turn out to be far more differences between crystal and ice than similarities. To set out in order the arguments that show the falsity of this opinion, I say: I. On their hypothesis, crystals could be found nowhere except where the mountain peaks are covered with perpetual snow, or at least where they last for years without melting. Yet it is certain, and proved by the unquestionable testimony of both the Ancients and the Moderns, that crystals are found even in the very hot regions of Asia, Africa and America, indeed in lands lying under the torrid zone. Garcias ab Horto, book 1, chapter 47, is willing to say that no crystal is found anywhere in the whole of India; and from this perhaps Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 143, asserts that it does not grow throughout India. Yet Pliny, Natural History, book 37, chapter 2, wrote that the East sends crystal, and that none is preferred to Indian crystal. Among the Moderns, Robert Boyle, On the Origin and Virtues of Gems, p. 26, reports that Madagascar and other regions of the torrid zone abound in crystal. And Vietheurn[?], Description of Exotic Things, p. 33, asserts that in the West Indies there are crystal-bearing mountains near the river Winacopora, which overflows into the Oranke and flows over the summit of a crystal-bearing mountain. Likewise in Peking, in the province of China, Neuhof, Sinische Reis-Beschreibung, p. 303. The Ceylonese too are recorded as having crystals, Acta Lipsiensia, p. 40. But why bring more testimonies to this point, when everyone recognises that the native places of the hardest and most precious gems lie right under the torrid zone? These gems are clearly of the same kind and origin as crystal, and differ from it only in hardness. Not to mention that crystals are found even in the deepest metal mines, where heat rather than cold reigns, and where at least no place is allowed for ice or frozen water. II. From the fact that crystals are found in the mountains themselves, which the Swiss call Glaciales or Gletscheros, because of the perpetual ice that is there without doubt, it does not follow at once that crystals are born of such ice. Indeed, what would follow from this hypothesis is that whole rocks and icy masses turn into crystal, which is completely contrary to experience. As a witness, Helmont, Inventa Tartarea, no. 14, cites Paracelsus, who says that he had seen in his Swiss rocks ice that had perhaps lain for a thousand years, bound by an immense cold, and yet it was not crystal but remained ice, as it was at the beginning. I myself, when I visited these glacial mountains out of curiosity, learned by experience that the ice, long hardened and perhaps indurated over many centuries, is indeed very hard and can be cut out only with difficulty, yet it melts at once, though more slowly if it is fresh, and so runs away until nothing solid or stony remains. I was also an eyewitness that crystals are not dug out of the old ice itself, or from under those glacial rocks, except perhaps rarely; they are taken from rocks and caverns not far from there, and even then they can be pried loose only with great force and iron tools. Hence, III. as an argument, the great difference between crystal and ice becomes plain: ice, though it has been for a thousand years and is constantly joined to new ice that is added to it, nevertheless melts with a gentle fire, whereas crystal can scarcely be dissolved by any force of fire, and it undergoes calcination sooner than liquefaction. Among the very rare, indeed accidental, experiments of the kind there are many for the Alchemists, and the following is counted among them: Joachim Becher, Physica Subterranea, book 1, section 3, chapter 2, p. 144. He says: "It happened to us that we dissolved crystal." He does not add the procedure itself, but only hints at the truth of the fact, adding this one circumstance: "that, with the solvent, or menstruum, drawn off, there remained at the bottom of the vessel a most transparent crystal of a jelly-like consistency, workable like wax and soluble with a gentle fire." That this is a most rare phenomenon is amply attested by the exclamation that he immediately adds, from a man otherwise most versed in the chemical art: "Truly a wonderful product! which we still keep among us as a kind of miracle." IV. Another circumstance that distinguishes ice from crystal is that ice floats on water, whereas crystal, like all other stones, sinks to the bottom. Everyone knows this, and it is easy to test. Yet Robert Boyle, On the Origin and Virtues of Gems, p. 26, examined it more precisely and hydrostatically, in a rock crystal wholly transparent and free of all colour (so as to give a probable reason for thinking that it was free of any foreign admixtures). Having weighed its weight in air with a delicate balance, and then in water, he found that its weight was to the weight of an equal quantity of water in the ratio of about 2 and 2/3 to 1. From this alone one can conclude how lightly and without reason many learned men, both ancient and modern, hold that crystal is nothing but ice, hardened by long and severe frost, when in fact a given quantity of ice is lighter than an equal quantity of water. V. The regularity of figure visible in gems and crystals, if it does not entirely overturn this opinion about origin from ice, at least weakens it considerably. For the production of so orderly and geometrical a figure requires either a suitable mould or a disposition of the matter itself to receive it; yet neither of these can be said of ice or of water frozen solid. Moreover, it is difficult to conceive, indeed, to speak truly, impossible, how either ice or water could cling to the sides and walls of the rocks in such a way that a figure, its sameness, and its regularity should result. VI. Finally, the emission of sparks observable when crystals are struck serves to overthrow this opinion. This can hardly be conceived in hardened ice or frozen water, and it necessarily implies the existence of sulphur, although the sulphur of crystals is purer, finer and less earthy than that which is in flints, because it is less foul-smelling, and its sparks are brighter and less coloured.

units.la: Reliquas quòd attinet Auctorum citatas opiniones, sunt illæ potius maximam partem ἐναυλιοφανεῖς[?], quàm reapse invicem oppositæ, & quia generaliter duntaxat rem exprimunt, facilè inter se & nobiscum conciliandæ; sive enim Crystalli dicantur ortum traxisse ex aqua, sive ex succo puro & purissimo, sive ex humore sui generis, sive ex terra & aqua, sive ab humido in terram mutato, sive ex unione diaphanorum corpusculorum per spiritum coagulativum, nobis perinde est, qui cum Boyle, & Recentioribus, gemmarum æquè ac Crystallorum è fluido ortum asserimus, facilè concedentes, quod sensus ipsi evincunt, humidum istud, sive fluidum, Scholastico loquendi more, in terram esse mutatum, sive, uti Recentiores exprimunt, in lapideam ac duram substantiam consolidatum. Circa causam concurrentem, & è fluido lapideam, sive Crystallinam duritiem efficientem, non erimus nec diffusi, nec scrupulosi, præsertim cum principium illud petrificum, nec quoad substantiam & structuram,nec quoad agendi modum ita fit ob oculos positum, ut nucleum potius,quàm corticem exinde attigisse dici queat animus curiosus,ut hinc non ullas intentemus lites Veteribus,lapidifico cuidam, vel petrifico succo,quem λιθοπηών[?] Græco idiomate vocabant,hanc operationem adscribentibus,vel Recentioribus,ad Chymica præsertim principia confugientibus, licèt & hi rem non eodem modo exponant. Ita Kirch: Mund: Subt: L.III. S.I.C.4. & 8. Liquorem & spiritum salinum statuit,& S.II. C.I. Succum nitrosum aquâ eliquatum: Daniel Major: Dissert: Epist:de Cancr. & Serpent: petrefactis. p.13. & 22. Sali in specie volatili, & ad statum fluoris jam redacto petrefactionem adscribit, adstipulante Philipp: Jacob: Sachs à Lövvenheim Diss: Respons: de admiranda lapidum natura. p. 65.. Philosophi Angli quidam Succum Calcarium sibi commendatum habent, plerique tamen ex illis Pyritam, sive succum vitriolicum, vel solum, vel cum lapide calcario subtili aura liquatum, ut Märt: Lifter: Præfat: Tract: de Cochlitis Angliæ, & Tract: de Therm: & Font: Med: Angl: C.VIII. p: 57. Erasm: Francisc: Im Vorgesprâch und Einleitung zu dem Ost-und West-Indischen/wie auch Chinesischen Lust-und Staats Garten. p.182. Sal, Nitrum, & Sulphur, pro petrificatione corporum inducit, ut illo pori corporis petrificandi aperiantur, isto repleantur, hoc humidum omne expellatur. Rob: Boyle tandem Hist: de Fluid: & Firmit: P.II. S. 72. & 73. Animalium, & ipsorum fluidorum in lapides conversionem fieri posse ostendit, à partium mutata structura, texturaque, exemplo aquarum, quæ quieti ad tempus permissæ fluere sponte desinunt, & in Saxum reipsa coagulantur, imò de Genm: Orig: & Virt: S.II. p.m. 46. 47. 48. 49. de ipsis etiam copiosis petrificis vaporibus in lapidem coagulari posse exemplis pluribus demonstrat. Nec nobis adversa est Antiquorum æquè ac Recentiorum è Peripato Philosophorum sententia, qui pro causa efficiente vel frigus, vel calorem admittunt. Cùm ex nostra Hypothesi nunc huic, nunc illi, nunc utrique ad hanc operationem accessus patet, & analogam Crystallisationi naturali Chymicam artificialem fieri. notum sit; æquè à constrictione pororum fluidi frigore induêta, ac evaporatione humidi per Ignem, sive calorem instituta. Quomodo tandem intelligat Crystalli è stellis nivosis Genefin Paracelsus, tam obscuris pro more expressit L. C. terminis, ut integri textus recensione Lectori tædio esse noluerim. Videtur autem ille, quantum conjectare licet, allusisse ad figuram nivis hexagonâ, & inde homogeneam Crystalli voluisse demonstrare, cùm tamen necunum, nec alterum probè & Philosophicè intellexerit, vel saltem scriptis ea non tradiderit, aut uti plurimis videtur, studio occultaverit, & rerum ejusdem figuræ possit, imò debeat sæpe concipi varia productio, sicuti id pluribus patescit ex Diff: Erasm: Bartholin:de Fig: Niv: Ut nunc taceam maximam omnino inter stellas nivosas sexangulares, & Crystallum hexagonam differentiam, & nullam ferè, nisi figuræ aliqualem duntaxat convenientiam. Vielheürn: tandem, Crystallorum productionem astrorum prædominio subjicientem, quòd attinet, eum intra pomœria Philosophiæ nostræ non admitto, usque dum, vel ipse, vel alii Astrologi; Astromantæ potius; influxum stellarum, & vires Conjunctionum vel Oppositionum &c. in hæc inferiora, solidioribus quàm hactenus argumentis demonstraverint. Propriam quòd attinet Hypothesin, quâ innixus Phænomena suprà recensita explicare conabor, ea non nova prorsus, & à suprà recensitis distincta est, sed ipsa, quam pleriq; Modernorum æquè ac Antiquorum ex humido, vel fluido derivant, quam speciatim Steno & Boyle, Viri in hoc rerum genere, ùt curiosissimi, ita subtilissimi, assumunt, ut proin-utriusque[?] textus, licèt diffusiores, suis quos vis locis recensere, iisque paginas nostras implere non pigeat.
units.tr: As for the other opinions of the authors cited, they are for the most part merely verbal [ἐναυλιοφανεῖς], rather than really opposed to one another. Since they express the matter only in general terms, they can easily be reconciled with each other and with us. Whether crystals are said to have arisen from water, from a pure and most pure juice, from a humour of their own kind, from earth and water, from something moist changed into earth, or from the union of transparent corpuscles through a coagulating spirit, it makes no difference to us. We, with Boyle and the more recent writers, maintain that gems as well as crystals arise from a fluid, and we readily concede what the senses themselves prove: that this moist or fluid substance, to use the Scholastic manner of speaking, has been changed into earth, or, as the more recent writers put it, has been consolidated into a stony and hard substance. As for the concurrent cause, the agent that makes the fluid into stony or crystalline hardness, we shall be neither diffuse nor scrupulous about it. This is especially so because that petrifying principle is not set so plainly before our eyes, either in its substance and structure or in its mode of action, that an inquiring mind could say it has reached the kernel rather than the rind. So we shall not pick quarrels with the Ancients, who ascribed this operation to a certain stone-making or petrifying juice, which they called λιθοπηών in Greek, nor with the more recent writers, who take refuge especially in chemical principles, although these too do not explain the matter in the same way. Thus Kircher, Mundus subterraneus, book III, section I, chapter 4 and 8, posits a liquor and a saline spirit, and section II, chapter I, a nitrous juice dissolved in water; Daniel Major, Dissertatio epistolaris de cancris et serpentibus petrefactis, pp. 13 and 22, ascribes petrifaction to salt especially volatile salt, reduced to the state of a flux, supported by Philipp Jakob Sachs von Lövenheim, Dissertatio responsoria de admiranda lapidum natura, p. 65. Some English philosophers hold that calcareous juice is to be commended to them, but most of them adduce pyrites, or vitriolic juice, either alone or with subtle calcareous stone dissolved in air, as Martin Lister, Praefatio to the tract De cochleis Angliae, and the tract De thermis et fontibus medicatis Angliae, chapter VIII, p. 57; Erasmus Francisci, In the preface and introduction to the East- and West-Indian as well as Chinese garden of pleasure and state, p. 182, introduces salt, nitre and sulphur for the petrifaction of bodies, so that the pores of the body to be petrified are opened by the first, filled by the second, and all its moisture driven out by the third. Finally, Robert Boyle, History of Fluidity and Firmness, part II, sections 72 and 73, shows that animals and their fluids can be converted into stones by a change in the structure and texture of their parts, using the example of waters which, when left at rest for a time, cease to flow of their own accord and really coagulate into rock. Indeed, in On the Origin and Virtues of Gems, section II, pp. 46–49, he demonstrates with many examples that even copious petrifying vapours can coagulate into stone. Nor does the opinion of the philosophers of the Peripatetic school, both ancient and recent, which admits cold or heat as the efficient cause, stand against us. For from our hypothesis it is plain that access to this operation is now by one, now by the other, and now by both, and that an artificial chemical process analogous to natural crystallisation is known. It is effected both by the constriction of the pores of a fluid induced by cold and by the evaporation of the moisture through fire or heat. As for how Paracelsus understood the origin of crystals from snowy stars, he expressed it in terms so obscure, as is his habit, in the passage I have cited, that I have not wished to weary the reader by reciting the whole text. He seems, as far as one may guess, to have alluded to the hexagonal shape of snow and to have wished from this to demonstrate the homogeneity of crystal. Yet he did not properly and philosophically understand either point, or at least did not hand them down in his writings, or, as most think, deliberately concealed them. Moreover, things of the same shape can and often must be produced in various ways, as is made clear to many from Erasmus Bartholin's dissertation De figura nivis. To say nothing for now of the very great difference between snowy six-cornered stars and hexagonal crystal, and of there being almost no resemblance beyond some slight similarity of shape. As for Vielheuer, who subjects the production of crystals to the predominance of the stars, I do not admit him within the boundaries of our philosophy, until either he or other astrologers (or rather astromancers) demonstrate the influence of the stars and the powers of conjunctions or oppositions upon these lower things by arguments more solid than any so far produced. As for our own hypothesis, on which I shall rely in trying to explain the phenomena recounted above, it is not entirely new, nor is it distinct from those recounted above. It is the very one which most of the moderns as well as the ancients derive from a moist or fluid substance, and which Steno and Boyle, men as subtle as they are curious in this kind of thing, specifically adopt. So I do not mind citing their texts at length, in whatever places you like, even if it fills our pages.

units.la: CAPUT V. Quo Phænomena Capite Tertio recensi- ta solvuntur.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. In which the phenomena set out in the third chapter are resolved.

units.la: I. INveniuntur Crystalli in Saxorum, Conchitarum, Cornuum Ammonis cavitatibus, in terra item, & collibus arenosis: Ut inde statim enascatur dubium de loco Crystalli Natali, in quo hi formentur; Manum autem ex hisce difficultatibus nos extricandi porrigere mihi videtur sororia artis & naturæ cognatio, i. e. Crystallisationem naturalem per Chymicam commodè illustrari, imò explicari posse, quum ex paritate effectûs jure inferatur identitas, vel saltem cognatio causæ, sicut jam olim Aretinus, & alii, exemplo Aluminis, Nitri &c. quæ post coctionem evaporato humido à terrestri materia in angulosas superficies congelantur probare annisus est, citante Boët. de Boot. p. 41. Ex hac autem operatione produci Crystallos non aliter quàm in fluido patet, sive nunc interveniat evaporatio liquoris sufficiens, sive constrictio pororum à frigore, sive repositio per aliquod tempus, sive aliud quid. Pari nunc modo videntur Crystalli naturales progigni, & materia earum colligi in fluido aqueo intra cavitates, seu Saxorum, seu luti, seu lapidum figuratorum contento; atque, ut exactiùs paulò hac de re loquar; placet mihi distinctio Stenoniana Diff: Prod:Cit:p.58. Inter locum, ubi prima concretio Crystalli incipit, & inter locum,ubi jam formata Crystallus crescit: de illo, an sit inter fluidum & solidum, an vero in ipso fluido,dubitat. Ego ex jactis modò fundamentis statuo postremum, inductus non solùm analogia Crystallisationis artificialis, sed & speciali Crystallorum utrinque acuminatarum Phænomeno, quod sanè explicari nequit, nisi in ipso fluido formatio concipiatur; quanquam nec productionis modum inter fluidum & fluidum improbaverim, imò cùm ultimo facilè conciliaverim. De loco verò, ubi jam formata Crystallus crescit, rectè statuit laudatus Auctor, esse solidum, qua parte Crystallus illi innititur; sive saxum sit, sive alia jam producta Crystallus, reliqua fluidum esse, si impedimenta tollas, quae ab inaequalitate saxi, vel aliis jam productis Crystallis, illi se offere poterunt. Ad objectionem autem, quam, circa locum productionis in cavitatibus Saxorum quaerendum, sibi ipsi movet, ex eo, quòd integri colles terrenâ materiâ constent Crystallis refertissimâ, ad nutum meum respondet. p.59. Quandoquidem in vicinia eorundem collium Saxei montes reperiantur, apti producendis Crystallis; & in ipsis collibus terrenæ materiæ insepulta eruantur majora Saxa à vicinis montibus avulsa; quorum quaedam fissuras ostendunt materiâ marmoreâ repletas, pari ratione ac in ipsis montibus saxeis stratorum fissuræ replentur, eadem autem causa, quæ à vicinis montibus avulsa stratorum fragmenta in colles devolvit, poterit itidem ex eorundem stratorum cavitatibus excussas Crystallos per eosdem colles disseminâsse. Interdum & aratro eruuntur, & in agris, Vineis, &c. colliguntur, haud dubiè, vel quia à possessore nihili aestimante rejectae, vel alio casu illuc delatae fuerunt. A torrentibus subinde deportantur, quatenus nimirum hi vel in montibus ortum ducunt, vel supra ipsa montium cacumina fluunt, Teste Vielheur: Descript: Exot: p.33. hocce modo secum vehunt & asportant. Crystalli adauctionem quòd spectat, appositè iterum Steno L.C. Crescit Crystallus, dum Crystalli jam delineatæ planis extremis apponitur nova materia Crystallina, quæ è parietibus lapidis continentis in cavitatem exsudare, vel sub vaporis specie exhalare potest, ut hinc rejicienda sit opinio eorum, qui autumant vegetando crescere, & nutrimentum attrahere, quo latere matrici adhaerent, adeoque à fluido saxi exceptas particulas, & in fluidum Crystalli transmissas, intrinsecus Crystalli particulis apponi. Ubi enim in Crystallo adsunt partes organicæ, vel succum nutritium vehentes, vel distendi aptæ? Ubi adsunt pori, vel canaliculi, per quos vel augeri possit plantarum, aut animalium instar Crystallus? Quòd autem Cocci minerales aliquando tanto crepitu disfringantur, & in minima dissiliant, rationem profert Fort: Licet: de Litheosph: C.52.p.265. Censeo, inquit, lapillos intra Coccum genitos esse à calore igneo, qui communisest causa lapidum omnium effectrix, sic autem calor in utero, cavitateve lapidis hujus maximè vigens, & vires suas exercens in humidam quampiam materiam eo loco residentem, ipsam attenuat in halitus; ac simul agens in terrenam consistentiam, ibidem majori libertate compertam, ex ea humidas exhalationes excutit, qui duo halitus ampliorem locum necessariò postulantes, quam habere valent intra caveam lapidis, ne detur corporum duorum invisa Naturæ penetratio, magno nisu lapidem diffringunt, ac veluti peculiari quodam terræmotu in lapide substantiam silicis aperiunt, & ipsam vi pellunt, excussa superjacente terra cum sonitu in aërem. Sed quia talis calor etiam vigere potest, & hujusmodi vapores & exhalationes multas procreare intra cavum lapidis, nondum lapillos illos alios in se gestantis, proinde fit, ut etiam inanes hujuscemodi lapides crepent, & ex terra sonantes in altum prosiliant. Non accidit autem hoc Aëtitibus, Ventribusque Crystallinis ab Imperato propositis, quia tanto non abundant interiore calore igneo, quanto est opus ad magnam vim exhalationum procreandam, quæ lapidem disrumpat, vel quia vulgares Aëtites obtinent porosum corpus, per cujus meatus, etsi visui non conspicuos, exeant sensim atque sensim halitus, qui generantur ab interno calore, qui longè major est in Indicis lapidibus, tum ratione temperaturæ, tum ratione majoris amplitudinis, & corpulentiæ densioris, poros non habentis, ullos ab interna cavæ superficie terminantes in exteriorem cutem, pervadentesque densiorem solidissimi lapidis consistentiam. Hæc Liceti verba, licèt fusiora, tanto lubentius recensere volui, quia opinionem fovent principiis Modernorum apprimè convenientem, ubi id saltem monendum, minùs recte adscribi calori interno intra lapidum cavitates conclusò, quod externo potius, seu solari, seu ignium subterraneorum debetur. Experimenta prostant analoga Æolipilæ, quæ aquâ admedietatem repleta, ac igni superpositâ disrumperetur omnino, si orificium occluderetur, & bullularum, seu sphærularum vitrearum, quæ itidem ad medietatem repletæ, & posteà hermeticè sigillatæ, si flammæ candelæ tamdiu exponantur, donec aquæ intus contenta in vapores abeat, cum sonitu sclopetorum æmulo disrumpuntur.
units.tr: I. Crystals are found in the cavities of rocks, of shells, and of ammonite horns, and also in the earth and in sandy hills, so that at once a doubt arises about the natural place where crystals are formed. It seems to me that a helping hand in extricating us from these difficulties is offered by the sisterly kinship of art and nature: natural crystallization can be well illustrated, and indeed explained, by chemistry, since from the parity of the effect one may rightly infer identity, or at least kinship, of cause. Long ago Aretinus and others, using the example of alum, nitre, and so on, which after boiling congeal from earthy matter into angular surfaces once the moisture has evaporated, tried to prove this, citing Boët. de Boot. p. 41. It is clear from this operation that crystals are produced only in a fluid, whether evaporation of enough liquor intervenes, or the pores are constricted by cold, or the liquor is left to stand for some time, or something else happens. In the same way, natural crystals seem to be generated, and their matter gathered, in an aqueous fluid contained within cavities, whether of rocks, of mud, or of figured stones. And to speak more precisely on this point, I am pleased with the distinction of Steno (Diff: Prod: Cit: p. 58) between the place where the first concretion of a crystal begins and the place where an already formed crystal grows. About the former he doubts whether it lies between fluid and solid or in the fluid itself. From the foundations just laid I hold the latter, moved not only by the analogy of artificial crystallization but also by the special phenomenon of crystals pointed at both ends, which cannot be explained unless their formation is conceived to occur in the fluid itself. Yet I would not reject the mode of production between fluid and fluid; indeed, I have readily reconciled it with the latter. As for the place where an already formed crystal grows, the author praised above rightly holds that "it is solid where the crystal rests upon it; the rest is fluid, if you remove the obstacles that may present themselves from the unevenness of the rock or from other crystals already produced." To the objection which he raises for himself, concerning where the production is to be sought within the cavities of rocks, namely that whole hills consist of earthy matter very full of crystals, he replies, to my liking: p. 59. "Since in the neighbourhood of those same hills there are rocky mountains fit for producing crystals; and in the hills themselves, among the earthy material, larger stones are dug up unburied, torn away from the nearby mountains, some of which show fissures filled with marble-like matter, just as the fissures of the strata are filled in the rocky mountains themselves. By the same cause which rolled fragments of strata torn from the nearby mountains down into the hills, the crystals shaken out of the cavities of those same strata could likewise have been scattered through the same hills." Sometimes they are dug up by the plough, and are gathered in fields, vineyards, and so on, no doubt either because they were thrown away by an owner who valued them at nothing, or because they were carried there by some other accident. Torrents sometimes carry them off, since these either rise in the mountains or flow over the very summits of the mountains, as Vielheur testifies, Descript. Exot. p. 33; in this way they carry and bear them away with them. As for the growth of a crystal, Steno again, in the same place, aptly says: "A crystal grows when fresh crystalline matter is applied to the flat ends of a crystal already outlined," which can exude from the walls of the containing stone into the cavity, or exhale in the form of vapour. Hence the opinion of those must be rejected who maintain that it grows by vegetation and draws nourishment, by which it adheres to its matrix at the side, and so that particles received from the fluid of the rock and passed into the fluid of the crystal are applied within the crystal's particles. For where in a crystal are there organic parts, or vessels carrying nutritive juice, or parts fit to be stretched? Where are there pores or little channels through which a crystal could be enlarged, as plants or animals are? As for why mineral nodules sometimes burst with such a crackling and split into tiny pieces, Fortunius Licetus (De Litheosphoris, c. 52, p. 265) gives this explanation: "I think," he says, "that the little stones generated within a nodule are caused by fiery heat, which is the common cause producing all stones. When such heat is at its strongest in the womb or cavity of this stone, and exerts its power on some moist matter residing in that place, it thins it into vapours; and at the same time, acting on the earthy substance found there in greater freedom, it shakes out moist exhalations from it. These two vapours, needing a larger space than they can have within the hollow of the stone, break the stone with great effort, lest there be a forbidden penetration of two bodies in nature, and, as if by a peculiar earthquake, they open the substance of the silex within the stone and drive it out by force, the overlying earth being thrown up into the air with a noise. But because such heat can also be active, and create many vapours and exhalations of this kind within the hollow of the stone, which does not yet contain those other little stones, it follows that even empty stones of this kind crack and leap up out of the earth with a sound. This does not happen to the eagle-stones and crystalline wombs put forward by Imperato, because they do not abound in so much internal fiery heat as is needed to generate a great quantity of exhalations to break the stone; or because common eagle-stones have a porous body, through whose passages, though invisible to sight, the vapours generated by the internal heat gradually escape. This heat is far greater in Indian stones, both by reason of temperature and by reason of greater size and denser bulk, which has no pores, and which closes off every internal cavity surface from the outer skin, and pervades the denser consistency of the very solid stone." I wished to record these words of Licetus, though lengthy, the more willingly because they favour an opinion most agreeable to the principles of the Moderns. Here it should at least be pointed out that it is less correct to ascribe this to the internal heat enclosed within the cavities of stones, which is rather due to external heat, whether of the sun or of subterranean fires. There are analogous experiments: the aeolipile, which, filled halfway with water and placed over the fire, would burst entirely if its opening were closed; and little glass bubbles, or spheres, likewise filled halfway and then sealed hermetically, which, if exposed to the flame of a candle until the water inside turns to vapour, burst with a noise like that of guns.

units.la: II. Figura Crystalli Hexagona multorum ingenia torsit, atque scopulus est, ad quem Scriptorum bene multi allidentes naufragium fecerunt. Negat Aretinus, & alii, figuram, ordinatam nempe, corporibus inanimatis inesse, quia fluida æquè ac solida figuris prædita esse observant, dicunt, illa cum per se fuerint rotunda fieri, aut à continente corpore figurari, hæc autem talia servari, qualia ex discissione fortuita prodeunt. In Crystalli autem productione divisionem admittunt, qualis sit in coagulatione, dum humida adhuc sunt corpora, & partes in diversa tendunt, fluida sursum, reflexa[?] ad fundum & latera, uniformem autem, sive regularem figuram produci ob puritatem, & æqualitatem succi lapidescentis, quam triplicem facit, triangularem, quadratam, & hexagonam, priores duas excludit, tertiam admittit, quia ad circuli naturam prope accedit. Hæc autem Aretini & assectatorum sententia cur mihi non satisfaciat indicabo.
units.tr: II. The hexagonal figure of crystal has tormented the minds of many, and is a rock on which quite a number of writers have struck and suffered shipwreck. Aretinus and others deny that a figure, namely an ordered one, is inherent in inanimate bodies, because they observe that fluids as well as solids are endowed with figures; they say that the former, when left to themselves, become round, or are shaped by a containing body, while the latter keep the shapes they come out with from fortuitous breaking. In the production of crystal, however, they admit a division of the kind found in coagulation, while the bodies are still moist and the parts tend in different directions: the fluid upwards, and the part that is reflected towards the bottom and sides. A uniform or regular figure, they say, is produced by the purity and evenness of the stony juice, and they make this threefold: triangular, square and hexagonal. They exclude the first two and admit the third, because it comes near to the nature of the circle. I will indicate why this opinion of Aretinus and his followers does not satisfy me.

units.la: Primo quidem, Opinio de Figura inanimatis deneganda nititur falsa Aristotelicorum, Latinorum præsertim, Hypothesi, Animas, Vegetativam in plantis, Sensitivam in brutis, figuras corporum illorum organicorum formare, cùm, excusso de animarum, quæ formæ nominis ipsis veniebant, prærogativa præjudicio, compertum nobis sit, figuram nullius plantulæ aut bruti, utpote intellectum atque ingenium spirantem, ab extenso quopiam, quale quid sunt animæ corporum animatorum, posse produci, sicuti id fusius ostenderem, si per tempus liceret. Falsum item est, inanimatis corporibus non aliam tribui debere figuram, quàm quæ ex divisione fortuita emergit, & vel exemplo Crystallisationis artificialis demonstrabile, solida à fluidis orta, juxta leges motûs naturæ impressas diversimodè & regulariter posse figurari, anima nulla, vel facultate, sive formativam eam nuncupes, sive αὐξητικήν, crescitivam, in subsidium vocata, cùm alias id genus facultatum nomina Modernis sint exosa. Hexagonam prodire figuram, quia ad circuli perfectionem propius accedit, precarium rursus est, & vel Mathesis Tyroni notum, figuras, quas vocant regulares, sive circulo sint inscriptibiles, sive circumscriptibiles, tantò propius ad circulum accedere, quantò plura habent latera, cùm hic rectissimè audiat polygonum infinitorum laterum & angulorum, ut hinc millecupla potius foret Crystalli figura, quàm hexagona, ea autem figuræ hexagonæ proprietas peculiaris, quòd latera sint æqualia, & centrum ab angulis & cujusque lateris medietate æquidistans, huc non quadrat, & paucissimis, imò forsan nullis, competit Crystallis; Ac posito etiam, hanc circulari esse præ aliis cognatam, nondum tamen positiva adest ratio, cur vel quomodo hæc Crystalli figuratio contingat.
units.tr: First, the opinion that figure must be denied to inanimate things rests on the false hypothesis of the Aristotelians, especially the Latin ones, that the souls, the vegetative soul in plants and the sensitive soul in brutes, form the figures of those organic bodies. For once the prejudice about the prerogative of souls, which were called forms, is set aside, it is clear to us that the figure of no little plant or beast can be produced from something extended, as souls are for animate bodies, since it breathes intellect and talent. I would show this more fully if time allowed. It is also false that inanimate bodies should be given no other figure than that which emerges from fortuitous division. This can be shown even by the example of artificial crystallisation: solids arising from fluids, according to the laws of motion impressed on nature, can be figured in various and regular ways, with no soul or faculty called in to help, whether you call that faculty formative or αὐξητικήν [auxētikēn], the crescitive faculty, since the Moderns detest that kind of faculty-name. That a hexagonal figure arises because it comes nearer to the perfection of the circle is again a precarious claim, and known even to a beginner in mathematics. The figures called regular, whether they can be inscribed in or circumscribed about a circle, come closer to the circle the more sides they have, and the polygon of infinitely many sides and angles is rightly spoken of here. Hence the figure of a crystal would be a thousand-sided figure rather than a hexagonal one. The peculiar property of the hexagonal figure, that its sides are equal and its centre is equidistant from the angles and from the middle of each side, does not fit here, and belongs to very few crystals, or perhaps to none. And even granting that this figure is more akin to the circle than the others, there is still no positive reason why or how this figuration of crystal comes about.

units.la: In diversa abit Boët: de Boot: p.44.45. & 220. Dum figurationem Crystalli Sali copiâ terrestrem materiam vincenti attribuit, quòd evaporato ex parte aqueo humido in angulos concrescat cum materia terrestri sibi unita. Cur verò ipsa salia in Hexagonam figuram abeant, difficile vult esse conjectu, exististimat tamen, quia salia homogeneæ naturæ non sunt, sed ex diversis partibus composita, omnes in congelatione ad medium quoddam, ubi initium coagulationis fit, ut eò uniantur, tendere, ac sic rotundam figuram tanquam perfectissimam ambire, sed in eo conatu heterogeneas partes, & quæ cæteris subtiliores, vel magis aereæ sunt, vel tardius ad medium properare, & in angulis relinqui, vel à reliquis ad angulos pelli, ac sic hexagonam figuram oriri, ut pote circulari proximam
units.tr: He departs from this view in Boët. de Boot, pp. 44–45 and 220, where he ascribes the figuring of crystal to a quantity of salt overcoming the earthy matter, because, with the watery moisture partly evaporated, it concretes into angles united with the earthy matter. Why salts themselves pass into a hexagonal figure, he thinks hard to conjecture, yet he suspects that since salts are not of a homogeneous nature but composed of different parts, all of them in congealing tend towards a certain middle point, where coagulation begins, so as to unite there and thus embrace the round figure as the most perfect. In that effort, however, the heterogeneous parts, and those finer than the rest or more airy, either arrive more slowly at the middle and are left behind in the angles, or are driven from the others to the angles; and so a hexagonal figure arises, as being nearest to the circular.

units.la: {*} Hæc Aretini & ... ximam. Tandem, postquam hexagonæ figuræ proprietates fusiùs commendavit, ingenuè fatetur, sibi non plane satisfacere, & naturam Crystallo hexagonam figuram dedisse autumat, non secus quàm arborum frondibus, & herbarum floribus peculiares figuras suas dat, quæ ab Architectonico Spiritu & formatrice facultate, ignoto nobis modo fabricantur. De hac Boëtii sententia, ut ingenuè quod sentio dicam, non me latet, Modernos plerosque, Chymicis præsertim principiis litantes, Ut Etthmyller: in Schröd: P.I. p.223: in figuratione non solùm Crystallorum, sed & quorumcunque lapidum figuratorum ad Sal, tanquam Sacram ancoram confugere. Verùm enim verò, cùm ipsa salia, considerirari debeant, & corpora figurata, & figuras, tam inter se, quàm à lapidibus figuratis, diversas habentia; Modus præterea, quo ad hanc vel illam figuram producendam hæc vel illa salia concurrant, ipsis hujus sententiæ patronis sit inexplicabilis, ad alia si confugiamus principia, nemo nobis vitio vertet, præsertim, cùm ipsorum etiam salium, quæ pro principio figurationis perperam illi agnoscunt, figuras earumque rationes geminas scire desideremus, atque hoc quod attinet subtiliter equidem ratiocinatur Boëtius, & in aliquibus consentit nobiscum, uti ex infrà dictis, cum citato Boëtii textu conferendis, melius patebit; Architectonicum tandem Spiritum & Formatricem facultatem cum aliis id genus speciosis nominibus, pro ignorantiæ habemus asylo; pluribus nunc ob brevitatem temporis non impugnando. Eandem quoque esse causam, quæ arborum frondes, herbarum flores, & Crystalli figuram producat, nimis longè petitum videtur, & ex modernorum, circa plantarum præsertim anatomen, institutis experimentis, & placitis, haud difficulter refutandum. Cæsalpino de Metall: L. II.C.19:p.96. De Crystalli figuratione eadem prorsus est cum Boëtio de Boot-mens, iisdem prorsus etiam verbis expressa.
units.tr: {*} These are the words of Aretinus and ... nearest. Finally, after he has praised the properties of the hexagonal figure at length, he frankly admits that he is not fully satisfied, and claims that nature gave crystal its hexagonal figure, just as it gives their particular shapes to the leaves of trees and the flowers of herbs, which are made by the Architectonic Spirit and the formative faculty in a manner unknown to us. As for this opinion of Boëtius, to say frankly what I think, I am not unaware that most of the moderns, especially those who cling to chymical principles, Ut Etthmyller: in Schröd: P.I. p.223: take refuge in salt, as in a sacred anchor, for the figuring not only of crystals but of all figured stones. But in truth, since salts themselves ought to be considered, both as bodies and as figures, and have figures different from one another and from figured stones; and since the manner in which these or those salts concur to produce this or that figure would be inexplicable even to the patrons of this opinion, if we take refuge in other principles, no one will blame us, especially as we also want to know the figures of the salts themselves, which they wrongly recognise as the principle of figuring. As far as this goes, Boëtius reasons subtly, and agrees with us in some points, as will be clearer from comparing what is said below with the cited text of Boëtius. As for the Architectonic Spirit and formative faculty, together with other such high-sounding names, we hold them as refuges of ignorance; I will not now refute them at length, for lack of time. That the same cause produces the leaves of trees, the flowers of herbs, and the figure of crystal seems far-fetched, and can be refuted without difficulty by the experiments and doctrines of the moderns, especially those concerning the anatomy of plants. Cæsalpino de Metall: L. II. C.19: p.96. On the figuring of crystal he is entirely in agreement with Boëtius de Boot-mens, and expresses it in virtually the same words.

units.la: Card: de Subt: L.VII.p.361. Opinionem, ab Ahton: Le Grand: Princ:: Philos: P.VI.p.313, quoque suffultam, quòd Crystalli sicuti, & apum capsulæ ab aliis circumdentur, adeóque & ipsæ hexagonæ sint, jam discussam videas à Scalig: de Subt: ad Card: Exerc.i.18. Quia non omnis Crystallus, sed infinita superficiebus ab alia tangitur, non autem ire liceat in infinitum, & mucrones Crystalloram itidem hexagoni ab aliis non tanguntur. Videtur hanc opinionem Cardano persuasisse conformitas figuræ hexagonæ cellularum in alvearibus apum, qui verò secum perpendit, quòd eadem figura in diversis subjectis, ex diversis possit oriri principiis, & insuper iis, quæ de hexagona favorum figura ex materiæ necessitate pura ad oculum demonstrabili, habet Eras: Bartholi: de Figur: Niv: p.18. vel parum attendit, statim luce clarius videbit, princi-pia. pia, ibi applicata Crystallo prorsus non quadrare eamque adeo ex aliis peti debere. Ipsa insuper conformitas figuræ favorum & Crystalli non haberi debet pro vera identitate, ibi enim est prisma hexagonum cavum absque pyramide iterum hexagona. Erasm: Bartholin: de Fig: Niv: p. 26. & 30. generatim quidem & incidenter de Crystallorum & Salium figuris regularibus judicat, vim internam motum partibus addere, partes quoque singulas pressas invicem figuram ordinare, speciatim autem, quod nos desideramus, nihil determinat, ut hic adeo verum, sed in genere tantum dixisse, salvo, quod de vi interna motum partibus addente formari posset, judicio, salvâque nostra Hypothesi infrà exponenda dici possit.
units.tr: Card: de Subt: L.VII. p.361. The opinion, also supported by Ahton: Le Grand: Princ. Philos: P.VI. p.313, that crystals, like the cells of bees, are surrounded by others and are therefore themselves hexagonal, you may already see discussed by Scalig: de Subt: ad Card: Exerc. i. 18. Because not every crystal is touched by another on all its surfaces, and one cannot go on to infinity, and the points of crystals are likewise hexagonal and are not touched by others. Cardan seems to have been persuaded of this opinion by the conformity of the hexagonal figure of the cells in beehives; but whoever weighs it for himself, that the same figure can arise in different subjects from different principles, and moreover from those things that Eras: Bartholi: de Figur: Niv: p.18. presents about the hexagonal figure of honeycombs, arising from the necessity of matter, demonstrable to the eye, if he pays even a little attention, will see at once, clearer than daylight, that these principles, applied there, do not at all fit crystal, and that its figure must therefore be derived from other causes. Moreover, the conformity between the figure of honeycombs and that of crystal should not be held to be a true identity, for there the hexagonal prism is hollow, without a pyramid that is again hexagonal. Erasm: Bartholin: de Fig: Niv: pp. 26 and 30. He does judge in general and incidentally about the regular figures of crystals and salts, that an internal force adds motion to the parts, and that the individual parts, pressed together, arrange the figure; but specifically, what we desire, he determines nothing, so that nothing here is true, but he has only said in general, saving the judgement that the figure could be formed by an internal force adding motion to the parts, and saving also our hypothesis, to be set out below, which can be stated.

units.la: Quare Crystalli sint cuspidatæ rationem affert subtilem Scalig: L C.Fxerc.[?] 119. §.2. Quòd nimirum concretionis opus procedat per minima & momenta naturalia idcirco in punctum desinat, aut punctum imitante fastigio terminetur, quam cum grano Salis & suo sensu intellectam Auctori iubens concedo.
units.tr: Why crystals are pointed, Scaliger gives a subtle reason, namely that the work of concretion proceeds through the smallest natural moments, and therefore ends in a point, or is terminated by a summit imitating a point, which I grant the author, taken with a grain of salt and in my own sense.

units.la: Kircherus, postquam Mund: Subt: T.I.L.VIII.S.I.C.VIII. p.24. ingenuè fatetur, nihil adeo Physicorum ingenia hucusque vexasse, quam hanc prodigiosam angulosæ sobolis progeniem, p.25. Quid vires ingenii sui pro eruendo gemmarum, & inspecie Crystallorum Polygonismo valuerint, aperit, atque pro fundamento ponit, omnes diaphanas gemmas, originem habere ex liquore salino — esse autem in Salinis Corporibus, virtutem quandam radiativam, sive actinobolicam, quâ Spiritus in Salis corpore abditus ex se, & sua natura appetitu quodam naturali ex Centro prodiens in circumferentiam corpuscula protrufione sua paulatim in radios quosdam dispescat — Supra radices autem in Crystallis sex Ichnographiæ loco fundata, postea sursum ἐξ τῆς ὀρχῆς[?] radiantes, nova corpusculorum accessione, tandem hanc formam sexangulam prodire — Quòd autem radiatio illa non in Circulum, sed in polygonas figuras degeneret, judicat id fieri ex proportionata diminutione virtutis radiativæ, quæ interjecti primis radii, semper magis magisque decrescant, id quod adjuncto schemate Geometrico ratiocinio ostendere allaborat — Posita hac virtutis Salinæ, veluti Ichnographica delineatione vult, statim reliqua corpuscula veluti magnetismo quodam impulsa attractàque se iis circumponere, quæ postea aliorum aliorumque accessu augmentata tandem in debitam Crystalli quantitatem exsurgent per continuum singulorum simili modo radiantium affluxum. Hæc Kircheri sententia, si verum fateamur, præ aliis nobis arridet, licèt & hic non reperiamus, quod nobis plenarie satisfaciat. Materiam gemmarum esse liquorem Salinum fusius quoque probare annititur, talibus tamen argumentis, quæ pro hypothesi hac stabilienda vix sufficere nobis videntur, magis placet vt Salium actinobolica, utpote egregiis confirmata experimentis; Hac tamen posita nondum habemus quod quaerimus. Cur enim diameter non dividitur in radios plures, vel pauciores quàm sex, sicut notum est, Crystallos ut plurimum esse hexagonas, licet non diffitendum sit, ab hoc angulorum numero varie deflectere? Cur non prodit potius unica superficies plana hexagona, quàm prisma integrum, idque satis longum? Cur nova corpusculorum accessio, sursum, ut vocat, radians, tam exactè sese ad Ichnographicam delineationem accommodat? Vel cur non potius Ichnographiæ, vel radiationes subsequentes angulos habent, & lineas, in situ à primis differentes? Quomodo tandem prodit vel unica, vel oppositæ duæ pyramides? Dum interim Kircheri hanc subtilem æquè ac curiosam de figuratione Crystalli Hypothesin objectis dubiis infringere allaboramus, non ita invita nati sumus modestiâ, ut nostram qualemcunque aliter quàm pro conjectura obtrudamus; siquidem eadem mihi mens est, quæ Accuratissimo ac Excellentissimo D.D. Scheuchzero, ex MSC. ejus eruta. Hisce, inquit, (generaliter nempe circa materiam, motum, methodum vel Scholasticam, vel Chymicam, vel Mechanicam &c:) praemonitis ab omni fastûs & ambitionis, si non audaciæ crimine alienus, suppono prius, cum ipsis Cartesianæ Philosophiæ patronis, motum particularum aquæ quaquaversum, sursum, deorsum, dextrorsum, sinistrorsum, extrorsum, introrsum, horsum, retrorsum, suppono item, massulas Crystalli antea per poros fluidi invisibiliter dispersas sese postea colligere, ac hinc inde ad Crystallos constituendas congregare, atque animo mecum concipiens, particulas aquæ, vel fluidi ambientis versus Centrum collectarum massularum undique prementes, in mente mea figuro genesin Sphaerae, vel siquidem pulsus, vel non sunt æquales, vel massa ipsa in Crystallum vertenda, vi gravitatis suæ deorsum quoque tendat, Cylindri superne ac inferne vel complanati, si pulsibus supernis ac infernis massa Crystallina cedat, vel rotundi, si massa solidior, & in se arctius coire inepta fortius resistat: Quòd si nunc pars quæpiam, vel latus Crystallini Cylindri, v.g. in Fig:7.a. fortius resistat præ aliis, sicut difficilis conceptu foret æqualis omnium partium consistentia, & resistentia; fiet omninò ut partes vicinæ pressioni eidem, vel modo fortiori reditæ cedat, ac angulum quendam, vel acutum, bac, vel rectum Fig:8. g f h, vel obtusum, Fig:9. l m n. constituant, dum interim hæperaguntur in hoc latere diametraliter opposito Fig:7.x. id quod quidem initio non videtur, quum vis ab a. versus x; majorem debeat exerere virtutem, & x eò lubentius cedere, quum nulla fit ab a. versus x. pressio contraria, & angulus, bac, asylum, in quod partes ab a. in x. pressæ sese recipere queant, verum si consideraverimus, angulos, bac, constitutos ab utroque latere, b a, et, ac. Oblique sursum versus x. premi partes diagonales, secundum lineas, r s, r s, &c. manebit omnino contrapressio τ̄ [?] a. & resistentia τ̄ [?] x. supra gratis asserta, nunc ad verticem τ̄ [?] x. ex eadem ratione, quæ supra data fuit, constitui potest, imò debet angulus Exγ. Opposito, b a c, quàm proximè æquales: Nunc habemus fontem trium ad minimum figurarum, quòd si enim oppositi anguli se claudant exactè, habetur pro basi quadratum, Fig:8. f g h i, vel oblongum, Fig:10. α β γ δ, vel Rhombus, Fig:9: l m n o, & productum corpus, vel Cubus, vel parallelipedum, vel corpus Rhomboideum, sicuti exempla talium prostant in Marcasitis Cubicis, ac Selenite Rhomboidali, quòd si autem talis sit distantia verticum, Fig:7. a. & x. ut anguli ab iis constituti b a c. & γ x z. sese claudere nequeant, oriuntur ad complementum figuræ novi anguli, b γ x. γ b a. a c z, & x z c. novàque latera, b γ. & c z. Sicque prodiit hexagonum, superne & inferne basi hexagona, circumcirca autem planis sex quadrangulis præditum, prorsus uti in Crystallis cuncta hæc hactenus supposita observantur, exceptis planitiebus, superna, infernáque, quarum loco adsunt duæ pyramides hexagonæ, vel una tantùm; Una, si Crystallus ante productionem, vel unius, vel utriusque pyramidis subsideat, ac parietibus cavitatis petrosæ adhærescat, quæ subsidentia, vel adhæsio fit plerumque Crystalli partibus nondum plenè consolidatis, vel cum insigni concussione, ut hoc arguunt bases Crystallorum vel diffractæ, & fissuras agentes, vel non pellucidæ, duæ & oppositæ prodeunt pyramides, ubi Crystallus plenariam nacta est figuræ suæ dispositionem in medio fluido, antequam scilicet fundum, vel latera petiit: quomodo autem producantur pyramides istæ, non ita facile dictu, ponatur quippe nova Crystalli materia superinfundi basi, seu superne, seu inferne, complanabitur illa, si satis fluida sit, atque sic prolongabitur quidem prisma, nullæ provenient pyramides; hoc ipsum igitur ratiocinium ansam dat, vel cogitandi, vel statuendi, materiam illam novam basibus affusam esse quidem fluidam & prismati cohærere aptam, non tamen ita, ut in planam abeat, & basi parallelam superficiem, sed tenaciorem & magis consistentem, ut in cumulum assurgat, pressionibus tamen aquæ obsequentem, hoc ipso prodibit statim pyramis, sicuti notum arenam, frumentum, & alia id genus in cumulum congesta talem figuram formare, eáque erit vel coniformis, si prisma foret Cylindricum, vel hexagona, uti hic, quia prisma ipsum est hexagonum, facile quippe concipere licet, identitatem figurarum prismatis, nunc fere consistentis, & pyramidis paulò fluidioris illi adnatæ; Cur vel quomodo pressio aquæ in omnes cumuli pyramidalis partes angulos hujus adaptet angulis prismatis, & plana planis, usque dum apex sit in eadem protrusione axeos prismatis. Et hoc quidem si punctum pyramidis resistens præcisè respondeat angulo prismatis (eodem quippe modo concipi potest ac debet Polygonismus pyramidis ac prismatis) id enim si fuerit alibi in medio e. g. plani prodibit equidem ex data ratione hexagona Pyramis (ab aliis in motu & pressione occurrentibus, variantibusq; causis in trigonam, pentagonam, aliamque mutanda) eaque talis, cujus plana non respondent planis columnæ, nec in situ, nec in magnitudine, sicuti id in pluribus Crystallis videre licet. Vel pro Genesi pyramidis in medium proferri potest massæ Crystallinæ levitas, cum certum sit, in positione quavis massæ Crystallinæ, ob heterogeneitatem partium, necessario supponendum esse, crassiorem impurioremque materiam versus medium propelli, leviorem, quæ hanc crassiorem & interiorem ambit, sursum magis ferri, ibique ab aqua ambiente undique compressam, pressionique ob subtilitatem facilius cedentem in pyramidem efformatam fuisse; Crassiore interim ad fundum se demittente, id quod in posteriore insuper confirmat pyramidis major puritas, pellucidi-tas[?], ac speciale Phænomenon Casat: de Igne, memoratum, Ph:XIII.
units.tr: Kircherus, after Mund: Subt: T.I.L.VIII.S.I.C.VIII. p.24. frankly admits that nothing has so exercised the minds of the natural philosophers hitherto as this strange offspring of angular progeny. On p.25 he explains how far the powers of his own mind have availed in unravelling the polygonal form of gems, and of crystals in particular, and he lays down as a foundation that all transparent gems derive their origin from a saline liquor. He holds that in saline bodies there is a certain radiative, or actinobolic, power, by which the spirit hidden in the body of the salt, of its own nature and by a certain natural appetite, issuing from the centre, gradually divides itself into rays by thrusting out little bodies towards the circumference. Upon the roots, moreover, laid down in the manner of a ground plan of six sides in crystals, afterwards radiating upwards [from the beginning, ἐκ τῆς ἀρχῆς], by a fresh accession of little bodies, this hexagonal form at last comes forth. That this radiation does not run out into a circle but degenerates into polygonal figures, he judges to happen from a proportionate diminution of the radiative power, so that the rays lying between the first rays grow ever smaller and smaller, which he labours to show by a geometrical argument with an attached diagram. Once this saline power is posited, as it were by a ground-plan delineation, he holds that at once the remaining little bodies, as if driven and drawn by a certain magnetism, place themselves around these, which afterwards, augmented by the approach of one after another, rise at last to the due quantity of a crystal, through the continual inflow of each of the rays in the same way. This is Kircher's opinion, and if we are to speak the truth, it pleases us more than the others, although here too we do not find anything that fully satisfies us. He also strives to prove more fully that the matter of gems is a saline liquor, but by arguments which seem to us hardly sufficient to establish this hypothesis. The actinobolism of salts pleases us more, as being confirmed by excellent experiments; yet even with this posited we do not yet have what we seek. For why, as is well known, does the diameter not divide into more or fewer than six rays, so that crystals are for the most part hexagonal, although it must not be denied that they vary from this number of angles in various ways? Why does a single flat hexagonal surface not come forth, rather than a whole prism, and that quite long? Why does the new accession of little bodies, radiating upwards as he calls it, accommodate itself so exactly to the ground-plan delineation? Or why rather do the subsequent ground plans or radiations not have angles and lines differing in position from the first? How, finally, does a single pyramid, or two opposite pyramids, come forth? Meanwhile, while we labour to break down this subtle and no less curious hypothesis of Kircher on the figuring of crystals with the objections raised, we were not born so unassuming in modesty that we press our own opinion, whatever it is, upon others otherwise than as a conjecture. For my mind is the same as that of the most accurate and most excellent Dr. Scheuchzer, drawn from his manuscripts. With these things, he says, (namely, in general, concerning matter, motion, and method, whether scholastic, chemical, or mechanical, etc.) premised, free from the crime, if not of audacity, at least of pomp and ambition, I suppose first, along with the very patrons of the Cartesian philosophy, that the particles of water move every way, upwards, downwards, to the right, to the left, outwards, inwards, hither, thither, backwards. I suppose likewise that the little masses of crystal, previously dispersed invisibly through the pores of the fluid, afterwards gather together and congregate here and there to constitute crystals; and conceiving in my mind with them, the particles of water or of the surrounding fluid, pressing from every side towards the centre of the gathered masses, I figure in my mind the genesis of a sphere, or, if the pushes are not equal, or if the mass itself, about to turn into a crystal, tends downwards also by the force of its gravity, cylinders, flattened above and below, if the crystalline mass yields to the upper and lower pushes, or round ones, if the more solid mass, unfit to cohere more tightly in itself, resists more strongly. But if now some part, or side, of the crystalline cylinder, for example in Fig. 7.a., resists more strongly than the others, since it would be difficult to conceive that the consistency and resistance of all parts are equal, it will entirely come about that the neighbouring parts yield to the same pressure, or to one returned in a stronger mode, and constitute some angle, acute, as bac, or right, Fig. 8, g f h, or obtuse, Fig. 9, l m n. Meanwhile they are driven in this side diametrically opposite, Fig. 7.x., which indeed does not seem so at first, since the force from a towards x ought to exert a greater power, and x yields the more willingly since there is no contrary pressure from a towards x, and no angle, bac, an asylum into which the parts pressed from a towards x could withdraw. But if we consider that the angles, bac, constituted from either side, b a, and a c, press obliquely upwards towards x, the diagonal parts along the lines r s, r s, etc., there will remain entirely the counter-pressure of a and the resistance of x, asserted above without proof; now, from the same ratio as was given above, an angle may be constituted at the vertex of x, indeed the angle Exγ ought to be constituted opposite to bac, as nearly equal as possible. Now we have the source of at least three figures. For if the opposite angles close exactly, a square base is had, Fig. 8, f g h i, or an oblong, Fig. 10, α β γ δ, or a rhombus, Fig. 9, l m n o, and the body produced is a cube, or a parallelepiped, or a rhomboid body, just as examples of such exist in cubic marcasites and in rhomboidal selenite. But if the distance of the vertices, Fig. 7, a and x, is such that the angles constituted by them, b a c and γ x z, cannot close together, there arise, to complete the figure, new angles, b γ x, γ b a, a c z, and x z c, and new sides, b γ and c z. And so there comes forth a hexagon, with a hexagonal base above and below and, all round, six quadrangular planes, exactly as all these things hitherto supposed are observed in crystals, except for the flat surfaces above and below, in place of which there are two hexagonal pyramids, or only one. One, if the crystal, before the production of one or both pyramids, subsides and adheres to the walls of a stony cavity; this subsiding or adhesion happens for the most part when the parts of the crystal are not yet fully consolidated, or with a notable concussion, as the bases of crystals show, which are broken and make fissures, or are not transparent. Two opposite pyramids come forth when the crystal has obtained the complete disposition of its figure in the middle fluid, that is, before it has reached the bottom or the sides. How these pyramids are produced is not so easy to say. If new crystalline matter is poured over the base, whether above or below, it will be levelled if it is fluid enough, and so the prism will indeed be lengthened, and no pyramids will arise. This very reasoning therefore gives occasion either to think or to state that this new matter poured on the bases is indeed fluid and fit to cohere to the prism, yet not so that it passes into a plane surface parallel to the base, but is tougher and more consistent, so that it rises into a heap, yet yielding to the pressures of the water. By this very fact a pyramid will come forth at once, just as we know that sand, grain, and other things of this kind, heaped into a pile, form such a figure; and it will be either conical, if the prism were cylindrical, or hexagonal, as here, because the prism itself is hexagonal. For one may easily conceive the identity of the figures of the prism, now nearly consistent, and of the pyramid, somewhat more fluid, adhering to it. How, or why, the pressure of the water adapts the angles of this pyramid to the angles of the prism, and plane to plane, until the apex lies in the same protrusion along the axis of the prism. And this indeed happens if the resisting point of the pyramid corresponds exactly to an angle of the prism (for in the same way the polygonal form of the pyramid and of the prism can and should be conceived); for if it is elsewhere, for example in the middle of a plane, there will indeed come forth, from the given ratio, a hexagonal pyramid (to be altered, by other causes occurring in motion and pressure, into a triangular or pentagonal one), and such a one whose planes do not correspond to the planes of the column, neither in position nor in size, as can be seen in many crystals. Or, for the genesis of the pyramid, there may be put forward in the middle the lightness of the crystalline mass; since it is certain that in any position of the crystalline mass, owing to the heterogeneity of its parts, it must necessarily be supposed that the thicker and impurer matter is driven towards the middle, while the lighter matter, which surrounds this thicker and interior part, is carried more upwards, and there, compressed on every side by the surrounding water and yielding more easily to the pressure because of its subtlety, is formed into a pyramid. Meanwhile the thicker matter sinks to the bottom, which the greater purity and transparency of the pyramid, and the special phenomenon of Casat. on fire, mentioned in Ph. XIII, further confirm for the latter.

units.la: Quòd Pyramis fere nullas, aut saltem paucas, contrà columna & basis multas & copiosas de se edat scintillas.
units.tr: That the pyramid produces almost no sparks, or at least few, whereas the column and the base give off many and copious sparks.

units.la: III. Variæ Crystallorum recensentur differentiæ, quæ in earum planis & angulis observantur, quæ non aliunde quàm à diversa particularum collocatione & dispositione dependet, atque si nobis liceret esse fusioribus, ansa daretur singula specialius explicandi. Propositiones ab ipso Stenone L.C.Phænomenis istis præmissæ sunt. I. Cresçit Crystallus, dum Crystalli jam delineatæ planis externis apponitur nova materia Crystallina. II. Nova hæc materia Crystallina non omnibus planis apponitur, sed ut plurimum solis planis apicis, seu planis extremis. III. Non eodem tempore, nec eadem quantitate omnibus planis extremis apponitur materia Crystallina. IV. Non semper totum planum materia Crystallina tegitur, sed interdum versus angulos, interdum versus latera, interdum in medio plano loca nuda relinquuntur. Nimirū, plana columnæ majora sunt, & oblonga, ubi Crystallus per appositionem continuam, ad plana pyramidis factam diu multumque crevit; Minora, ubi parum; Nulla, ubi materia nova Crystallis appositæ fluida nimis extitit, ut ab utroque latere bases pyramidum in unam abierint. Plana intermedia; sive columnæ; ut plurimum non striata, ad minimum unum, vel duo, quando scilicet materia appositæ, propter crassitiem aliqualem non potuit explanari, quin in continio columnæ & pyramidis vestigia relicta fuerint; Axis pyramidum, ubi deviat à rectitudine cum axe columnæ, dicendum videtur, in prima Crystalli formatione hoc ita contigisse, ut prælio unius lateris prævaluerit, & apicem versus oppositum latus detorserit, vel uni præsertim plano pyramidis, ad quod nempe magis inclinat apex, appositam fuisse materiam, atque ob hanc ipsam causam fit, ut plana pyramidis raro sint æqualia inter se, cum difficile sit concipere, materiam novam æqualiter omnibus planis sese apponere, vel appositam fuisse, & ex eodem fonte derivanda est varietas figuræ, in planis tum pyramidis, tum columnæ, ipsaque resolutio angulorum solidorum,tum extremorum,tum intermediorum,in plures alios; Sic partes plani ejusdem, seu pyramidalis, seu columnaris, non semper in eadem sunt superficie, licet in alia parallela, ubi materia nova propter aliquam crassitiem, vel aliud impedimentum, sese non diffudit per totam plani planitiem; gibbum in medio fit planum, quando materia nova medio ipsius plani fuit apposita, indeque sensim versus latera, sive bases extenuata. Tandem in planis intermediis inæqualitates observantur scalarum gradibus similes, quando nempe materia nova planis pyramidalibus affusa non tota illa occupavit, sed nunc per has, nunc per illas partes illorum defluxit, sicque nunc has, nunc illas partes planorum columnarinm adauxit.
units.tr: III. Various differences among crystals are listed, which are observed in their planes and angles, and which depend on nothing other than the diverse placement and arrangement of the particles. If we were permitted to be more expansive, an opening would be given to explain each one more particularly. Steno himself, in the work already cited, set out the propositions premised to these phenomena: I. A crystal grows when fresh crystalline matter is applied to the outer planes of a crystal already formed. II. This new crystalline matter is not applied to all the planes, but for the most part only to the planes of the apex, that is, the extreme planes. III. Crystalline matter is not applied to all the extreme planes at the same time, nor in the same quantity. IV. The whole plane is not always covered by crystalline matter; sometimes bare spots are left near the angles, sometimes near the sides, and sometimes in the middle of the plane. Namely, the planes of the column are larger and oblong where the crystal has grown for a long time and to a great extent by continuous apposition onto the planes of the pyramid; they are smaller where it has grown little, and there are none where the new matter applied to the crystal was too fluid, so that the bases of the pyramids ran together into one from either side. The intermediate planes, or those of the column, are for the most part not striated, at least one or two, namely when the applied matter, because of some thickness, could not be spread out without leaving traces at the junction of column and pyramid. Where the axis of a pyramid departs from straightness with the axis of the column, it seems right to say that this happened in the first formation of the crystal in this way: the push of one side prevailed and twisted the opposite side toward the apex; or matter was applied especially to one plane of the pyramid, namely the one toward which the apex leans more. For this very reason the planes of the pyramid are rarely equal to one another, since it is difficult to conceive of new matter applying itself, or having been applied, equally to all the planes. From the same source must be derived the variety of figure in the planes of both pyramid and column, and the breaking up of the solid angles, both extreme and intermediate, into several others. Thus parts of the same plane, whether pyramidal or columnar, do not always lie on the same surface, though they lie on another parallel one, where the new matter, because of some thickness or other impediment, did not spread over the whole flatness of the plane. A hump becomes a plane in the middle when the new matter was applied to the middle of the plane, and it thins gradually toward the sides or bases. Finally, in the intermediate planes there are inequalities resembling the steps of a staircase, when the new matter poured onto the pyramidal planes did not occupy them all, but flowed down now through these parts, now through those, and so increased now these, now those parts of the columnar planes.

units.la: IV. Sicuti omne rectum est norma sui curvi, ita non impossibile, licet operosum erit ei, qui genesin Crystalli hexagonæ, in superioribus jam expositam, attentè perlegerit, irregulares quoque innumeras angulorum & planorum ab ordinaria deflectentes Crystallorum figuras explicare. Quoniam autem ansam daret argumentum hocce in amplum & longum excurrendi campum, si vellemus singulas in hoc Phænomeno recensitas figurarum varietates enucleare, satis nobis; &, ut spero, aliis faciemus, si fontes duntaxat solutionum generales ex superioribus indicaverimus, nimirum, sicuti conceptu est facile, materiam Crystallinam non esse ubique ejusdem constitutionis & texturæ, resistentiæ, vel cessionis, crassitiei vel subtilitatis, extensibilitatis, sive tenacitatis, & fragilitatis, ita in fluido ambiente, cui non minimam figurationis partem detulimus, magna omnino potest esse varietas, ut pressio non sit sufficiens, non ubique æqualis, sed ab uno latere major, quam ab altero, impedita vel libera. Facile quoque inde judicare licet, ex innumeris forte modis, variante activi fluidi ad passivam materiam Crystallinam applicatione, non posse non varias induci figuras. Ipse quoque locus, prout est vel amplus, vel angustus, oblongus, angularis, vel rotundus, undique clausus, vel alicubi apertus, non parum quoque ad diversitatem figuræ contribuit.
