Porrò Crystallus, licet primigenia sit hexagona, insigniter potest variari à varia cohæsione, compressione aliarum Crystallorum, à celeri vel tarda, ad fundum vel latera cavitatis detrusione & allisione, præsertim etiam in sui augmento, prout nova materia Crystallina apponitur, vel omnibus undique planis, vel uni duntaxat, aut duobus planis, vel alterutris, vel utriusque pyramidis, ut vel hinc ad confirmationem tantò majorem nostræ Hypotheseos pateat, quàm ampla foret occasio ex hisce generalibus causis ad specialia phænomena applicandis fusiùs differendi, non solùm de Crystallorum variis figurationibus, sed & ipsorum salium[?], juxta varias Crystallisationis ἐγχειρήσεως[?], multùm variantibus figuris, quæ cuncta tædii ex ambagibus forte oriundi evitandi ergo hac vice prætermitto.
units.tr: IV. Just as every straight line is the rule of its curve, so it is not impossible, although it will be laborious for one who has read carefully through the genesis of the hexagonal crystal set out above, to explain also the countless irregular figures of crystals that deviate from the ordinary angles and planes. Since this subject would open a wide and lengthy field if we wished to unfold each of the varieties of figure listed in this phenomenon, it will suffice for us, and, as I hope, for others, if we indicate only the general sources of solution from what has gone before. Namely, as is easy to conceive, the crystalline matter is not everywhere of the same constitution, texture, resistance or yielding, thickness or fineness, extensibility or tenacity, and brittleness. So in the surrounding fluid, to which we have assigned no small part of the shaping, there can be great variety: the pressure may be insufficient, not everywhere equal, but greater from one side than from the other, and either hindered or free. It is also easy to judge from this that, through perhaps countless modes of applying the active fluid to the passive crystalline matter, various figures cannot but be induced. The place itself, whether it is wide or narrow, oblong, angular or round, enclosed on all sides or open somewhere, contributes not a little to the diversity of figure. Furthermore, the crystal, although primarily hexagonal, can be notably varied by differences in cohesion, by the compression of other crystals, by quick or slow thrusting and dashing against the bottom or the sides of the cavity, and especially in its growth, as new crystalline matter is applied either to all the planes on every side, or to one only, or to two planes, or to one or the other, or to either pyramid. From this the confirmation of our hypothesis may appear all the greater. There would be ample occasion to discuss at length, by applying these general causes to special phenomena, not only the various figurations of crystals but also those of the salts themselves, whose figures vary much according to the various attempts at crystallisation. All of this I now omit, to avoid the tedium that perhaps arises from circumlocutions.

units.la: V. Qui perspicuitatis in Cœlo, aëre, vitro, gemmis, &c. observabilis rationem ex modernorum principiis reddere novit, ei non difficile erit & pelluciditatem nostrarum Crystallorum explicare, nimirum, cùm materia ipsa Crystallos constituens, per ipsos saxorum poros filtrata quasi & percolata durissima necessariò evadat, mirum non est eam in concretione adeò regulariter disponi, ut materia secundi elementi liberè sine ulla radiorum infractione, vel reflexione eam pertransire possit, & hoc ipsum est ratiocinium quod Anton. Le Grand: Princip: Phil: P.VI. p.312. de lapidibus pellucidis, & speciatim Crystallo, hisce verbis exprimit.
units.tr: V. Whoever knows how to give an account, from the principles of the moderns, of the transparency observable in the sky, the air, glass, gems, and so on, will not find it difficult to explain also the pellucidity of our crystals. Namely, since the matter constituting crystals, filtered and as it were percolated through the very pores of rocks, necessarily becomes very hard, it is no wonder that it is disposed in its concretion so regularly that the matter of the second element can pass through it freely, without any breaking or reflection of the rays. This is the very reasoning which Anton. Le Grand: Princip: Phil: P.VI. p.312. expresses in these words concerning transparent stones, and particularly crystal.

units.la: Lapides pellucidi generantur, non ex multarum arenarum congerie, ut vulgares, sed ex materia quadam fluida, quæ unum duntaxat granum constitueret; modò in tanta sit copia, ut ad alicujus magnitudinis molem assurgat, & tale Corpus pellucidum fieri necesse est. Quia cum exhalationes in Terrarum imis vel cavitatibus, in guttam collectæ, lubricis & fluidis illarum particulis abeuntibus, paulatim sibi mutuò adhærescunt, globuli secundi elementi, luminis actionem transferentes, undique per earum meatus satis valide pertransire possunt; Quod tamen non fieret, si ex multis granis hujusmodi lapides compingerentur, quia quarumvis postmodum mollia redderentur, nunquam inter se ita conjungi possent, quin aliqua inter illa esset interruptio, quæ illorum transparentiam impediret. Ac proinde hujusmodi exhalationes secundum diversos duritiei gradus, variamque partium suarum dispositionem, incertos quosdam lapides abeunt, ut Crystallum &c. Quando nunc in Crystallis frequenter observatur diaphaneitas corrupta & interrupta, attribuendum id est crassitiei & impuritati ipsius materiæ Crystallinæ, cui plurimæ, vel metallicæ, vel terrestres, particulæ sunt intermixtæ, quod autem in una eademque Crystallo pyramis cum parte Columnæ aquæ adinstar limpidissimæ sit pellucida, inferior autem Columnæ pars cum basi vel nebulosa vel nivosa, plurimisque fissuris inquinata, uti id haud raro observare licet, contingit id, vel à violenta Crystallorum ad fundum cavitatis detrusione, unde in Crystallo ad basin percussa pororum ordo & dispositio necessariò infringitur, radiique intercipiuntur, quò minùs rectâ viâ progredi queant, vel ab impuritate & terrestreitate materiæ, quæ vi gravitatis suæ fundum petit, & sese purioribus partibus intimiùs permiscet, vel etiam ob inæqualitatem fundi, quâ partes quædam extantiores ad basin Crystalli sese insinuant, & partim mutatione pororum, partim ipsis terrestribus particulis Crystallum inquinant.
units.tr: Transparent stones are generated not from a heap of many sands, as common stones are, but from a certain fluid matter which would constitute only a single grain; provided there is so much of it that it rises to a mass of some size, and such a transparent body must needs be made. For since exhalations collected into a drop in the lower parts or cavities of the earth, passing into the slippery and fluid particles of those, gradually cling to one another, the globules of the second element, transmitting the action of light, can pass quite forcefully through their pores on all sides. This would not happen if such stones were put together from many grains, because, being made soft afterwards, they could never be joined together so that there was no interruption between them, which would impede their transparency. And so exhalations of this kind, according to the different degrees of hardness and the varying arrangement of their parts, become certain stones, such as crystal, and so on.

units.la: VI. De colorum natura non est ut pluribus disquiramus, vel variorum Auctorum de iis sententias congeramus. Eam quæ reliquis antecellere videtur, exponam. Ei, qui vel unicum perlegerit Róberti Boyle Tract: de Colorib: manifestum fiet, colores non tam esse qualitatem Corporibus inhærentem, uti Scholastici volunt, vel sulphuri adscribendos, ut Chymici somniant, quàm lucem variè modificatam, prout nimirum variant, vel ipsæ figuræ partium superficialium in Corporibus coloratis, vel situs & motus earundem, vel profunditas parvularum cavitatum inter extantes particulas interceptarum, hanc autem modificationem variam ut ad Crystallos variè coloratos applicem, dico cum eodem Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virt: p.8. Illam dependere à quodam succo minerali colorato, sive à quadam minerali exhalatione tingendi virtute prædita, Crystallis participata, quoad erant vel in solutis principiis, vel constabant ex textura satis aperta, ut per eum penetrarent vapores minerales. Cui vel minimum hanc ob rem exorietur dubium, is veritatem asserti agnoscet, ubi ingressus fuerit Germaniæ, vel Hungariæ fodinas metallicas, ibique vel oculis usurpaverit, vel manibus collegerit Crystallos montanas, sive fluores, omni pulcherrimorum colorum genere ita splendentes, ut ipsas gemmas, Sapphiros, Smaragdos, Rubinos &c. prorsus æmulentur, & ab his feré nonnisi duritie differant, ut vel hinc ἐν πεδίῳ[?] consectarii loco inferre quis possit, Alpes nostras non esse metallorum feraces, quoniam Crystalli ibi reperiundæ omnes, vel maximam partem sint colore omni destitutæ. Confirmat porrò hoc suum assertum Boyle Lib: Cit: p.13. Ex modo tingendi Crystallos petrosas pulchris coloribus per vapores minerales — Licet colores hoc modo producti non soleant Crystallos illas multùm pervadere, penetratioque illorum adjuvetur non debili gradu caloris, quoniam considerandum proponit partes illas Crystalli obtinuisse plenariam suam duritiem — Cùm tamen gemmæ supponantur fuisse tinctæ in locis subterraneis, cùm adhuc essent fluidæ, aut minimùm molles. Specialis nimis & præceps nobis videtur Kircherus, dum Mund: subt: L.VIII.P.I.C.V. Colorum in lapidibus varietatem deducit ex varietate Salium Sulphuri commixtorum, & cœruleos, v. g. deducit à Vitriolo, Virides à succo Æruginis &c. Cùm probabile mihi videtur, tincturas coloratas esse generales, & mineralibus omnibus communes, ita ut Vitriolum æquè possit dici tinctum colore Sapphirino, & Ærugo colore Smaragdi &c. Ex hisce nunc de Crystallorum coloribus generaliter præmissis facilè solvi possunt variæ quoque circumstantiæ. Ita antequam Boyle Lib: C.p.13. meminit Crystalli in vertice Viridis, et in basi colore omni cassæ, jam p.12. exposuit, quomodo gemmæ possint esse tinctæ, partim colore carentes. Quasi, inquit, tingens pigmentum commixtum uni parti materiæ, ex qua lapis constabat, dum esset liquidus, vel mollis, non satis copiosus fuerit, ut se diffunderet in totum, & omni illi portioni, quam tingit, præberet æquè intensum colorem, non diffitetur, quandoque in quibusdam casibus diffusionem posse sisti per petrescentes succos coagulatos prius in alia parte ab ea, cui tinctura fuit commixta. Et forsan in aliis casibus diversos colores pertinere ad diversas particulas materiæ coagulatas vel agglutinatas ad singulas illas diversis temporibus, ut tamen unicus solidus lapis videretur. Rarius & curiosius est, quod Steno refert L.C.de Crystallis in iisdem lapidis lamellis nonnullis aqueis, aliis lucidissimis, quibusdam albis, multis Amethystinis sibi invicem immixtis, [?]ine ulla colorum confusione. Cui tamen analogum prorsus ex Crystallisatione artificiali refert experimentum, quo Vitriolum & Alumen in eadem aqua dissoluta, post consumtam aquæ partem seorsim concreverunt singula absque ulla partium miscela, difficile tamen est vel ex ipsa nostra hypothesi concipere, vel demonstrare, quomodo, vel cur in eadem solutione & evaporatione eodem tempore instituta particulæ tingentes Cœruleæ, vel virides potius sese imiscuerint Crystallis Vitrioli quàm Aluminis, nisi occultus statuatur quasi magnetismus, vel Philosophica magis locutione, partes, vel vapores minerales tingentes propter structuram Aluminis & Vitrioli differentem, & illius forte majorem laxitatem, vel strictiorem compagem, cujusque proportionatam angustiam in Vitriolo potius quàm Alumine invenerit adhærendi & in poris subsistendi dispositionem; Vel quod in eadem licet solutione Crystalli Vitrioli, ob terrestreitatem majorem ante Crystallos Aluminis compingi aptæ ( interveniente forsan ipsa structuræ Vitrioli proportionata aptitudine) particulas minerales tingentes receperint, Crystallis postea nulla Aluminis tinctura relicta; Cui tamen ratiocinio experimentum à me ipso ob id constitutum, Crystallos Aluminis ante coagulationem Vitrioli exhibens, & ad fundum mittens, quadantenus contrariari videtur. Quoniam autem unius ejusdemque effectus, plures possunt esse causæ, nobisque Crystallisationi naturali interesse haud licet, aliam porrò phænomeni hujus rationem: Ita concipere possumus, ut dicamus, in una eademque cavitate Crystallos, non eodem omnes tempore esse productos, sed priores hac vaporum mineralium tinctura imbutos, posteriores aliis noviter accidentibus: imprægnatos, vel etiam ejusdem Cavitatis Crystallos, eodem licet tempore productas à vaporibus mineralibus duntaxat cavitatis mediam, vel aliquam partem pertranseuntibus, ex parte saltem & aliquas tinctas fuisse, aliis manentibus colore omni destitutis. Quod attinet colorum apparentium Phænomenon, posset id equidem ex Opticorum principiis, & speciali eorundem colorum in prismate triangulari (quod aliqui haud inepte Paradisum stultorum vocare solent,) & omni corpore diaphano anguloso, Iride item, meteoro, notissimo observabilium Phænomeno fuius[?] explicari, & schematismis illustrari, quoniam vero ejus conditionis hæc est res, ut in Opticorum celebrium libris passim reperiatur, libet digressionis forte tædiosæ evitandæ ergo generaliter duntaxat indicare, dependere hunc variantem colorum lusum in corporibus diaphanis ex varia lucis five radiorum refractione in ingressu ad perpendiculum, & egressu a perpendiculo propter medii variantem tenuitatem & crassitiem facta, cui addunt alii, ut P. Joh: Zahn: Oculo Artific: Teledioptric: Fund: I. Syntag: II. C.12. p.123.124. Et Ath: Kirch: Mund: Subt: L. VIII.S.I.C.6.p.15.16. Radiorum in transitu diaphani per Umbras, tum à partibus elementaribus, opacis ipsius diaphani, tum maxime angulorum solidorum, corpus diaphanum complectentium, projectas, fœdationem, obfuscationem, vel modificationem. In isto tandem Phænomeno, quod colores variegatos in fissura Crystalli interna quasi fixos repræsentat, videtur admittenda lucis non solùm refractio densitati medii attribuenda, sed & reflexio, partibus ipsius Crystalli fisfis adscribenda. Artificium denique quòd spectat, quo Crystallus, limpida licèt, & aquea supposito aliquo colore infecta videtur, ut inexpertis vel eminus aspectantibus, gemma colorata putetur. Lubet id ipsius Kirch: verbis Arte magna Lucis & Umbræ. p.80. reperiundis, solvere. Coloribus, inquit, per Crystalli densitatem fractis radiis transmissus in ipsa tantisper hærere, ac fluitantis in modum ludere videtur, quousque ad optatum perveniat. Deinde ea Crystalli planities, quæ subjecto colorie diametro opponitur, radios coloris sursum elevatos ab interna, seu cava sui parte suscipit, eosdem ad infimam Crystalli superficiem remittit, quidam hinc rursus ad oculos redeunt, primis radiis permixti saturationem Crystalli densitate, quam in circumfuso aere ostendunt, quo fit, ut Crystallus universa tincta videatur.
units.tr: VI. There is no need for us to inquire at length into the nature of colours, or to gather together the opinions of various authors on them. I will set out the view that seems to surpass the rest. Anyone who reads even a single work, Robert Boyle's Tract on Colours, will see clearly that colours are not, as the Scholastics maintain, a quality inhering in bodies, nor to be ascribed to sulphur, as the Chymists dream, but rather light variously modified: namely, according to whether the figures of the superficial particles of coloured bodies, or their position and motion, or the depth of the tiny cavities lying between the projecting particles, vary. I say, with the same Boyle, On the Origin and Virtues of Gems, p. 8, that this modification, so far as I apply it to variously coloured crystals, depends on a certain coloured mineral juice, or on a certain mineral exhalation endowed with a power of tinging, which the crystals have shared, so long as they were either in dissolved principles or consisted of a texture open enough for mineral vapours to penetrate through them. Whoever has the slightest doubt about this assertion will recognise its truth once he has entered the metal mines of Germany or Hungary, and there either seen with his eyes or gathered with his hands the mountain crystals, or fluors, shining with every kind of most beautiful colour, so that they rival the gems themselves, sapphires, emeralds, rubies and so on, and differ from them almost only in hardness. Hence one might even draw as a corollary in the plain [ἐν πεδίῳ] that our Alps are not rich in metals, since almost all the crystals found there are, for the most part, wholly devoid of colour. Boyle, Tract cited, p. 13, further confirms this assertion of his. From the manner of tinging stony crystals with beautiful colours by means of mineral vapours: Although colours produced in this way do not usually penetrate those crystals very far, and their penetration is aided by no slight degree of heat, since he proposes that those parts of the crystal had acquired their full hardness, yet gems are supposed to have been tinted in subterranean places while they were still fluid, or at least soft. Kircher, in his Mundus subterraneus, Book VIII, Part I, Chapter V, seems to us far too particular and hasty, when he derives the variety of colours in stones from the variety of salts mixed with sulphur; he derives blues, for example, from vitriol, and greens from the juice of verdigris, and so on. It seems probable to me that tinctures of colour are general and common to all minerals, so that vitriol could equally be said to be tinted with a sapphire colour, and verdigris with the colour of an emerald, and so on. Now that we have laid down these general points about the colours of crystals, various other circumstances can also be easily resolved. Thus, before Boyle, Tract cited, p. 13, mentions that crystals are green at the top and wholly colourless at the base, he has already explained on p. 12 how gems can be tinted while partly lacking colour. As if, he says, the tinging pigment, mixed with one part of the matter of which the stone consisted while it was liquid or soft, was not copious enough to diffuse itself through the whole and give equally intense colour to every portion it tinges; he does not deny that sometimes, in certain cases, diffusion can be checked by petrifying juices coagulated first in a part other than that into which the tincture was mixed. And perhaps in other cases the diverse colours belong to diverse particles of matter coagulated or agglutinated at different times, so that nevertheless a single solid stone appears. What Steno reports in his work on crystals is rarer and more curious: in the same plates of stone, some watery, others most clear, some white, many amethyst-coloured, mixed with one another without any confusion of colours. Yet he reports an experiment from artificial crystallisation wholly analogous to this, in which vitriol and alum, dissolved in the same water, after a part of the water was consumed, crystallised separately, each without any mixture of parts. It is difficult, however, either to conceive or to demonstrate, even from our own hypothesis, how or why, in the same solution and evaporation carried out at the same time, the blue or rather green tinging particles mixed themselves with the crystals of vitriol rather than of alum, unless we posit a hidden magnetism, or, to speak more philosophically, that the tinging mineral particles or vapours, because of the different structure of alum and vitriol, and the greater looseness or tighter compactness of the one, found in vitriol rather than in alum a proportionate narrowness of each, a disposition for adhering and for remaining in the pores. Or else, although in the same solution the crystals of vitriol, because of their greater earthiness, were fitted to be compacted before the crystals of alum (perhaps through the proportionate aptitude of the very structure of vitriol), they received the tinging mineral particles, and afterwards the crystals of alum were left with no tincture at all. Yet this reasoning seems in some measure to be contradicted by an experiment I myself made for this purpose, in which I exhibited the crystals of alum before the coagulation of the vitriol and sent them to the bottom. But since one and the same effect may have several causes, and since we are not permitted to meddle with natural crystallisation, we may conceive another explanation of this phenomenon, as follows: that in one and the same cavity the crystals were not all produced at the same time, but the earlier ones were imbued with this tincture of mineral vapours, and the later ones were impregnated by other newly arising circumstances; or else that crystals of the same cavity, produced at the same time, were tinged in part only, by mineral vapours passing through the middle or some part of the cavity, while the others remained devoid of all colour. As for the phenomenon of apparent colours, this could indeed be explained and illustrated with diagrams from the principles of optics, and from the special behaviour of those colours in a triangular prism (which some not unaptly call the paradise of fools), in any angular transparent body, and likewise in the rainbow, a meteor and a very well-known observable phenomenon; but since this matter is of such a kind that it is found everywhere in the books of the famous writers on optics, I shall, to avoid a perhaps tedious digression, indicate it only in general terms: this varying play of colours in transparent bodies depends on the varying refraction of light or rays, made on entering the medium perpendicularly and on leaving it away from the perpendicular, owing to the varying thinness and thickness of the medium. To this others add, as Father Johann Zahn, Oculus Artificialis Teledioptricus, Fundamentum I, Syntagma II, Chapter 12, pp. 123, 124, and Athanasius Kircher, Mundus subterraneus, Book VIII, Section I, Chapter 6, pp. 15, 16, the darkening, obscuring or modification of rays in passing through a transparent body, cast by the elementary particles of the transparent body itself, which are opaque, and above all by the solid angles surrounding the transparent body. Finally, in that phenomenon which presents colours variegated, as it were fixed, within the internal fissure of a crystal, it seems that we must admit not only a refraction of light attributable to the density of the medium but also a reflection, to be ascribed to the split parts of the crystal itself. As to the artifice by which a crystal, although clear and watery, is made to appear as if tinted with some colour, so that to the inexperienced or to those who look at it from afar it is thought to be a coloured gem, it pleases me to explain this in Kircher's own words, to be found in The Great Art of Light and Shadow, p. 80. The rays, he says, broken by the density of the crystal, seem to linger for a while in the transmitted colour and to play as if fluttering, until they reach the desired point. Then that plane of the crystal which lies opposite the coloured base, receiving the rays of colour raised upward from its inner or hollow part, sends them back to the lowest surface of the crystal; some of these return again to the eyes, mixed with the first rays, and by the density of the crystal they show a saturation such as they display in the surrounding air, so that the crystal appears wholly tinted.

units.la: VII. Crystalli Islandicæ Phænomena ita ex principiis Opticis deduxerunt Celebratissimi Viri, Bartholinus et Hugenius, ut eorum solutionibus acquiescere quivis possit, imò ob demonstrationem ocularem vi convictus debeat. Figuram autem quòd spectat in massis æquè integris, ac particellis etiam minimis Rhomboidalem vel Rhombicam, (de cujus genesi physica in eitatis Libris, ne γεν[?] quidem occurrit) exhibuimus jam supra aliquem, eumque simplicissimum formationis conceptum. Unicum duntaxat de hac figuræ productione & multiplicatione addo, quòd unico Rhombo, vel Rhomboide, tanquam rudimento formato non difficile sit concipere, quomodo nova materia Crystallina, seu selenitica apposita, planis & angulis jam factis sese accomodans, nova eaque plurima ejusdem figuræ progignat Rhomboidalia corpora. Annexa quòd attinet Phænomena Optica, Crystallo Islandicæ propria, ejus sunt illa subtilitatis & sublimitatis, ut absque intimiori Opticæ ipsius notitia nec solvi, nec soluta intelligi queant, sicuti id ex citatis hac de re Auctoribus patebit. Uti autem non ex re mihi videtur Lectorem curiosum dimittere, nisi aliquid saltem, ad sui satisfactionem hauserit ex fonte, unde solutionum rivuli emanant, ita sufficiet fere indicasse, quod pleraque, imò cuncta Crystalli, vel Selenitæ hujus Phænomena derivanda sint è structura & textura ipsius lapidis singulari, quâ is non frustum unicum saltem, aut absolutè continuum, sed compositum ex distinctis laminis, seu bracteis diversimodè contiguis, adeò ut in quibusdam locis distinctæ istæ laminæ saltem unam refractionem, in aliis duas, vel plures efficiant, prout hæc omnia accuratius & fusius inquirunt, atque demonstrant Laudati Viri, Bartholi & Hugeni: ad quos Lectorem proin relego.
units.tr: VII. The phenomena of Icelandic crystal have been derived from the principles of optics by the most celebrated men, Bartholinus and Huygens, so that anyone can accept their solutions, and indeed ought to be forced to assent by the evidence of their own eyes. As for the figure, which is rhombic or rhomboidal both in whole masses and in the smallest particles (on whose physical genesis the books cited say not even a word [γεν[?]]), we have already set out above a single and very simple concept of its formation. I add only this about the production and multiplication of this figure: once one rhomb or rhomboid has been formed as a rudiment, it is not hard to conceive how new crystalline or selenitic matter, applied to it, adapts itself to the planes and angles already formed and gives rise to many new rhomboidal bodies of the same figure. As for the optical phenomena peculiar to Icelandic crystal, they are of such subtlety and loftiness that they can neither be solved nor, once solved, understood without a deeper knowledge of optics itself, as will be clear from the authors cited on this matter. It does not seem right, however, to send the curious reader away without his having drawn at least something from the source from which the streams of solutions flow. It will therefore be enough to indicate briefly that most, indeed all, of the phenomena of this crystal or selenite are to be derived from the peculiar structure and texture of the stone itself, by which it is not a single fragment or absolutely continuous, but composed of distinct laminae or flakes lying in various ways against one another, so that in some places these distinct laminae produce only one refraction, in others two or more. The celebrated men Bartholinus and Huygens investigate and demonstrate all this more carefully and at greater length, and I therefore refer the reader to them.

units.la: VIII. Inæqualitates quòd spectat, & heterogeneitates in planis Crystalli conspicuas, debentur illæ causis externis, nimirum, vel succo minerali & metallico, Crystallo jam formatæ accedenti, vel arenulis aliisque terrestribus particulis è tabulato cavitatis superioris in Crystalli præsertim pyramides delapsis. A succo metallico fit, ut Crystalli habeantur obductæ, vel ipso puro puto Auro, vel Cœruleo, &Chrysocolla, vel Spato, vel illis insideant Pyritarum, sive Marcasitarum cubi, de quarum generatione speciatim videatur Steno, p.75. & Sqq. Atque hac occasione notari meretur, Crystallum durante adhæsione extraneæ materiæ posse existere vel adhuc parum fluidam, & quasi mollem, vel jam plenè induratam; Prius si statuatur, potest formari conceptus probabilis de foveolis in superficie lapidis conspicuis, ut arenæ, vel aliæ terrestres particulæ delapsæ sese in molliusculam adhuc Crystallinam massam insinuaverint, postea autem duritie inducta, & poris magis constrictis, fuerint vel sponte elapsæ, vel, seu arte, seu natura, quasi elotæ, remanentibus postea exiguis illis foveolis, sive cavitatibus, nisi malueris dicere, quòd Crystalli superficies, jam plenè indurata, à succo quodam acri Aquæ forti æmulo fuerit erosa. Posterius locum invenit, ubi materia Crystallos obducens superficiei externæ adhæret quidem, nulla tamen sui vestigia imprimit, quo casu lentor quidam & viscidi-tas ipsius materiæ adhærescentis, vel saltem gluten aliquod interveniens potest admitti. Exigua tandem tubercula quòd attinet variolas æmulantia, oriri ea possunt, dum in fluido particulæ solidæ Crystallinæ hinc inde errantes, in ipso actu Crystallisationis ad prisma pressæ superficiei postea adhæserunt, vel, ut Steno, p.62. autumat, à particulis minutis oleofis, quæ fluido supernatârunt, sese poris istis Crystalli insinuârunt.
units.tr: VIII. As for the inequalities and heterogeneities visible on the faces of the crystal, they are due to external causes, namely either to a mineral and metallic juice coming to a crystal already formed, or to grains of sand and other earthy particles that have fallen from the upper roof of the cavity, especially onto the pyramids of the crystal. Through metallic juice it happens that crystals are seen to be coated, either with pure gold itself, or with blue copper ore and chrysocolla, or with spar, or else Pyrites or Marcasite cubes sit upon them; on how these arise, see Steno, p. 75 and following. On this occasion it deserves to be noted that, while a foreign matter adheres to it, a crystal may exist either while still fairly fluid and somewhat soft, or when already fully hardened. If the first is supposed, a probable concept can be formed of the little pits visible on the surface of the stone: grains of sand or other earthy particles, having fallen, may have insinuated themselves into the still soft crystalline mass; afterwards, when hardness set in and the pores were more tightly closed, they either slipped out of their own accord or were washed out, by art or by nature, leaving those small pits or cavities behind, unless you prefer to say that the surface of the crystal, already fully hardened, was eroded by some sharp juice rivalling aqua fortis. The second possibility applies where the matter coating the crystals adheres to the outer surface but leaves no trace of itself impressed on it; in that case a certain stickiness and viscosity of the adhering matter, or at least some intervening glue, may be admitted. As for the small tubercles resembling pustules, they can arise when, in the fluid, solid crystalline particles wandering here and there have afterwards adhered to the surface pressed against the prism during the very act of crystallisation; or, as Steno, p. 62, suggests, they have insinuated themselves into those pores of the crystal from small oily particles that floated on top of the fluid.

units.la: IX. Heterogeneitatibus superficiei externæ, in Phænomeno præcedente expositis, ad ea accedimus, quae in ipso Crystallini corporis medio conspiciuntur, & variis etiam nominibus ansam praebuerunt. Sunt autem hae, generaliter loquendo, nihil aliud quam particulae crassiores non pellucidae, in fluido externo Crystallos ambiente vagantes, & ipsi postea Crystallinae massae penitius immixtae. Atque hic non praetereundum esse puto, heterogenea illa varia, festucas, paleas, herbas, folia, aquam, aerem, pilos &c. manifestissimo indicio, gemmas omnes, etiam durissimas, (quum de Adamante ipso idem testentur Historiae) initio fuisse fluidas. Modus autem, quo includi queant id genus heterogenea, non ita proclivis; Urget hinc Steno p.58[?]. Non posse dici in fluido aqueo concrevisse Crystallum, quum 1. Certum sit una cum aqua aerem ibi contineri. 2. Dari multas Crystallos solum aerem includentes. 3. Si in fluido aqueo concrevisset Crystallus, omnia spatio undique clausa plena essent aqua, quandoquidem eo modo detentam aquam nullo seculorum numero evanescere constans observatio sit. Ast quod attinet. 1. Hoc non tam pro Stenone, quam pro nobis militat, quum omnibus modernae, experimentalis, praesertim philosophiae Sectatoribus extra omne dubium sit, omni aquae intermisceri aerem, qui adeo simul cum aqua Crystalli cavitati facile potuit, imo debuit includi. 2. Speciosius quidem, non tamen invictum, quum durante constrictione Crystallinae materiae ab ambiente fluido aqueo aqua correpta & incarcerata facile potuit particulis suis laevibus, oblongis ac flexibilibus per rimas Crystalli nondum consolidatae elabi, aere interim, ob figurae suae ramosae inaequalitatem, ad penetrandum inceptoris, intus manente. 3. Itidem non stringit, quoniam non supponitur spatium, (sive materia Crystallos ambiens) ita arcte clausum, ut aqua, vel fluida, vel in vapores resoluta transire nequeat, & saepissime fissurae in id genus lapidibus Crystallum continentibus oculis ipsis observantur, imo his licet oculis nudis non conspiciantur, aqua tamen residua statim a calore subterraneo attenuata exhalare potest. Ipse Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virtut: p.15. Ex lapidibus Crystallinis in cavitatibus lapidum reperiundis colligit, extitisse ibi liquorem, in quo concurrerint nitidae particulae, quamquam progressu temporis residua & incoagulabilis pars ejus forsan fuerit imbibita per materiam ambientem, nisi per eandem evolavit, virtute peculiaris cujusdam congruitatis cum poris lapidis. Quod non videatur impossibile, quandoquidem experientia nos docuit, solidos quosdam lapides (excipio gemmas) posse (quanquam lente) penetrari ab aqua, vel aquam posse texturam illarum alterare. Non interim hisce meis ratiociniis improbarim illarum cavitatem, aquam vel aerem continentium genesin a Stenone p.63. memoratam. Quod scilicet, In illis planis, ubi nova materia Crystallina relicta fuerit, accedens nova materia Crystallina, & super eadem loca extensa, cavitates ibi formet, interdum lamellas plures producat, nonnunquam externi fluidi partem includat, quod modo purus aër est, modo cum aëre aqua. Cui opinioni tantò lubentius subscribimus, quia nec nostræ, nec Stenoniana Hypothesi est adversa, & aliis heterogeneis inclusis, ut herbis, paleis &c. æque applicari potest. Nec improbabimus sententiam de Aqua in Crystallo contenta Fortunii Liceti de Spontan: Vivent: Ort: p.314. Quòd à frigore aqueum illum humorem in lapideam duritiem cogente solum concretæ fuerint partes exteriores, quas undique ambiebat, ejus vi fracta, & actione intermissa priusquam intimas humoris partes congelaret, in quibus sub prioris aquæ specie remanentibus forte fortuna consistens fragmentum corporis atri permanserit inclusum ab ambiente Crystallo. Quinimo fieri etiam potuit, ut humoris illius partibus exterioribus agenti frigori propinquioribus in Crystallum perfectè mutatis intimiores in glaciem solum minori gradu concretionis riguerint, ac postea remoto frigore, calor ambientis non ita vehemens glaciem internam dissolvere potuerit in aquam; Externum verò Crystallum eliquare minimè potuerit. Ratiocinio favet experimentum vini Oligophori, quod vehementissimo frigori expositum, atque glaciatum, in medio massæ glacialis exhibet partem Vini spirituosissimam congelari ineptam. Potest autem hoc Phænomenon Sp. Vini ab aquosioribus partibus separati & in meditullio concentrati ad aquam in Crystallo contentâ commodè applicari, & Hypothesi nostræ de Crystalli ortu ex fluido accommodari; Interim tanquam falsam rejicimus Hypothesin Liceti ex glacie ortum Crystalli derivantis. Antimonii tandem Crystallisati fila & striàs corpori Crystallino inclusas quòd attinet, statuendum est, quòd nominatæ Antimonii Crystalli fundo cavitatis jam adnatæ, & acuum adinstar rigentes, Crystallos ibi delapsas, & adhuc ex parte fluidas perfoderint, sicuti hoc inspectiones talium Crystallorum, & particulæ Antimonii in medio Crystalli quasi diffractæ à posteriori confirmant.
units.tr: IX. From the heterogeneities of the outer surface, set out in the preceding phenomenon, we come to those that are seen in the middle of the crystalline body itself and have also given occasion for various names. These, speaking generally, are nothing other than thicker, non-transparent particles wandering in the external fluid surrounding the crystals, and later mixed more deeply into the crystalline mass. Here I think it should not be passed over that these various heterogeneous things, such as straws, chaff, grass, leaves, water, air, hairs, etc., are a very clear indication that all gems, even the hardest (as histories also testify concerning the diamond itself), were at first fluid. The manner, however, in which heterogeneous things of this kind can be enclosed is not so easily explained. Steno, p. 58[?], presses the point: it cannot be said that the crystal grew in a watery fluid, since (1) it is certain that air is contained there together with the water; (2) there are many crystals enclosing only air; (3) if the crystal had grown in a watery fluid, all the enclosed spaces would be full of water, since it is constant observation that water so held never vanishes in any number of ages. But as for these points: (1) this tells not so much for Steno as for us, since it is beyond all doubt for all adherents of the modern, experimental philosophy, especially, that air is mixed into all water, and so it could easily, indeed must, have been enclosed in the cavity of the crystal along with the water. (2) This objection is more specious, but not unanswerable: while the crystalline matter was still soft, water caught up from the surrounding watery fluid could easily have slipped out, with its smooth, elongated and flexible particles, through the cracks of the crystal not yet consolidated, while the air, because of the branching irregularity of its shape, remained inside, being unable to penetrate. (3) Nor does this objection press hard, since it is not supposed that the space (or the material surrounding the crystals) is so tightly closed that water, whether fluid or resolved into vapours, cannot pass through; and very often cracks are observed with the eyes themselves in stones of this kind containing crystals; indeed, even when they are not seen with the naked eye, the remaining water, at once thinned out by subterranean heat, can exhale. Boyle himself, in On the Origin and Virtues of Gems, p. 15, from crystalline stones found in cavities of rocks, infers that a liquor existed there in which bright particles came together, although in the course of time its residual and non-coagulable part was perhaps soaked up by the surrounding matter, unless it flew out through the same by virtue of a certain peculiar congruity with the pores of the stone. This does not seem impossible, since experience has taught us that certain solid stones (I except gems) can be penetrated, though slowly, by water, or that water can alter their texture. Nor, by these reasonings of mine, do I wish to reject the genesis of those cavities containing water or air that Steno, p. 63, mentions: namely, that in those planes where new crystalline matter has been left behind, new crystalline matter that comes later and extends over the same places forms cavities there, sometimes produces several lamellae, and sometimes encloses a part of the external fluid, which is now pure air, now water with air. To this opinion I subscribe all the more willingly, because it is opposed neither to our hypothesis nor to Steno's, and it can equally be applied to other heterogeneous things enclosed, such as grass, straw, etc. Nor shall I reject the view of Fortunio Liceti, On Spontaneous Generation, p. 314, concerning the water contained in crystal: that when the cold compelled that watery humour to harden into stony hardness, only the outer parts that surrounded it on all sides were congealed, their force broken and their action interrupted before the inner parts of the humour froze; and that, among these inner parts which remained in the form of the former water, by chance a fragment of a dark body remained enclosed by the surrounding crystal. Indeed, it could also have happened that, when the outer parts of that humour, nearer to the external cold, had been wholly changed into crystal, the inner parts stiffened into ice only to a lesser degree of congealing; and afterwards, once the cold was removed, the not very vehement heat of the surroundings could dissolve the inner ice into water, but could not melt the outer crystal at all. The experiment with Oligophorus's wine favours this reasoning: when wine is exposed to the most intense cold and frozen, it shows, in the middle of the mass of ice, the most spirituous part of the wine unable to freeze. This phenomenon of spirit of wine separated from its more watery parts and concentrated in the centre can be conveniently applied to the water contained in the crystal, and fitted to our hypothesis of the crystal's origin from a fluid. Meanwhile, we reject as false the hypothesis of Liceti that derives the origin of the crystal from ice. Finally, as for the threads and streaks of crystallised antimony enclosed in the crystalline body, it must be held that those crystals of antimony, already attached to the bottom of the cavity and stiffening like needles, pierced through the crystals that had fallen there and were still partly fluid; as the inspection of such crystals and the particles of antimony, as if broken off in the middle of the crystal, confirm from the outcome.

units.la: X. Crystalli in magnitudine variatio non aliunde feré dependet quàm à materiæ ipsius Crystallinæ in fluido existentis abundantia, vel defectu, ubi simul attendi debet textura & constitutio materiæ solidæ ambientis, sive ea metallica fuerit, sive lapidea, inde enim arcessi debet materia nova Crystallis jam formatis apponenda, ita ut Crystalli majores majoresque evadant, si illius pori fuerint particulis Crystallinis caloris ope in cavitatem expellendis repleti. Nec silentio involvenda est conditio loci ipsius, sive cavitatis, in qua formari debent Crystalli, prout enim illa magna fuerit, vel parva, puto progigni etiam majores, vel minores Crystallos, sicuti Chymici etiam observant, Crystallos tantò majores fieri, quantò vas ipsum in quo Crystallisatio fit, majus est, & amplius. Tandem, ratio quoque habenda est ipsius fluidi, in quo Crystallisatio naturalis debet peragi; prout enim illud fuerit vel copiosum, vel paucum; citæ, vel tardæ; quietæ, vel turbatæ evaporationi expositum, variabit ipsa quoque Crystallorum magnitudo, & ipsa quoque in diaphaneitate perfectio. Audiamus Bohn: de Crystallisatione Chymica Differt: Chymico-Phys: XIII. §.24. Ita differentem. Encherisis Operationis hujus potissima in proportionata humiditatis aquæ separatione consistit, quam evaporatio utplurimum, rarius distillatio præstat, cujusque terminum pellicula, seu crusta tenuior, superficiei solutionis innatans, tanquam primum Crystallisationis inchoamentum, monstrat: quem qui non attingit, propter nimis discontinuatas & commotas adhuc particulas salinas, Crystallos frustra expectabit, aut exilissimos tantum sibi comparabit; qui transit, seu excedit, loco Crystallorum diaphanorum crassamentum inconditum, & ab illorum forma sæpe quàm alienissimum acquiret, vel quòd particulæ salinæ per spatii, seu medii fluidi angustias confusè magis sibi adigantur, vel quòd illo aquæ dimenso, quam ad Crystallisationem postulant, defraudentur.
units.tr: X. The variation in the size of crystals depends almost entirely on the abundance or scarcity of the crystalline matter present in the fluid. At the same time, one must consider the texture and constitution of the surrounding solid matter, whether metallic or stony, for new matter to be added to crystals already formed must be drawn from there. Thus the crystals become larger and larger if their pores are filled with crystalline particles, which are driven into the cavity with the help of heat. Nor should the condition of the place itself, that is, of the cavity in which crystals are to form, be passed over in silence. For I think that larger or smaller crystals are produced according as that place is large or small, just as chemists also observe that crystals become larger the bigger and roomier the vessel in which crystallisation takes place. Finally, account must also be taken of the fluid in which natural crystallisation is to be carried out. According as it is abundant or scanty, quick or slow, at rest or disturbed, and exposed to evaporation, the size of the crystals and their perfection in transparency will also vary. Let us hear Bohn, On Chemical Crystallisation, Chymico-Physical Dissertation XIII, §24, who speaks as follows: "The chief management of this operation consists in separating the water from the moisture in due proportion, which evaporation mostly, and more rarely distillation, accomplishes. Its limit is shown by a thin skin or crust floating on the surface of the solution, as the first beginning of crystallisation. Whoever does not reach this point, because the saline particles are still too loose and agitated, will wait in vain for crystals, or will obtain only very tiny ones. Whoever passes beyond it, will instead of transparent crystals acquire a shapeless crust, quite unlike their form, either because the saline particles are driven confusedly together through the narrowness of the space or medium of the fluid, or because they are deprived of that measure of water which they need for crystallisation."

units.la: XI. Qui è principiis Physicis generalem hausit duritiei conceptum, quòd nimirum illa præsertim consistat in partium solidarum firma compactione, & fluidarum molliumque exclusione, & insuper ad ea, quæ de petrefactione suprà generatim expositimus, vel parùm attendit, ei non difficile est, Crystallorum in duritie differentias, & explicare, & concipere. Quòd si rotundæ Crystalli aliis sint duriores, dependet id manifestè ab homogeneitate ipsarum particularum solidarum, & æquali undique pressione versus medium facta, quo ipso pororum structura non solùm multò compactior evasit, sed imprimis partes Centrum ambientes solidiores, durioresque evasisse oportuit, ut nunc taceamus, esse hanc proprietatem omnibus corporibus sphæricis communem, quòd ictibus præ aliis magis resistant, ex aliis Physico-Mathematicis principiis deducendam.
units.tr: XI. Whoever has drawn from physical principles the general concept of hardness, namely that it consists chiefly in the firm compaction of solid parts and the exclusion of fluid and soft parts, and has paid little attention to what we have set out above in general about petrifaction, will not find it difficult to explain and understand the differences in the hardness of crystals. If round crystals are harder than others, this clearly depends on the homogeneity of their solid particles and on the equal pressure exerted from every side towards the centre. By this very means the structure of the pores has become not only much more compact, but the parts surrounding the centre must especially have become more solid and harder. To say nothing now of the fact that this property, by which spherical bodies resist blows more than others, is to be derived from other physico-mathematical principles.

units.la: XII. Sicuti ad propagationem generis humani, et bruti, plantarum item, necessaria est partium Organicarum decens textura, & Ovulorum, unde formari debent, tum perfectio, tum in loco, vel matrice convenienti augmentatio; ita ad novam mineralium, metallorumque, vel consumptorum, vel excisorum regenerationem nihil aliud requiritur, quàm nova ejus generis particularum præsentia, & in loco debito adhæsio. Ex hisce facillimè inferri potest, quid statuendum sit de Crystallorum regeneratione, & quomodo sententiarum circa hanc rem divortia sint concilianda, nimirum, si cavitates Saxis inclusæ talem habeant ambientem solidamque materiam, quæ non solùm materia, sive semifeminio quasi Crystallino sit prægnans, sed & pororum habeat talem structuram, ut externo motore accedente partes illæ Crystallinæ possint è poris suis in cavitatem dictam protrudi, non difficile omnino est, quomodo cavitas Crystallo exhausta de novo possit id genus lapidibus adimpleri, præsertim si alia quoque Crystallisationis debitæ adsint requisita, ut fluidum in decenti quantitate ibi existens, &c. Ubi contrà lapidea massa cavitatem includens Crystallina omni materia sit vacua, & pori obstructi, fluidum item nullum adsit (sicuti certè raro cunctæ hæ conditiones ad Crystallisationem necessariæ postant, adeoque regeneratio Adamantum non abs re Stenoni tantùm non pro impossibili habetur) non mirum productioni novæ locum nullum esse.
units.tr: XII. Just as the propagation of the human race, of animals, and likewise of plants requires a suitable texture of organic parts, and both the perfection of the eggs from which they are to be formed and their growth in a suitable place or womb, so for the new regeneration of minerals and metals, whether consumed or cut away, nothing else is required than the presence of new particles of that kind and their adhesion in the proper place. From these points it can very easily be inferred what must be held about the regeneration of crystals, and how the disagreements of opinion on this matter are to be reconciled. Namely, if the cavities enclosed in rocks have a surrounding solid matter which is not only pregnant with crystalline matter, as it were a half-seminal substance, but also has such a structure of pores that, when an external mover approaches, those crystalline parts can be pushed out of their pores into the said cavity, it is not at all difficult to see how a cavity emptied of crystal can be filled again with such a stone, especially if the other requisites for crystallisation are also present, such as fluid existing there in a suitable quantity, and so on. Where, on the contrary, the stony mass enclosing the crystalline cavity is empty of all matter and its pores are blocked, and no fluid is present (for indeed all these conditions necessary for crystallisation are rarely present together, and so the regeneration of diamonds is by Steno not without reason regarded as almost impossible), it is no wonder that there is no room for new production.

units.la: XIII. Crystallum substantiæ & Originis esse lapideæ, & mineralis potius, quàm glacialis, & aquæ, vel hoc unico constat argumento, quòd percussa scintillas edat, ut hinc ratio hujus Phænomeni Cartesianis æquè ac Veteribus eadem sit, quæ prosilientis ignis è silice percusso, quòd nempe, propter structuræ firmam compagem, à violenta collisione pori aperiantur, ut particulæ igneæ (vel Chymicorum Sulphur) prosilire queant, & à subtilissima primi elementi in motum citatissimum rapi. Experimentum Cafato memoratum, quòd Crystalli basis plures emittat scintillas, quàm pyramis, ita solvi potest. Quòd illa Sulphure, vel particulis igneis imprægnata copiosioribus & fixioribus, hæc autem, quia est purior, laxior, pauciboribus[?], & fere nullis. Quòd tandem in lentes formata rem sibi objectam facilè inflammabilem accendat, ratio est eadem quæ aliarum lentium, ex Opticis principiis arcessenda, refractio, nempe, & concentratio radiorum solarium in focum à lente magis vel minùs distantem.
units.tr: XIII. That the substance and origin of crystal is stony and mineral rather than icy and watery is established by this single argument alone: when struck it gives off sparks. So the explanation of this phenomenon is the same for the Cartesians as for the ancients, as with fire leaping out of struck flint. Namely, because of the firm compactness of its structure, the pores are opened by violent collision, so that the igneous particles (or the Sulphur of the chemists) can leap out and are snatched into very rapid motion by the most subtle first element. The experiment of Cafato mentioned above, that the base of a crystal gives off more sparks than its point, can be solved thus: the one is impregnated more abundantly and more fixedly with sulphur or igneous particles, while the point, because it is purer and looser, gives fewer, and almost none. Finally, that when formed into lenses it readily sets fire to an object placed before it, the reason is the same as for other lenses and must be drawn from optical principles: namely refraction, and the concentration of the solar rays into a focus at a greater or lesser distance from the lens.

units.la: XIV. Crystalli nomen qui Vitro imposuerunt, non valdè meo judicio errârunt, tanta quippe inter hæc duo, in colore, diaphaneitate, fragilitate, & haud dubiè etiam textura est affinitas, ut facilè unum pro altero accipi possit; Ut Vitra Veneta in Littore Murano parari solita, quæ aliis præstantiora, ad Crystallum proximè accedunt, vulgò etiam vitra Crystallina nuncupantur. Qui igitur modum, vel rationem fracti ab infuso calido liquore vitri intellexerit, is non amplius mirabitur, Crystallo idem obtingere posse, sive nunc fragilitas Vitri, & sic etiam Crystalli, cum Cartesianis inde desumenda sit, quòd superficies, secundùm quas eorum particulæ se invicem tangunt, sint admodum exiguæ & parvæ, sive, juxta Nulandum, Cartesianarum Hypothesium impugnatorem, Element. Phys. p. 511. Vitri particulæ constent figuris magnum vacuum admittentibus, invicem tamen firmiter connexis, sive cum Chymicis dicatur structura vitri fragilis dependere à Sale, cujus particulæ rigidiores sunt quàm ut ad flexionem corpus aliquod disponant,sive cum Morhoff: de Scyph: Vitreo &c. C.III.p.53. statuatur, vitri texturam ex armillis rigidiusculis constare, facile ipsa fractio Vitri vel Crystalli, ex singulis his Hypothesibus explicari potest, Ut e.g. Armillæ hæ parùm flexiles ab externo impellente, quale est aqua fervida, ultra resiliendi potentiam compressæ dissiliant, ipseque aër vi quadam erumpens, vel irruens, ipsum Vitrum rumpat, sicuti ita ratiocinatur Morhoff: C.L.C.VIII.p.120.
units.tr: XIV. Those who gave crystal its name to glass were, in my judgment, not greatly mistaken. There is such a great affinity between the two in colour, transparency, fragility, and undoubtedly also in texture, that one can easily be taken for the other. Thus the Venetian glasses usually made on the shore of Murano, which surpass the others and come closest to crystal, are commonly also called crystal glasses. Whoever therefore understands the manner or reason by which glass breaks when hot liquid is poured into it will no longer be surprised that the same can happen to crystal. Whether the fragility of glass, and so also of crystal, is to be derived, with the Cartesians, from the fact that the surfaces by which their particles touch one another are very small and slight; or, according to Nuland, an opponent of the Cartesian hypotheses, Elements of Physics, p. 511, the particles of glass consist of figures admitting a large void yet firmly connected with one another; or whether, as the chemists say, the structure of fragile glass depends on salt, whose particles are too rigid to dispose the body to bending; or whether, as Morhof, On Glass Drinking Vessels, ch. III, p. 53, holds, the texture of glass consists of somewhat stiff rings. The breaking of glass or crystal can easily be explained by each of these hypotheses. For example, these rings, not very flexible, when pressed by an external impelling force, such as boiling water, beyond the power of springing back, burst apart; and the air itself, breaking out or rushing in with a certain force, breaks the glass, as Morhof reasons in ch. VIII, p. 120.

units.la: XV. Posse liquorem aliquem facilè in momento quasi alterare corporis alicujus colorem, experimento Crystalli excandefacti in frigida restincti, & ex pellucido album induentis colorem, pulchrè ostendit Illust: Boyle, & ex sua Colorum Hypothesi, Tractat: De Gemm: Orig: & Virt: p.8.9. Ut & Tract: de Coloribus p.m.50.96. facilè explicat, quod nimirum mutatio illa fuerit inducta divisione Crystalli in multitudinem minutissimarum partium, seu totidem distinctarum superficierum, quæ valdè reflectunt lumen quaquaversum, extrorsum, & sic albo tinctum colore Corpus reddunt, eoque vel magis, vel minus vivido,quò vel plures, vel pauciores fuerint particulæ, vel grandiores, vel minutiores, aut alio modo aptæ diffundendis radiis luminis, sicut videre est in limatulo Vitro Veneto redu&to in pulverem, quod album referet speciem. Quòd si nunc frigidæ loco sumatur tinctura Cochinellæ, vel alia colorata, non mirum videri debet, si ab ejus particulis intra Crystalli fissuras sese insinuantibus pulcher ei concilietur color.
units.tr: XV. That a liquid can easily alter the colour of a body almost in a moment, the illustrious Boyle has nicely shown by the experiment of crystal heated until red and quenched in cold water, which from transparent takes on a white colour. From his own hypothesis of colours, Treatise on the Origin and Virtues of Gems, pp. 8, 9, and Treatise on Colours, pp. 50, 96, he easily explains that this change was brought about by the division of the crystal into a multitude of very minute parts, or as many distinct surfaces, which strongly reflect light in every direction outward, and so render the body white in colour, more or less vivid according as the particles are more or fewer, larger or smaller, or otherwise suited to scatter the rays of light. This can be seen in Venetian glass filed into powder, which presents a white appearance. But if instead of cold water a tincture of cochineal or another coloured liquid is used, it should be no wonder if a fine colour is imparted to the crystal by its particles insinuating themselves into the fissures of the crystal.

units.la: XVI. Porositatem Vitri atque Crystalli diu multumque pro & contra ventilatam adstruere videtur & hoc experimentum, quo Crystallus Chymicâ arte, etiam absque ignitione, coloribus aliquantùm pervadentibus tingi potest, ita ut pro solutione Phænomeni statuendum necessariò sit, poros Crystalli satis esse patentes pro vaporum mineralium vel tingentium admissione.
units.tr: XVI. The porosity of glass and crystal seems to be established by the long and much-debated arguments both for and against it; and this experiment, in which crystal can be tinted by chemical art, even without fire, with colours that penetrate it somewhat, also points that way, so that to solve the phenomenon it must necessarily be held that the pores of crystal are open enough to admit mineral vapours or tinting agents.

units.la: XVII. Et hoc Phænomeno porositatem Crystalli probari posse concedat, qui attractionum magneticarum, vel Electricarum, modum atque rationem ex modernorum Philosophia didicit, ubi nempe statuitur subtilis quædam materia ipsum corpus pervadere, vel sponte, vel poris attritu magis apertis, tantâ copiâ, ut aër vicinus loco pulsus levicula adsita ad Corpus magneticum pellat. Ipse Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virtut: s.II.p.m.34. Ut in gratiam Medicorum, præsertim Antiquiorum, afferat exspirationem effluviorum ex ipsis gemmis pellucidis, testatur sibi esse adamantem, qui leviter frictus, valdè, & ad admirationem spectatorum attrahit, & p.35. Se asservare alium Adamantem, cujus facultas electrica excitatur non tantùm frictione, sed & languido gradu caloris adventitii.. Et Velsch: Hecat: I. Obs: 85. Uti adamantes, itaque gemmas, & lapides quosvis magneticos reddi posse magnetis affrictu frequentiori autumat.
units.tr: XVII. Let this phenomenon also be granted as proof that crystal is porous, for one who has learned from the philosophy of the moderns the manner and reason of magnetic and electrical attractions, where it is namely held that a certain subtle matter permeates the body itself, either spontaneously or with its pores opened more by rubbing, in such quantity that the neighbouring air, pushed out of place, drives a light object placed near the magnetic body. Boyle himself, in De Gemmarum Origine et Virtutibus, sect. 2, p. 34, to oblige the physicians, especially the ancient ones, asserts that there is an emanation of effluvia from transparent gems themselves; he testifies that he possesses a diamond which, when lightly rubbed, attracts strongly and to the astonishment of onlookers, and at p. 35 that he keeps another diamond whose electrical power is excited not only by friction but also by a feeble degree of adventitious heat. And Velschius, Hecatontas I, obs. 85, holds that diamonds, and thus gems and any stones whatever, can be made magnetic by more frequent rubbing with a magnet.

units.la: CAPUT VI. Crystalli Usum Medicum subjciens.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. Setting out the medical use of crystal.

units.la: Gemmas, pretiosiores præsertim, tam multas & insignes possidere in morbis profligandis virtutes, quantas iis adscripserant Veteres, audacter asserere non audeo, innixus æquè ratione, ac modernorum, Celeberrimorumque Practicorum auctoritate, has ad Aurifabrorum Ossicinas potius, quàm Medicorum, Pharmacopolarumque repositoria relegantium. Non negans interim Illustr: Boylio, posse Virtutes gemmarum, tam pellucidarum, quàm opacarum, si quæ adforent, speciosè & Philosophiæ modernæ convenienter applicari ex ipsa nostra, quam supra in Phænomenorum solutione fusius expositimus, Hypothesi, speciatim ex ingenti specifica gravitate gemmarum ex mineralibus & Metallicis substantiis, quæ gemmis insunt, & ab iis obtineri & separari possunt, ex effluviis item variis, quæ, non obstante eorum subtilitate, insignes valent in humores nostros & Spiritus exerere virtutes; Sicuti, cuncta hæc pro more subtiliter & latè deducit Vir Laudatissimus S.II. Integra.p.m.30-58. Quoniam autem gemmæ expeti possunt, vel propter substantiam & consistentiam, quâ constant, vel propter colorem & tincturam, quâ imbuuntur, illa autem, ut supra hinc inde monui, cùm nihil aliud sit, quàm Crystallus ad majorem evecta duritiem, hæc autem tam pauca sit, ut vix mereatur considerationem, omnino recte egerunt Recentiores, substituendo omnibus aliis gemmis, nostram tanquam gemmarum mollissimam, de cujus viribus, pro exiguitate temporis mihi relicti, paucula quædam proferre lubet, nec tamen confarcinare ea, quæ Auctores passim de Crystalli viribus prædicârunt, sed sontes duntaxat indicare ex quibus vires hujus lapidis probatæ, eæque restrictæ derivari queant; sunt autem generaliter loquendo, partim adstringentes, partim aperientes, ubi tamen statim notandum, habendam esse rationem temporis, & contrarietatem hanc non tam esse veram, quàm apparentem. Enimverò adstringere potest, uti cuncta Veteribus dicta frigida & sicca, quæ Recentioribus audiunt terrea, absorbentia, præcipitantia, quæ vel partium suarum crassitie, & figura, alterius corporis partes constringunt, spicula acida, vel salina, in corpore prædominanminantia[?] diffringunt, vel humores mobiles nimis & efferos concentrant, constringunt, & ad quietem reducunt ; Aperire, quatenus absorbendo coagulum impediunt; vias patulas præstant, & poros reddunt liberos. Ob adstringendi virtutem, & inde dependentes alias vires, commendatur ad temperandum quodvis acidum acrius, ad corrigendam bilem æruginosam, adeoque in atrocioribus infantum torminibus, pavoribus eorum nocturnis, Cholera, Diarrhoea, Dysenteria, Melancholia, Mania, Febre quartana, Gonorrhoea, tum simplici, tum virulenta, Cancro &c. Specificum perhibetur Antidotum, Arsenici, Mercurii sublìmati, Aquæ fortis ; Aperitiva vis Crystallum commendat in obstructionibus viscerum, Menstruum, Febribus, affectibus Capitis, Calculo, Arthritide; Præsertim specifica, & valde decantata est lac augendi vis, ceu quæ inter [?]τὰ πολυγαλακτικὰ[?] præcipuè eminet. Licèt vulgata quoque sit persuasio, Crystallum dorso applicatam lac potius imminuere, scilicet vi frigoris repellendo, ut influxurus in mammas liquor avertatur, vel, quod vero videtur similius, ob eandem rationem nervos è spinali medulla prodeuntes, & ad mammas tendentes constringendo, quo ipso Spirituū, alias, pro lactis secretione peragenda, jugiter & vividè influentium, motus atque influxus non parum retardatur. Ut autem ad optatum, sibique præfixum pervenirent scopum Medici, Crystallum variè præparârunt, sive diversimodè ignis torturæ subjecerunt, unde prostant, Crystallus præparata in specie sic dicta, Sal. Magisterium, Oleum, seu Liquor, Elixir, Essentia, Cremor, Syrupus Crystalli &c. Quibus tamen omnibus præfert Accuratissimus Pharmaciæ Corrector, Daniel Ludovicus, Pharm: Differt: I. p.415. Crystallum simpliciter saltem pulverisatam & præparatam, quam porro aliis pro lubitu intermiscere licet. Ita celebratur Exc: D.D.Theod: Zvinger. Sicher und geschwinder Arzt. p.m.§99.
