units.tr: I do not dare to assert boldly that gems, especially the more precious ones, possess as many and as remarkable powers for overcoming diseases as the ancients ascribed to them. I rely on reason and on the authority of modern and very celebrated practitioners, who relegate these stones to the workshops of goldsmiths rather than to the storerooms of physicians and apothecaries. Meanwhile I do not deny that the Illustrious Boyle can apply the powers of gems, both transparent and opaque, if they have any, in a plausible way and in keeping with modern philosophy. This can be done according to our own hypothesis, which I set out more fully in the solution of the phenomena above. In particular, it can be done through the great specific gravity of gems, which comes from the minerals and metallic substances contained in them and which can be drawn out and separated from them, and also through various effluvia which, despite their subtlety, exert remarkable powers on our humours and spirits. That most praiseworthy man, S. II. Integra, pp. 30–58, deduces all this subtly and at length, as is his custom. Since gems may be sought either for the substance and consistency of which they consist, or for the colour and tint with which they are imbued, and since the former (as I have pointed out here and there above) is nothing other than crystal raised to a greater hardness, while the latter is so slight that it hardly deserves consideration, the more recent writers have rightly acted in substituting our crystal for all other gems, as the softest of them. Given the brevity of the time left to me, I am pleased to set forth a few things about its powers. I will not, however, cram together everything the authors have claimed in various places about the powers of crystal, but will only point out the sources from which the proven powers of this stone, and those limited ones, can be derived. Generally speaking, these powers are partly astringent and partly opening, though here it must be noted at once that this contrariety must be considered with regard to the time, and that it is not so much real as apparent. For it can astringe, as all the things the ancients called cold and dry, which the moderns call earthy, absorbent and precipitating, do. They constrict the parts of another body either by the thickness and shape of their own parts, or they break up the acid or saline spicules that predominate in the body, or they concentrate and constrict humours that are too mobile and wild and bring them back to rest. It opens, inasmuch as by absorbing it impedes coagulation; it provides open passages and makes the pores free. Because of its astringent power, and the other powers that depend on it, crystal is commended for tempering any acid that is too sharp, for correcting verdigris-like bile, and so in the more severe colics of infants, their night terrors, cholera, diarrhoea, dysentery, melancholy, mania, quartan fever, gonorrhoea, both simple and virulent, cancer and so on. It is said to be a specific antidote to arsenic, sublimate of mercury and aqua fortis. Its aperient power commends crystal for obstructions of the viscera, menstruation, fevers, affections of the head, stone and arthritis. Especially specific and much celebrated is its power of increasing milk, which stands out above the other galactagogues. Although it is also a common belief that crystal applied to the back rather diminishes milk, namely by repelling with the force of cold, so that the fluid that would flow into the breasts is turned away, or, what seems truer, for the same reason by constricting the nerves that issue from the spinal marrow and run to the breasts, whereby the motion and influx of the spirits, which flow continually and vigorously for the production of milk, are not a little slowed. But so that physicians might reach the desired goal they had set themselves, they prepared crystal in various ways, or subjected it in different ways to the torture of fire. From this come the preparations of crystal known by that name: salt, magisterium, oil or liquor, elixir, essence, cream, syrup of crystal and so on. Yet the most accurate corrector of pharmacy, Daniel Ludovicus, Pharmacopoeia Differentiae I, p. 415, prefers to all of these crystal simply powdered and prepared, to which other things may be mixed at will. So the most excellent Dr. Theodore Zwinger is celebrated in Sicher und geschwinder Arzt p. 99, [illegible] of Dr. Wepfer the elder, Powder for Arthritis. Take: crystal powder compound, 11 ounces; prepared earthworm, 115 ounces; oriental bezoar, 15 ounces; sugar candy, 11 ounces. Mix and make a powder. Dose: 1 scruple to 3 scruples. A powder of crystals is prepared in this way: take the powder of crystal (or of the crystal stone) macerated for 24 hours in juice of citron or vinegar, 1 ounce; prepared root of arum, 1 ounce; 3 drachms; starch of arum and of bryony, of each 5 drachms; crystal, white, calcined three or four times and quenched in betony water; white succinum; Mandeville's tablets, Christ's, of each 11 ounces. Mix and make a fine powder. The Powder of Hertodt, from the Tartarus-Mastix Moravian, p. 65, can be conducive to the generation of milk. Take: prepared crystal, 2 drachms; lunar milk, 15 drachms; prepared pearl, 1 scruple; seeds of nigella, cardamom, Mary's thistle and fennel, of each 2 scruples. Mix and make a powder. Or with a sufficient quantity of sugar, dissolve in fennel-milk water, and make into lozenges. For appetite, or pain of the stomach: Dr. Michael and Dr. Sachs. Take: prepared crystal, 1 drachm; white chalk, 2 drachms; prepared eye-crab, 69 [sic], 1 drachm; prepared coral, 2 scruples. Mix and make a powder.

units.la: CAPUT VII. Usum Crystalli Mechanicum & Magi- cum indicans.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. Showing the Mechanical and Magical Use of Crystal.

units.la: Æstimium, quod Crystallis ab artibus Mechanicis, Sculptura, Cœlatura, arte tornandi, Optica, Perspectiva, aliisque pluribus accedit, si quis in latitudine sua extollere desideraret, amplissimam haberet materiem segetem; Parantur quippe ex Crystallo varia ornamenta & vasa, ut pocula, Scyphi, conspicilla, patinæ, monilia, Armillæ, Candelabra &c. Qui Antiquitatis flagrat studio, ei de Crystalli æstimatione sufficiat textus Plin: Hist: Nat: L.37. C.2. Magnitudo amplissima adhuc visa nobis erat, quam in Capitolio Livia Augusta dicaverat, Librarum circiter quinquaginta. Xenocrates Auctor est, vas amphorale visum, & aliqui ex India Crystallum sextariorum quatuor. Paulò infrà. Postremò auctoritas imponere est. Invenio Medicos, quæ sunt urenda Corporum, non aliter utilius id fieri putare, quàm Crystallina pila adversis solis posita radiis. Alius hic furor, HS.C.L.M. Trullam unam non ante multos annos mercatam à matre-familiâs, nec divite. Idem Nero amissarum rerum nuntio accepto, duos Calices Crystallinos in suprema ira fregit illisos. Hæc fuit ratio seculum suum punientis, ne quis alius ex his biberet, fragmenta nullo modo farcire queunt. Summa præsertim fuit Auctoritas calicibus & poculis Crystallinis, de quibus videantur Joh: Bruyerin: Lib:3. Dipnosoph: C.9. & Guilb: Stuckius. L.3. Antiq: Conviv: C.12. §. Vitris simillima sunt Crystallina. Et Simon: Majol: Lib: I. Canicul: dier: Colloq: 18. Existimat autem Henric: Salmuth: Comment: ad Guidon: Panciroll: Rerum deperditarum & recens inventarum. P. II.T.II.p.75. Tantum Crystallinis pretium fecisse ipsam fragilitatem, & in Testem adducit Senec: L.VII. De Beneficiis.C.9. Ipsumque Plinium Lib:33. In Prooëmio, &c. Curiosum est id, quod refert Athanas: Kirch: Mund: Subt: L.VIII.S.I.p.19. Ex Historia Regni Chile ex iis tractibus, in profunda quadam valle, quam Andium juga determinant, in medio prægrandis fluminis Insula ingentem rupem totam Crystallinam, in qua ab incolis paganis fanum integrum mira arte sit exsculptum, ex omni parte diaphanum. Alia, eaque recentiora, & forsan veriora, de arte factis ex Crystallo nunc prætereo, quia sat opinor temporis esse consumptum.
units.tr: The esteem that crystal gains from the mechanical arts (sculpture, engraving, the art of turning, optics, perspective and many others) would, if someone wished to set it out in full, give him a very rich field of material. Indeed, from crystal are made various ornaments and vessels: cups, goblets, spectacles, dishes, necklaces, armlets, candelabra, and so on. Whoever burns with love of antiquity will find enough on the value of crystal in the text of Pliny, Natural History, Book 37, chapter 2: The size of a crystal still seemed very great to us, which Livia Augusta had dedicated in the Capitol, weighing about fifty pounds. Xenocrates reports having seen a vessel the size of an amphora, and some from India a crystal of four sextarii. A little further on: Lastly, authority is decisive. I find that physicians think that the bodies to be cauterised are best treated with crystal balls placed in the rays of the sun. That was another madness: a certain mother of a household, not a rich one, bought a single bowl not many years ago. The same Nero, on hearing news of lost property, in his supreme anger broke two crystal cups by smashing them together. This was his reason for punishing his age, so that no one else might drink from them; fragments can in no way be mended. Indeed, crystal cups and drinking vessels were held in especially high regard; on these see Joh. Bruyerinus, Book 3, Dipnosophists, chapter 9, and Guilielmus Stuckius, Book 3, Antiquities of the Banquet, chapter 12, §. Crystal is very like glass. And Simon Majolus, Canicular Days, Colloquy 18. Moreover, Henricus Salmuth, Commentary on Guido Pancirollus, Lost and Recently Discovered Things, Part II, Title II, p. 75, thinks that its very fragility gave crystal such a high price, and he cites as witness Seneca, Book 7, On Benefits, chapter 9, and Pliny himself, Book 33, in the Preface, etc. It is a curious thing that Athanasius Kircher, Mundus Subterraneus, Book 8, section 1, p. 19, reports from the history of the Kingdom of Chile: in a certain deep valley among those mountain ranges that the Andes define, in the middle of a very large river there is an island with a huge rock made entirely of crystal, in which a whole temple has been carved with wonderful skill by the heathen inhabitants, and it is transparent on every side. Other accounts, more recent and perhaps more reliable, of works made from crystal I now pass over, because I think enough time has already been spent.

units.la: Κρυσταλλομαντείαν[?], seu Crystalli usum Magicum in abditis detegendis, furibus ostendendis, &c. iis relinquimus, qui superstitione & Dæ-monis monis præstigiis delusi, sibi, aliisque imponendo, saluti animarum suarum non attendunt, & veritatem rerum obscurare potius quàm proferre satagunt. De quibus interim videantur Martin: Delrio Disquis: Mag: T.II. L.IV. C.II. Q.VI. S.IV. p.400. Barthol: Anborn: Magiolog: P.II. C.V. §.2.p.512. Felix Malleolus Can: Tig: De Exorcis: Anno 1454.
units.tr: Crystallomancy [Κρυσταλλομαντείαν], or the magical use of crystal for uncovering hidden things, for exposing thieves, and so on, I leave to those who, deceived by superstition and the tricks of the demon, impose on themselves and others, do not attend to the salvation of their souls, and strive to obscure the truth rather than bring it forward. On these matters, meanwhile, see Martin Delrio, Disquisitions on Magic, Vol. II, Book IV, chapter II, Question VI, §IV, p. 400. Bartholomaeus Anhorn, Magiologia, Part II, chapter V, §2, p. 512. Felix Malleolus, On Exorcisms, Cantor of Tigurum, Anno 1454.

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Crystalli Locum Natalem specificans.
units.tr: Specifying the native place of crystal.

units.la: CRystallorum foecunda mater & nutrix est totus terrarum orbis, & singulæ forte ejus, montosæ præsertim, & metalliferæ regiones, licet non extent de singulis testimonia. Notum quippe est iis, qui curiofitatis ergo mineras metallorum adeunt, & conquirunt, nullam ferè esse, ditiorum præsertim, seu nobiliorum metallorum venam, ubi non copiosæ eruantur Crystalli. Atque de Helvetia nostra asserere audeo, vix esse in Cantonibus, præsertim Romanæ fidei addictis, jugum excelsius, sive Alpem, ubi fodiendo erui nequeant Crystalli in gratiam τῶν Κρυσταλλοφιλῶν [?], Exterorum. Loca Crystallorum naturalia in variis regionibus variis Scriptoribus memorata Geographico ordine apponam. Faciem Europæ quòd attinet, Hispaniam intelligo, scripsit jam olim Plin: Hist: Natur: L.37.C.2. Cornelio Boccho Auctore, & in Lusitania nasci perquàm mirandi ponderis, immensis jugis depressis ad libramentum aquæ puteis. In montibus Pyrenæis, qui Galliam ab Hispania segregant, Crystallos Copiosas reperiri, sicut nullum est dubium, ita passim Auctores testantur.
units.tr: The whole round of the earth is the fruitful mother and nurse of crystals, and perhaps every one of its regions, especially the mountainous and metal-bearing ones, although testimonies do not exist for each. Those who visit and search out metal mines from curiosity know well that there is scarcely any vein of metal, especially of the richer or nobler metals, where crystals are not dug up in abundance. And I dare to say of our Helvetia that there is hardly a high ridge or Alp in the Cantons, especially those attached to the Roman faith, where crystals cannot be dug out for the sake of the crystal-lovers [τῶν Κρυσταλλοφιλῶν], that is, foreigners. I shall list the natural places of crystals, as various writers have recorded them in various regions, in geographical order. As for the face of Europe, I mean Spain: Pliny wrote long ago, on the authority of Cornelius Bocchus, Natural History book 37, chapter 2, that in Lusitania crystal is born of very remarkable weight, dug from deep wells sunk to the level of the water among immense ridges. That abundant crystals are found in the Pyrenees, which separate Gaul from Spain, is as certain as it is widely attested by authors.

units.la: Ita memorat de Vallemont Traité de la Baguette divinatoire. C.15. p.173. In Catalogo Venarum mineralium ope Virgulæ divinatoriæ detectarum. Inter sequentia Loco primo. Aux monts Pyrenées à demy lieuë. de S. Bertrand, une grande miniere de Crystal. Dans la Comté de Foix. Au lieu de Carbanes, une miniere de Crystal. En Languedoc. A Lodève une miniere de Crystal. Audivit jam olim Gesner: de Figur: Lap: p.25. inveniri Crystallos in provincia Galliæ monte Marinaux dicto.
units.tr: Thus de Vallemont, Traité de la Baguette divinatoire, chapter 15, p. 173, in a catalogue of mineral veins detected by means of the divining rod, lists first among the following: In the Pyrenees, half a league from St Bertrand, a great mine of crystal. In the county of Foix, at the place Carbanes, a mine of crystal. In Languedoc, at Lodève, a mine of crystal. Gesner, On the Figures of Stones, p. 25, heard long ago that crystals are found in the province of Gaul called Mont Marinaux.

units.la: In Anglia observavit Joh: de Mey Comment: Phys: p.nr. 161. in montibus circa Urbem ac flumen Bristolis adhærentes Crystallos. Quæ forte eædem sunt cum Adamantibus Bristoliensibus, quarum mentionem facit Robert: Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virtut: p.4.5. In agro Derbiensi Crystallum effodi scribit. Christ: Merrett: Pinace Rerum Britan: p.209. In Monte Sancti Vicentii in Anglia. Mus: Worm. p.100.
units.tr: In England, Joh. de Mey, Commentarii Physici, p. nr. 161, observed crystals adhering to the hills around the city and river of Bristol. These are perhaps the same as the Bristol diamonds, which Robert Boyle mentions in De Gemmarum Origine et Virtutibus, pp. 4 and 5. Christopher Merrett, Pinax Rerum Britannicarum, p. 209, writes that crystal is dug up in the Derbyshire country; he gives Mount St Vincent in England. Museum Wormianum, p. 100.

units.la: Prope Arnhemum Geldriæ Oppidum, Clabequii prope Bruxellam Crystallos duriores, sive Pseudo-adamantes reperiri scribit Ansb: Boët: de Boot: de Lapid: & Genr. L.II.C.73.p.217. Et Kunkel de Art: Vitr: P. II. p. 121.
units.tr: Anselm Boëtius de Boot, De Lapidibus et Gemmis, book II, chapter 73, p. 217, writes that harder crystals, or pseudo-diamonds, are found near Arnhem, a town of Gelderland, and at Clabeck near Brussels; so also Kunkel, De Arte Vitraria, part II, p. 121.

units.la: In Helvetia nostra vix esse montem excelsiorem Crystallis vacuum jam supra attigi. Præ aliis tamen locis memoratur à Celeberr: D. D. Wagnero Helvet: Curios: p.325. Apud subsylvanos Mons, der Schneyden dictus, Parochiæ Saxlensis, Crystalli ferax. Apud Glaronenses, Mons der Lei- terberg dictus, prope Wichlam pagum, & Mons, Roßmatt dictus, in valle Crazera, apud Lepontios in Grinsula, Gotthardo, Furca, apud Rhætos in valle Ætuatia, valle Massinensi, Monte rubro, qui est in inferiore Engadina &c. In Valesia prope Gasam &c. Et jam supra laudatus Exc: D. D. Muralt: Act: Philosoph: Transact. A.1669.p.250. Prope Valesiam & Augustam, in Nomarchia Bernensi, prope Taminium & Tavetsch, Rhætorum, Item in montis Gotthardi ascensu, Item montibus prope Valesiam, Urselen [?], prope montem schellinin. Inveni & ego in Monte Crispalto Rhetiæ, in Valesiæ omnibus fere jugis, præsertim Schluhen / in monte prope Ober Wald /in Glaronensi ditione, in monte Wiechlen dicto; In monte, Groß Albrig ab incolis denominato, prope Lachen / &c.
units.tr: I have already noted above that there is hardly any mountain in our Helvetia higher than the crystal-bearing ones. Among other places it is recorded by the most celebrated Mr Wagner, Helvetic Curiosities, p. 325: among the Subsylvani, a mountain called der Schneyden, in the parish of Saxlen, rich in crystal; among the people of Glarus, a mountain called der Leiterberg, near the village of Wichlam, and a mountain called Roßmatt, in the valley of Crazera; among the Lepontii, in Grinsula, Gotthard and Furca; among the Rhaetians, in the valley of Ætuatia, the valley of Massino, Red Mountain, which lies in Lower Engadine, and so on. In Valais near Gasa, etc. And the excellent Mr Muralt, already cited, Acta Philosophica, Transactions 1669, p. 250: near Valais and Augusta, in the Bernese district, near Taminium and Tavetsch of the Rhaetians, likewise on the ascent of the Gotthard, likewise on the mountains near Valais, Urselen [?], near the mountain Schellinin. I too have found it on Mount Crispalt in Rhaetia, on almost all the ridges of Valais, especially at Schluhen, on the mountain near Ober Wald, in the Glarus territory, on the mountain called Wiechlen, on the mountain named by the inhabitants Groß Albrig near Lachen, and so on.

units.la: Crystalluum variis in locis Italiæ nasci scribit Worm: Mus: p.100. Circa Genuam Jacob: Mirx: p.79. Circa Pisam in quodam Torrente, qui ex Monte Magno fluit, in Verruca etiam monte propinquo. Andr: Cæsalp: de Metall: L.II. C.19. p.99. Ansb: Boët: de Boot: L. C. p.221. In Baldo monte prope Veronam Conrad: Gesn: de Fig: Lap: p.18. In ditione Bergomensi, in monte, quem Salvinum accolæ nominant, Bened: Cerut: ad Mus: Calceolar: P. III. In montibus Mediolanensibus, Chauvini Lexic: Philos: sub titulo Crystalli.
units.tr: Crystal is said to be born in various places in Italy: Museum Wormianum, p. 100; near Genoa, Jacob Mirx, p. 79; near Pisa, in a certain torrent flowing from Monte Magno, and also on the nearby mountain Verruca. Andreas Cesalpinus, De Metallicis, book II, chapter 19, p. 99; Anselm Boëtius de Boot, loc. cit., p. 221. On Mount Baldo near Verona, Conrad Gesner, De Figuris Lapidum, p. 18. In the Bergamo district, on the mountain which the locals call Salvinum, Benedetto Cerutti, to the Museum Calceolarium, part III. On the mountains of Milan, Chauvin's Philosophical Lexicon under the title Crystal.

units.la: In Norvegia Worm: Mus: p. 100. Crystallum Islandicam (quæ Selenites est noster Rhomboidalis) Incolæ Islandiæ, & mercatores nostrates Crystallum hanc in variis regionibus istius loci reperiri affirmant, imprimis vero ex monte præalto, prope Sinum Roerfiord in Elevatione Poli 65. Gr. sito à fossoribus erui, montis ejusdem ad Austram vergentis superficiem totam exteriorem ex materia hac compositam esse Oliger: Jacobæ: Mus: Reg: Dan: S. VII. p. 35. Erasm: Barth: Exper: Cryst: Island: p. 60. Ex Infulis Feroënsibus Mus: Worm: p. 100.
units.tr: In Norway: Museum Wormianum, p. 100. The Icelanders and our merchants affirm that the rhomboidal crystal of Iceland, which is our Selenites, is found in various regions of that island, and especially that it is dug by diggers from a very high mountain near the bay Roerfiord, situated at latitude 65 degrees, the whole outer surface of that mountain, which slopes to the south, being made of this material: Oliger Jacobaeus, Museum Regium Danicum, S. VII, p. 35; Erasmus Bartholin, Experimenta Crystalli Islandici, p. 60. From the Faroe Islands: Museum Wormianum, p. 100.

units.la: Per Universam Indiam Crystallum nullam reperiri scribit Garcias ab Horto. C. 47. Cui tamen contradicunt Plin: Hist: Natur: L. 36. C. 26. Strabo Geograph: L. 15. Robert: Boyle de Gemm: Orig: & Virt: p. 26. Qui Insulam Madagascar, aliasque regiones Zonæ torridæ Crystallo abundare asserit. Athanas: Kirch: Mund: Subt: L. VIII. S. I. p. 9. Qui in Infulis, Zeilan, & Sumatra Crystallum provenire scribit. In Cypro, Infula, Plin: Hist: Nat: L. 37. C. 2. In quadam Infula Rubri maris ante Arabiam sita, quæ Neron (aliis Necron) vocatur. In Scythia. Sol: p. 15. & Salmas: in Solin: p. 143. In Regione Peking Sinensium, Neuhoff Sinische Reißbeschreibung/p. 303.
units.tr: Garcias ab Horto, chapter 47, writes that no crystal is found throughout India. Yet this is contradicted by Pliny, Natural History book 36, chapter 26; Strabo, Geography book 15; and Robert Boyle, De Gemmarum Origine et Virtutibus, p. 26, who asserts that the island of Madagascar and other regions of the torrid zone abound in crystal. Athanasius Kircher, Mundus Subterraneus, book VIII, section I, p. 9, writes that it arises on the islands of Ceylon and Sumatra. In Cyprus, an island: Pliny, Natural History book 37, chapter 2. On a certain island of the Red Sea lying off Arabia, called Neron (by others Necron). In Scythia: Solinus, p. 15, and Salmasius on Solinus, p. 143. In the region of Peking of the Chinese: Neuhoff, Sinische Reisebeschreibung, p. 303.

units.la: Ex Montibus Lunæ Africæ, Zonæ torridæ subditæ, ingentem extrahi Crystalli copiam, Ath: Kirch: L.C. refert.
units.tr: Athanasius Kircher, loc. cit., reports that an immense quantity of crystal is extracted from the Mountains of the Moon in Africa, which lie under the torrid zone.

units.la: In India Occidentali, sive America, præsertim Circa Winacapora Vielhëurn: descript: Mat: Exotic: p. 33. In Regni Chile tractibus esse Vallem, quam Andium juga determinant, in media prægrandis fluminis Infula ingentem Rupem Crystallinam. Ath: Kirch: L.C. Brasilia. Worm: Mus: p. 100. Hartnacc: admirand: Phys: p. 411. Zwischen Wayanawassan und dem Südmeer ist der große Chrystallberg/welcher so hoch/daß er sich in die Wolken verbirgt/ und so gech/daß niemand darüber kommen kan/ 10. Tag sihet man den Berg/ eh man darzu komt/und wann die Sonn scheint/kan man wegen des Glanzes gegenschein nicht dargegen wandlen. sebast: Munster: Cosmograph: p. 1731.
units.tr: In the West Indies, or America, especially around Winacapora: Vielheurn, Descriptio Materiae Exoticae, p. 33. In the regions of the kingdom of Chile there is a valley, bounded by the ridges of the Andes, in the middle of a very great river's island a huge crystalline rock: Athanasius Kircher, loc. cit. Brazil: Museum Wormianum, p. 100; Hartnack, Admiranda Physica, p. 411. Between Wayanawassan and the South Sea is the great crystal mountain, which is so high that it hides itself in the clouds, and so steep that no one can get over it; one sees the mountain ten days before one comes to it, and when the sun shines one cannot walk opposite it because of the glare of its reflection. Sebastian Münster, Cosmographia, p. 1731. [The German passage is given here in English.]

units.la: Tu interim, Benevole Lector, ea quæ minùs ἀκριβῶς[?], sed παχυ-λῶς[?] & rudi Minerva à me dicta sunt, pro humanitate & benevolentia Tua corrige, omissa supple, reliqua tanquam leves conjecturas benignè accipe. Meliora, favente Numine, maturescentibus studiis & annis, meliores & perfectiores cum tempore redditi, forte dabimus,
units.tr: Meanwhile, kind Reader, correct with your courtesy and goodwill whatever I have said less accurately [ἀκριβῶς] and more crudely [παχυλῶς], with my rough Minerva; supply what I have omitted, and take the rest kindly as slight conjectures. With God's favour, as my studies and years mature, I may perhaps one day offer better and more perfect work.

units.la: Μόνῳ τῷ Θεῷ ἡ δόξα.
units.tr: To God alone be the glory [Μόνῳ τῷ Θεῷ ἡ δόξα].
